Since $M_i^x\ge0$ and $\rho_{E_i}^{x'}\ge0$, this implies $M_i^x\rho_{E_i}^{x'}=0$ on the support of $\rho_{E_i}^{x'}$. Also
$$
\operatorname{Tr}(M_i^x\rho_{E_i}^{x})=1.
$$
Because $0\le M_i^x\le1$, this forces $M_i^x$ to act as the identity on $\operatorname{supp}\rho_{E_i}^{x}$. Therefore the support of $\rho_{E_i}^{x}$ is orthogonal to the support of $\rho_{E_i}^{x'}$ for $x\ne x'$, which is equivalent to (M.6.11.9). This proves the spectrum-broadcast form.

The three-layer statement is only a restatement of the roles of Theorem G.1.7, Theorem M.6.11b, and the present theorem. ∎

<a id="corollary-m611f-objectivity-without-perspective-independent-ontology"></a>**Corollary M.6.11f (Objectivity Without Perspective-Independent Ontology).** Under Theorem M.6.11e's strict-cost and dephasing hypotheses, a classical fact shared by many perspectives is a PCE-minimal broadcast record. It is objective because many disjoint fragments independently recover the same minimal statistic $X$, not because the framework adds a perspective-free state of affairs.

*Proof.* Theorem M.6.11e identifies exact public objectivity with redundant fragment recovery and conditional independence in spectrum-broadcast form. Its strict-cost premise and Theorem M.6.11b(5) select $X$ as the unique PCE-minimal sufficient record up to relabeling. ∎

<a id="theorem-m611g-finite-process-tensor-construction-of-minimal-spectrum-broadcast"></a>**Theorem M.6.11g (Finite Process-Tensor Construction of Minimal Spectrum Broadcast).** Let $X=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ be the PCE-minimal classical quotient of Theorem M.6.11b, with system basis $|x\rangle_S$. Prepare one discarded dephasing register $E_0$ and $N\ge1$ public fragments $E_1,\ldots,E_N$, each of dimension $m$, in $|0\rangle$. At successive fixed-order slots apply unitary extensions of
$$
U_i|x\rangle_S|0\rangle_{E_i}=|x\rangle_S|x\rangle_{E_i}
\qquad(i=0,\ldots,N),
\tag{M.6.11g.1}
$$
and discard $E_0$. These channels define a normalized deterministic process tensor by Theorem M.6.14b. For every input $\rho_S$, its retained output is
$$
\sum_{x=1}^m\langle x|\rho_S|x\rangle
|x\rangle\!\langle x|_S
\otimes
\bigotimes_{i=1}^N|x\rangle\!\langle x|_{E_i}.
\tag{M.6.11g.2}
$$
Thus the discarded copy derives exact dephasing, and the retained copies derive spectrum-broadcast structure. Every nonempty fragment subset recovers $X$ exactly, so the redundancy is $N$ and any $N-1$ fragments may be lost.

For the registered exact classical storage cost $C_{\log}(R)=\log|R|$, every record sufficient for all point-identification tasks on $X$ has at least $m$ values and cost at least $\log m$. A strict sufficient refinement has at least $m+1$ values and costs at least
$$
\log(m+1)-\log m>0
\tag{M.6.11g.3}
$$
more per refined record. Hence total public-fragment cost is at least $N\log m$, and (M.6.11g.2) saturates the bound.

*Proof.* Each displayed rule is an isometry on an $m$-dimensional subspace and extends to a unitary. Before tracing $E_0$, an off-diagonal $|x\rangle\langle x'|$ is accompanied by $|x\rangle\langle x'|_{E_0}$; its trace is zero for $x\ne x'$, giving (M.6.11g.2). Measuring any retained fragment in its displayed basis recovers $x$. Exact point identification requires an injective code and hence at least $m$ record values; a strict refinement splits at least one fiber and has at least $m+1$. ∎

### M.6.12 PCE Information-Bottleneck Universality

<a id="definition-m612a-finite-predictive-bottleneck"></a>**Definition M.6.12a (Finite Predictive Bottleneck).** Let $X$ be a finite substrate variable, let $Y$ be a finite task or protocol-outcome variable, and let $Z$ be a finite effective description variable generated by a stochastic kernel
$$
p(z\mid x).
$$
The PCE information-bottleneck functional is
$$
\mathcal B_\beta[p(z\mid x)]
=
I(X;Z)-\beta I(Z;Y),
\qquad
\beta\ge0.
\tag{M.6.12.1}
$$
A statistic $Z$ is sufficient for predicting $Y$ from $X$ when
$$
p(y\mid x)=p(y\mid z)
$$
for all $x,z$ with $p(x,z)>0$.

<a id="theorem-m612b-minimal-sufficient-predictive-bottleneck"></a>**Theorem M.6.12b (Minimal Sufficient Predictive Bottleneck).** For finite random variables $X,Y$, use the effective substrate alphabet $X_+=\{x:p(x)>0\}$ and discard zero-probability statistic outputs. Write $X$ for this effective alphabet in the quotient below; all claims of recovery or conditional equality are almost sure under the registered joint law. Define an equivalence relation on these substrate states by
$$
x\sim x'
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p(y\mid x)=p(y\mid x')
\text{ for every }y.
$$
Let
$$
Z_*=X/{\sim}
$$
be the quotient statistic. Then:

1. $Z_*$ is sufficient for predicting $Y$.
2. Every sufficient statistic $Z$ determines $Z_*$ by a deterministic post-processing.
3. Consequently,
$$
I(X;Z)\ge I(X;Z_*)
$$
for every sufficient $Z$.
4. Equality holds only up to operational relabeling and null refinements.

*Proof.* If $Z_*=[x]$, then by construction all elements of the class $[x]$ have the same conditional distribution $p(y\mid x)$. Therefore
$$
p(y\mid Z_*=[x])=p(y\mid x),
$$
so $Z_*$ is sufficient.

Let $Z$ be any sufficient statistic. If two substrate states $x,x'$ can produce the same value $z$ with positive probability, sufficiency gives
$$
p(y\mid x)=p(y\mid z)=p(y\mid x')
$$
for all $y$. Hence $x\sim x'$. Therefore each value of $Z$ lies inside one equivalence class of $Z_*$, and $Z_*$ is determined by a deterministic map from $Z$.

Because $Z_*$ is a deterministic function of $Z$, the chain rule gives
$$
I(X;Z)
=I(X;Z,Z_*)
=I(X;Z_*)+I(X;Z\mid Z_*)
\ge I(X;Z_*).
$$
Equality holds if and only if $I(X;Z\mid Z_*)=0$, equivalently $X$ and $Z$ are conditionally independent given $Z_*$. Thus an equality case may add only conditionally independent random refinement or relabeling within a $Z_*$ class; such added data are operationally null for both $X$ and the retained prediction of $Y$. ∎

<a id="corollary-m612c-lossless-predictive-bottleneck-endpoint"></a>**Corollary M.6.12c (Lossless Predictive-Bottleneck Endpoint).** Among finite descriptions constrained to be exactly sufficient for $Y$, $Z_*=X/{\sim}$ minimizes $I(X;Z)$. It is therefore the lossless endpoint of the predictive bottleneck. For finite $\beta$, a minimizer of (M.6.12.1) may discard predictive information; identifying classical records, RG variables, effective fields, or perspective summaries with such a minimizer requires solving the corresponding model-specific bottleneck problem.

*Proof.* Theorem M.6.12b gives $I(X;Z)\ge I(X;Z_*)$ for every exactly sufficient $Z$. This proves the first two sentences. The Lagrangian (M.6.12.1) optimizes over all kernels $p(z\mid x)$, including insufficient ones, so the theorem supplies no characterization of its finite-$\beta$ minimizers. ∎

<a id="theorem-m612d-exact-finite-beta-bottleneck-and-the-deterministic-readout-sector"></a>**Theorem M.6.12d (Exact Finite-$\beta$ Bottleneck and the Deterministic-Readout Sector).** Keep Definition M.6.12a with a registered joint law of the finite variables $X,Y$, the effective alphabet of Theorem M.6.12b, and descriptions $Z$ generated by kernels $p(z\mid x)$ on finite alphabets. Put
$$
\eta_{XY}:=\sup\left\{\frac{I(Z;Y)}{I(X;Z)}:I(X;Z)>0\right\},
\tag{M.6.12d.1}
$$
with $\eta_{XY}:=0$ when $X$ is almost surely constant.

1. $0\le\eta_{XY}\le1$, and every description satisfies $\mathcal B_\beta[p(z\mid x)]\ge(1-\beta\eta_{XY})I(X;Z)$. If $\beta\eta_{XY}<1$, the minimum of $\mathcal B_\beta$ is $0$ and its minimizers are exactly the descriptions with $I(X;Z)=0$. If $\beta\eta_{XY}>1$, some description has $\mathcal B_\beta<0$, so no $X$-independent description is optimal.
2. Suppose $Y=f(X)$ almost surely and $H(Y)>0$. Then $\eta_{XY}=1$, the statistic $Z_*$ of Theorem M.6.12b is an injective relabeling of $Y$, and
$$
\mathcal B_\beta=I(X;Z\mid Y)+(1-\beta)I(Z;Y).
\tag{M.6.12d.2}
$$
Consequently, for $0\le\beta<1$, $\min\mathcal B_\beta=0$, attained exactly by the $X$-independent descriptions; for $\beta=1$, $\min\mathcal B_1=0$, attained exactly by the descriptions with $I(X;Z\mid Y)=0$; and for $\beta>1$, $\min\mathcal B_\beta=(1-\beta)H(Y)$, attained exactly by the descriptions with $H(Y\mid Z)=0$ and $I(X;Z\mid Y)=0$. The last class consists of the exactly sufficient descriptions that determine $Z_*$ and are conditionally independent of $X$ given $Z_*$, namely the relabelings and null refinements of $Z_*$; its deterministic members are exactly the injective relabelings of $Z_*$.
3. In the record sector of Theorem M.6.11b, take the substrate $X:=R$ with its registered law and the task variable $Y:=\Pi(R)$ of (M.6.11.1). Then $Y$ is a deterministic function of $R$ and $Z_*$ is the risk-equivalence class $[R]$ of (M.6.11.2). Whenever two retained records have distinct profiles, every $\beta>1$ has the quotient map $r\mapsto[r]$ of $\mathcal M_{\min}$ as its deterministic bottleneck minimizer, unique up to relabeling, and every $\beta<1$ has only $R$-independent minimizers.

*Proof.* Every description gives the Markov chain $Z-X-Y$, so data processing gives $I(Z;Y)\le I(X;Z)$ and $0\le\eta_{XY}\le1$. If $I(X;Z)=0$, then $I(Z;Y)=0$ and $\mathcal B_\beta=0$. Otherwise $I(Z;Y)\le\eta_{XY}I(X;Z)$ gives the displayed lower bound. When $\beta\eta_{XY}<1$ that bound is strictly positive whenever $I(X;Z)>0$, which proves the first case. When $\beta\eta_{XY}>1$, the definition of the supremum supplies a description with $I(Z;Y)>I(X;Z)/\beta$, hence $\mathcal B_\beta<0$.

For item 2, on the effective alphabet $p(y\mid x)=\mathbf 1[y=f(x)]$, so $x\sim x'$ exactly when $f(x)=f(x')$ and $Z_*$ is an injective relabeling of $Y$. Since $Y$ is a function of $X$, the chain rule gives $I(X;Z)=I(X,Y;Z)=I(Y;Z)+I(X;Z\mid Y)$, which is (M.6.12d.2). The choice $Z=Y$ has ratio $H(Y)/H(Y)=1$, so $\eta_{XY}=1$. The three cases follow from $I(X;Z\mid Y)\ge0$ and $0\le I(Z;Y)\le H(Y)$, with $I(Z;Y)=H(Y)$ exactly when $H(Y\mid Z)=0$; the constant description attains $0$, and $Z=Y$ attains $(1-\beta)H(Y)$. If $H(Y\mid Z)=0$, then $Y=g(Z)$ almost surely, so $p(y\mid x)=\mathbf 1[y=g(z)]=p(y\mid z)$ whenever $p(x,z)>0$; thus $Z$ is exactly sufficient and determines $Z_*$ by Theorem M.6.12b. The condition $I(X;Z\mid Y)=0$ is conditional independence of $X$ and $Z$ given $Z_*$, which is the null-refinement equality case of Theorem M.6.12b. For a deterministic $Z=\phi(X)$, $I(X;Z\mid Y)=H(Z\mid Y)$, so the two conditions make $Z$ and $Y$ functions of each other on the support.

For item 3, $p(y\mid r)=\mathbf 1[y=\Pi(r)]$, so the equivalence of Theorem M.6.12b coincides with (M.6.11.2) and $Z_*=[R]$. Two distinct retained profiles give $H(Y)>0$, and item 2 applies to the quotient map of (M.6.11.3). ∎

**Finite bottleneck scope.** For every finite joint law and $\beta\ge0$, Theorem M.6.12d gives the universal triviality threshold $\beta<1/\eta_{XY}$. In a deterministic-readout sector with $H(Y)>0$, the exact threshold is $\beta=1$: for $\beta>1$ the effective variable is sufficient and minimal, unique up to relabeling and response-null refinement. The following theorems treat stochastic readouts and the declared Gaussian continuum source.

<a id="theorem-m612e-complete-algebraic-global-certificate-for-rational-finite-readouts"></a>**Theorem M.6.12e (Complete Algebraic Global Certificate for Rational Finite Readouts).** In Definition M.6.12a, fix a finite effective substrate alphabet of size $n$, a positive rational prior $p_i$, a rational column-stochastic readout matrix $W_{yi}=p(y\mid X=i)$ and rational $\beta\ge0$. Zero entries of $W$ are allowed. Optimize over every stochastic description kernel on every finite alphabet. Use natural logarithms, write $\Delta_n=\{q\in\mathbb R^n:q_i\ge0,\ \sum_iq_i=1\}$, and put
$$
f(q)=\beta H(Wq)-H(q),\qquad q\in\Delta_n.
\tag{M.6.12e.1}
$$
Choose an integer $L\ge1$ such that $b_{yi}:=L\beta W_{yi}$ are nonnegative integers. The following finite algebraic certificate is sound and complete for the global optimum.

Choose positive real algebraic numbers $c_1,\ldots,c_n,d$; the normalization $c_n=1$ is available. For every nonempty support $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, use variables $q_i>0$ for $i\in I$, set the other coordinates to zero, and impose $\sum_{i\in I}q_i=1$. Let
$$
J_I=\{y:W_{yi}>0\text{ for some }i\in I\},\qquad
r_y=\sum_{i\in I}W_{yi}q_i,\qquad
M_i(q)=\prod_{y\in J_I}r_y^{b_{yi}}.
$$
Every $r_y$ and $M_i$ in this formula is positive on the relative interior of the face. Fix one pivot $j\in I$ and define the polynomial equations and value test
$$
F_{I,i}=q_i^L c_jM_j-q_j^L c_iM_i=0\quad(i\in I\setminus\{j\}),
\qquad V_I=q_j^L-dc_jM_j.
\tag{M.6.12e.2}
$$
Require that the semialgebraic set
$$
\left\{q_i>0,\ \sum_{i\in I}q_i=1,\ F_{I,i}=0\ (i\ne j),\ V_I<0\right\}
\tag{M.6.12e.3}
$$
is empty for every nonempty $I$. Let $\mathcal T$ be the union of the same face sets with $V_I=0$ replacing $V_I<0$. Finally supply $k\le n$ points $q^{(a)}\in\mathcal T$ and positive algebraic weights $w_a$ satisfying
$$
\sum_{a=1}^kw_a=1,\qquad
\sum_{a=1}^kw_aq^{(a)}=p.
\tag{M.6.12e.4}
$$
Then the global minimum equals
$$
H(p)-\beta H(Wp)+\frac{\log d+\sum_i p_i\log c_i}{L}.
\tag{M.6.12e.5}
$$
Every global minimizer, on an arbitrary finite effective description alphabet, is exactly a finite mixture of points of $\mathcal T$ with barycenter $p$: if its weights are $w_z>0$ and posterior points are $q^{(z)}$, its kernel is
$$
p(z\mid X=i)=\frac{w_zq_i^{(z)}}{p_i}.
\tag{M.6.12e.6}
$$
Relabeling the output atoms and splitting an atom into outputs with the same posterior are precisely the relabelings and null refinements of this posterior description. At least one optimizer uses at most $n$ outputs. The least output cardinality is the smallest $k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ for which (M.6.12e.4) has a solution. A larger finite alphabet attains the optimum by null splitting. The bound of $n$ is an existence bound; an optimal kernel may have more than $n$ distinct posterior points when $\mathcal T$ has a positive-dimensional component.

For every registered rational input in the theorem, such a certificate exists and can be found by a terminating exact real-algebraic procedure. The procedure includes every support face and all positive-dimensional critical loci. It gives a finite semialgebraic description of every posterior contact set and hence of all finite-alphabet minimizers, without assuming that a stationary iteration finds a global minimum.

*Proof.* Write $w_z=p(z)$ and $q_i^{(z)}=p(X=i\mid z)$, discarding zero-probability outputs. Bayes' formula gives $\sum_z w_zq^{(z)}=p$ and (M.6.12e.6). Conversely, those two conditions define a normalized stochastic kernel. The Markov chain $Z-X-Y$ gives
$$
\mathcal B_\beta
=H(p)-\beta H(Wp)+\sum_z w_zf(q^{(z)}).
\tag{M.6.12e.7}
$$
The graph of the continuous function $f$ is compact. Its convex hull is compact in the finite-dimensional affine space containing $(q,f(q))$, so the least attainable mean value at prior $p$ exists. Equivalently it is the lower convex envelope of $f$ at $p$. Since $p$ is in the relative interior of the simplex, the finite convex envelope has a supporting affine function $\gamma+\lambda\cdot q$ there. This follows from finite-dimensional separation of its epigraph; a finite supporting slope exists at an interior point of its finite convex domain. A representation of the lower boundary point by graph points uses only contacts with this supporting plane: a positive weighted sum of nonnegative support gaps can vanish only when every gap vanishes. These contacts lie in an affine space of dimension at most $n-1$. In a representation with more than $n$ positive-weight contacts, an affine dependence permits changing their weights while keeping their sum and barycenter fixed until one weight vanishes. Repetition gives a representation with at most $n$ contacts.

It remains to replace the global support inequality by the polynomial certificate rather than leaving it as an unevaluated convex-envelope problem. Set
$$
\lambda_i=L^{-1}\log c_i,\qquad \gamma=L^{-1}\log d,
\qquad \phi(q)=f(q)-\lambda\cdot q.
$$
On the relative interior of face $I$, all active output probabilities are positive and $\phi$ is differentiable. Its partial derivative at an active coordinate is
$$
\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial q_i}
=\log q_i-\beta\sum_{y\in J_I}W_{yi}\log r_y-\lambda_i+1-\beta.
$$
At a constrained critical point these derivatives are equal. Exponentiation after multiplication by $L$ gives exactly (M.6.12e.2): all quantities being divided or exponentiated are positive, so no branch or spurious solution is introduced. At such a point the common value of
$\log q_i-\beta\sum_yW_{yi}\log r_y-\lambda_i$
is $\phi(q)$, because multiplication by $q_i$ and summation yields $f(q)-\lambda\cdot q$. Consequently
$$
e^{L\phi(q)}=\frac{q_j^L}{c_jM_j(q)}.
\tag{M.6.12e.8}
$$
Thus $V_I<0$ is exactly $\phi(q)<\gamma$ on that critical locus.

The continuous function $\phi$ attains its minimum on the closed simplex. At a minimizer, take $I$ to be its positive support. It is a relative-interior minimizer on that face and satisfies its critical equations. Therefore emptiness of (M.6.12e.3) on all faces is equivalent to $\phi\ge\gamma$ everywhere. The same argument shows that its equality set is precisely $\mathcal T$. This includes vertices, faces with absent readout outcomes and positive-dimensional critical sets. Equations (M.6.12e.4) and (M.6.12e.7) now prove (M.6.12e.5). Conversely every optimizing mixture has zero average support gap, so each of its positive-weight posteriors lies in $\mathcal T$. Bayes' formula proves the complete kernel classification. Outputs sharing a posterior are conditionally independent refinements given that posterior label; distinct posterior points cannot be merged by a null refinement. The cardinality statements follow from the contact representation and from exact real-algebraic feasibility of (M.6.12e.4) at each $k$.

For completeness and effectivity, first use the real supporting plane established above, with $c_i=e^{L\lambda_i}$ and $d=e^{L\gamma}$. Subtracting $\lambda_n$ from every $\lambda_i$ and adding it to $\gamma$ fixes $c_n=1$ without changing the plane on the simplex. The contact points and weights supplied by the convex-hull argument satisfy the certificate over the reals. The entire certificate condition, including all universally quantified no-undercut clauses, is a first-order formula over the rationals: (M.6.12e.2)--(M.6.12e.4) contain polynomial equalities and inequalities only. Effective quantifier elimination over real closed fields decides this formula and supplies algebraic sample points (Basu, Pollack and Roy 2006, Chapters 13--14). Since it has a real solution, it has a solution over the real algebraic numbers. The logarithms defining the original dual variables need not be algebraic; their positive exponentials in this equivalent formula have an algebraic witness.

A proof-carrying form of each emptiness check is also finite and exact. Introduce variables $u_i,v$ and replace the strict inequalities in (M.6.12e.3) by
$$
q_i u_i^2-1=0\quad(i\in I),\qquad -V_Iv^2-1=0.
\tag{M.6.12e.9}
$$
Together with the normalization and critical equations, these have a real solution exactly when (M.6.12e.3) does. A real-algebraic infeasibility certificate is a polynomial identity
$$
-1=\sum_\ell h_\ell F_\ell+\sum_b s_b^2,
\tag{M.6.12e.10}
$$
where $F_\ell$ lists these equations. The identity is checked by exact coefficient arithmetic and is sound because a common real zero would make its right-hand side nonnegative. The real Nullstellensatz supplies such an identity for every empty real algebraic set (Stengle 1974). Positive weighted squares are equivalent after adjoining their square roots. All finitely many coefficients lie in one effectively represented real algebraic number field. Additional reciprocal-square equations for polynomials proved strictly positive on the face preserve the same equivalence.

One terminating certificate search enumerates exact real-algebraic fields, positive certificate scalars, finite contact/weight records and finite polynomial identities, and checks (M.6.12e.2)--(M.6.12e.4) and (M.6.12e.10). Existence of an algebraic certificate proves termination; quantifier elimination provides a direct alternative. Neither procedure assumes isolated critical points or a strict optimizer. The optimum value is then the exact logarithmic expression (M.6.12e.5), and the computed polynomial contact sets describe all minimizers. ∎

<a id="theorem-m612h-computable-finite-operatornamelaw-bottleneck-approximation"></a>**Theorem M.6.12h (Computable Finite-$\operatorname{Law}$ Bottleneck Approximation).** In Definition M.6.12a fix finite alphabets of sizes $n,m\ge1$, a joint probability law $p_{xy}$ and finite $\beta\ge0$. A precision name for these data is a procedure that, on input $k$, returns rational approximations to every $p_{xy}$ and to $\beta$, each with absolute error at most $2^{-k}$. The procedure is required to satisfy this promise for every $k$; no procedure deciding equality of named reals is supplied. Computability in this theorem is uniform in these names and the two alphabet sizes. Zero probabilities are allowed, and the names need not decide their support.

The minimum over all finite stochastic descriptions is attained by a kernel with at most $n$ outputs. Its value is a computable real, and for every positive rational $\epsilon$ a terminating procedure returns a rational stochastic kernel on $n$ outputs with objective at most $\epsilon$ above the global minimum, together with a rational interval of width at most $\epsilon$ containing that minimum.

Here is an explicit finite search and its error certificate. Put $h_2(t)=-t\log t-(1-t)\log(1-t)$, with the continuous endpoint convention, and $g_d(t)=h_2(t)+t\log d$. Obtain any rational $b\ge\beta$ from its precision name. If $n=1$, return the constant kernel and value zero. Otherwise choose an integer $N$ with $\delta=(n-1)/N\le1/2$, together with a certified rational number $\overline\omega_N$, such that
$$
\omega_N=(1+b)g_n(\delta)+g_{n^2}(\delta)+b g_{nm}(\delta)
\le\overline\omega_N\le\epsilon/2.
\tag{M.6.12h.1}
$$
Enumerate every row-stochastic $n\times n$ matrix whose entries have denominator $N$. Compute a rational value $\widehat B_K$ for each matrix with $|\widehat B_K-\mathcal B_\beta(K)|\le\epsilon/4$. If $\widehat v=\min_K\widehat B_K$, return one minimizing matrix and
$$
[\widehat v-\epsilon/4-\overline\omega_N,\ \widehat v+\epsilon/4].
\tag{M.6.12h.2}
$$
Both endpoints are rational because the certified upper bound $\overline\omega_N$ is rational. Its bound by $\epsilon/2$ preserves both conclusions. Every constant description is available in the grid, so its exactly known score zero can also tighten the upper endpoint.

*Proof.* Discard zero-probability substrate states for the existence argument, writing $s\le n$ for the resulting size. Its prior $p$ is in the relative interior of $\Delta_s$. Write $W_{yi}=p(y\mid i)$ on this support and $f(q)=\beta H(Wq)-H(q)$. A finite description gives posterior atoms $q^z$, weights $w_z>0$ and barycenter $\sum_z w_zq^z=p$. Conversely every such finite family gives the kernel $K(z\mid i)=w_zq_i^z/p_i$. Direct entropy expansion gives
$$
\mathcal B_\beta(K)=H(p)-\beta H(Wp)+\sum_z w_zf(q^z).
$$
The graph of continuous $f$ on compact $\Delta_s$ is compact, and its convex hull is compact in the finite-dimensional affine space of pairs $(q,t)$. The lowest point of this hull above $p$ therefore exists. The lower convex envelope has a finite supporting affine function at its relative-interior point $p$: separation of its epigraph gives a support plane, and finiteness on an open neighborhood of $p$ in its affine domain excludes a vertical support plane. Each atom in a representation of this point must contact that plane, since its nonnegative vertical gap has weighted sum zero. These contacts lie in an affine space of dimension at most $s-1$. If there are more than $s$ positive weights, affine dependence supplies real coefficients $a_j$, not all zero, with $\sum a_j=0$ and $\sum a_jq^j=0$. Move the weights by a scalar multiple of $a$ until a first one becomes zero; positivity of the other weights and the barycenter are preserved. Repeat until at most $s$ remain. This proves attainment by at most $n$ outputs without requiring an algorithm to detect the effective support. Set arbitrary stochastic rows at the discarded zero-probability inputs and add null output labels to reach $n$.

For each row of an arbitrary $n$-output kernel, round its first $n-1$ entries down to multiples of $1/N$ and put the remaining mass in its last entry. The rounded matrix $K'$ is stochastic, and each row's total variation distance is at most $(n-1)/N=\delta$. Consequently the joint laws $p_{xy}K(z\mid x)$ and $p_{xy}K'(z\mid x)$ have total variation at most $\delta$, as do all their marginals.

For probability vectors $u,v$ on $d$ labels at total variation distance $t\le\delta\le1/2$, couple them with mismatch probability $t$: put common mass $\min(u_i,v_i)$ on the diagonal and distribute the residual masses between unequal labels. If $U,V$ are the resulting variables and $E$ indicates mismatch, then $H(U\mid V)\le H(E)+t\log d$ and the same holds with $U,V$ interchanged. The entropy chain rule gives $|H(U)-H(V)|\le h_2(t)+t\log d\le g_d(\delta)$. This argument includes one-point alphabets; the stated bound remains valid there.

The marginals of $X,Y$ remain fixed when rounding a kernel. Expanding both mutual informations as joint and marginal entropies yields
$$
|\mathcal B_\beta(K)-\mathcal B_\beta(K')|
\le (1+\beta)g_n(\delta)+g_{n^2}(\delta)+\beta g_{nm}(\delta)
\le\omega_N.
$$
Since $g_d(\delta)\to0$ effectively as $\delta\downarrow0$, an $N$ satisfying the certificate can be found. A safe implementation requires a strict margin, such as a certified upper bound below $\epsilon/2$, so equality testing of logarithmic expressions is unnecessary.

Every objective value in the finite grid is uniformly computable from the precision names. Indeed, its joint probabilities are finite sums and products of named reals and rational kernel entries. The function $-x\log x$ is computable on $[0,1]$, including zero: for $0\le x\le a<e^{-1}$ its absolute value is at most $-a\log a$, while on $[a,1]$ the logarithm has a convergent rational series with an explicit remainder. This gives a uniform rational approximation algorithm on the full interval. Finite summation and multiplication by the named finite $\beta$ preserve effectivity. No support decision or division by a probability is used by the grid algorithm.

Let $v$ be the global minimum, $v_N$ the grid minimum and $\tau=\epsilon/4$. An attaining kernel and its rounded version show $v\le v_N\le v+\omega_N$. Uniform value errors give $|\widehat v-v_N|\le\tau$. Since $\omega_N\le\overline\omega_N$, (M.6.12h.2) contains $v$ and has width $2\tau+\overline\omega_N\le\epsilon$. For the selected grid matrix, $\mathcal B_\beta(K)\le\widehat v+\tau\le v+\omega_N+2\tau\le v+\overline\omega_N+2\tau\le v+\epsilon$. All enumerations and approximations are finite. ∎

<a id="theorem-m612i-exact-decision-boundary-for-irrational-nonbinary-laws"></a>**Theorem M.6.12i (Exact Decision Boundary for Irrational Nonbinary Laws).** Under the precision-name representation of Theorem M.6.12h, there is no algorithm that terminates on every computable finite law and decides whether its bottleneck minimum equals zero or is strictly negative. The obstruction already holds with $|X|=3$, $|Y|=4$, fixed rational $\beta=2$, a fixed full-support irrational prior, and a genuinely stochastic readout. Every nonzero entry of the joint laws in the obstructing family is irrational. Equivalently, neither exact optimality of the constant description nor the minimum optimal output cardinality admits such a uniform decision procedure.

Fix
$$
p=\left(\sqrt2-1,\ 1-\frac{\sqrt2}{2},\ 1-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right),
\qquad Y\in\{*,1,2,3\}.
\tag{M.6.12i.1}
$$
For $0<c<1$, independently draw a Bernoulli variable of mean $c$; reveal $Y=X$ when it is one and output $Y=*$ otherwise. For every finite description kernel, including all stochastic refinements,
$$
I(Z;Y)=cI(X;Z),\qquad
\mathcal B_\beta=(1-\beta c)I(X;Z),\qquad
v=\min\{0,(1-\beta c)H(X)\}.
\tag{M.6.12i.2}
$$
For $\beta c<1$ the minimizers are precisely $X$-independent descriptions. At $\beta c=1$ every description is a minimizer. For $\beta c>1$ the minimizers are precisely the descriptions with $H(X\mid Z)=0$; their minimum output cardinality is three.

*Proof.* The erasure indicator is independent of $(X,Z)$ and is determined by $Y$. Conditional on an erasure, $Y$ contains no substrate information, and conditional on a reveal it is exactly $X$. Applying the mutual-information chain rule to the indicator and revealed label proves the first identity in (M.6.12i.2). The second follows from the definition. The attainable interval satisfies $0\le I(X;Z)\le H(X)$, with endpoints attained by a constant and by $Z=X$. Their equality cases are independence and $H(X\mid Z)=0$, respectively. All three prior masses are positive, so exact recovery from $Z$ requires at least three nonnull outputs and the identity description attains that bound. This proves the global optimizer classification over every finite output alphabet.

For a program $e$ on a fixed input, let $h\ge1$ be its first halting step when it halts, and define
$$
c_e=\begin{cases}
\frac12+2^{-(h+4)},&e\text{ halts at step }h,\\
\frac12,&e\text{ never halts}.
\end{cases}
\tag{M.6.12i.3}
$$
These parameters have uniformly computable precision names, despite the undecidability of their equality with $1/2$. To approximate $c_e$ at precision $2^{-k}$, simulate $e$ for $k$ steps. If it halts, return its exact displayed rational value; otherwise return $1/2$. A later first halt has $h>k$ and changes the answer by at most $2^{-(k+5)}<2^{-k}$. Standard integer square-root bracketing provides a precision name for the fixed prior (M.6.12i.1), and multiplication supplies names for the complete joint law. If a prescribed joint-entry precision requires a smaller error after multiplication, request that finer precision before forming the rational products.

For every $e$, $1/2\le c_e\le17/32<1$, so both reveal and erasure have strictly positive probability. The prior entries are positive irrational numbers. Since $c_e$ and $1-c_e$ are positive rational numbers for each program, all six nonzero joint entries $p_xc_e,p_x(1-c_e)$ are irrational. The three reveal labels have distinct conditional laws, so the model has three effective substrate states; it is not a binary alphabet with a null third state. Zero cross-reveal entries are part of its fixed stochastic readout grammar.

At $\beta=2$, (M.6.12i.2) has value zero precisely when $e$ never halts and strictly negative value precisely when it halts. A total decision procedure for either event would decide halting. To recall the contradiction, if an algorithm decided whether an arbitrary program halts on its own code, a program could run forever exactly when that algorithm predicts it halts and halt exactly when it predicts otherwise. Applying the algorithm to that program's code contradicts its answer. The fixed-input halting problem used here contains this diagonal problem by compiling the program and its code into a fixed-input program. Thus the assumed bottleneck decision algorithm cannot exist.

In the nonhalting case the constant description is optimal and the minimum optimal alphabet has size one; in the halting case the minimum size is three and every constant description is suboptimal. The same reduction proves the two equivalent decision obstructions. Theorem M.6.12h still computes the value and arbitrarily accurate optimizing kernels on every member of this family. Exact rational inputs with algebraic certificates in Theorem M.6.12e retain that theorem's decision procedure; a precision name supplies a different input interface. ∎

Theorems M.6.12h--M.6.12i resolve approximation and exact-decision effectivity for the declared computable-real finite-law interface. The continuum RG discrepancy, limiting response dictionary, physical effective-variable source and complete clock/resource records are not covered by these theorems.

<a id="theorem-m612k-smooth-gaussian-continuum-bottleneck-and-actual-finite-operatornamelaw-bridge"></a>**Theorem M.6.12k (Smooth Gaussian Continuum Bottleneck and Actual Finite-$\operatorname{Law}$ Bridge).** All information quantities use nats. The continuum sector is separately declared from Definition M.6.12a; its actual finite laws in part6a are instances of that definition.

**Exact statement.** Let $(\xi _i,\eta _i)$ be independent standard Gaussian pairs with $\eta _i=\rho _i \xi _i+\sqrt{1-\rho _i^2}N_i$, $0<\rho _i<1$, $\rho _i\to 0$, and $\sum \rho _i^2<\infty$. Realize these coefficients as smooth stationary fields as below. For each finite $\beta \ge 0$, minimize $B=I(X;U)-\beta I(Y;U)$ over standard-Borel kernels $U-X-Y$ with finite $I(X;U)$, without side information or a cardinality bound. The infimum is attained using just the finitely many modes $\beta \rho _i^2>1$. It is the sum of their scalar minima. Spectral-cutoff optima eventually equal that value exactly, and their chosen optimal response kernels stabilize after independent tail lifting. The infimum over the union of all finite output alphabets is the same; if any mode is active, no finite output attains it. Quantized-input, dyadic-table finite-output encoders approach it with the explicit bounds below. Thus a fixed-output-memory contract is not solved by the continuum formula.

#### 1. Independently specified nonempty source and regularity

Use the circle of circumference $2\pi$, normalized Haar measure, and real orthonormal Fourier basis $e_0=1$, $e_{n,c}=\sqrt{2}\cos(nx)$, $e_{n,s}=\sqrt{2}\sin(nx)$. Both sine/cosine copies have

$$
a_n=\exp(-2n^2), \lambda _n=n^2+\ln2, \rho _n=\exp(-\lambda _n)=(1/2)\exp(-n^2).
$$

Let independent stationary scalar OU processes satisfy

$$
d \xi _i(t)=-\lambda _i \xi _i(t)dt+\sqrt{2\lambda _i}dW_i(t),\quad \operatorname{Var} \xi _i(t)=1.
$$

Define $F_t=\sum_i \sqrt{a_i}\xi _i(t)e_i$, $X=F_0$, $Y=F_1$. The spatial length and temporal lag 1 are supplied units, not derived scales. This is a stationary process in time and jointly translation-invariant in space. Its conditional readout noise has coefficients $\sqrt{a_i(1-\rho _i^2)}N_i$; every mode is strictly noisy. The canonical correlation operator is diagonal with eigenvalues $\rho_{i}$, hence compact, and $\sum \rho _i^2<\infty$ with multiplicity.

On $H=L^2$, set $Ae_i=-\lambda _i e_i$, $D(A)=\{x:\sum \lambda _i^2|x_i|^2<\infty\}$, $Qe_i=2\lambda _i a_i e_i$, and $Ce_i=a_i e_i$. Q and C are trace class, $S(t)$ is exponentially stable, and $Q_t e_i=a_i(1-\exp(-2\lambda _i t))e_i$. These explicitly satisfy Theorem 12.5.5n's hypotheses and Lyapunov identity.

For every real $s$, $\sum_i(1+n_i^2)^s a_i<\infty$. Thus each $F_{t}$ and each conditional noise field belongs almost surely to every Sobolev space, hence has a $C^\infty$ representative. On every compact time interval one also has continuous paths with values in every fixed Sobolev space: the second increment moment is bounded by $2|t-s|\sum_i(1+n_i^2)^s \lambda _i a_i$, Gaussian fourth moments bound the fourth increment by three times its square, and the Banach/Hilbert Kolmogorov argument applies. Taking countably many integer $s$ gives the simultaneous smooth spatial version. Coefficient recovery from the field is measurable and invertible on its full-measure Fourier image; mutual information therefore equals that of the coefficient sequences. One must not treat the whitened sequence $\xi$ as an $\ell^{2}$-valued random variable.

The law is specified independently of $\beta$. For example $\beta =8$ activates just $n=0$. This has $d_0=3/7$, $U=\sqrt{4/7}\xi _0+\sqrt{3/7}Z$, $I(X;U)=(1/2)\ln(7/3)$, $I(Y;U)=(1/2)\ln(7/6)$, and negative optimum $(1/2)\ln(7/3)-4\ln(7/6)$. Every other mode remains genuinely present in X,Y and genuinely noisy. If a spatially nonconstant effective field is wanted, the same independently specified source at $\beta =64$ activates exactly $n=0$ and the two $n=1$ real modes, because $e^2<16<e^8$. Its gains have $d_0=1/21$ and $d_1=(4e^2-1)/63$. Thus the witness is not restricted to a constant-mode summary; this second separated rational-$\beta$ case also supports the constructive finite-table statements.

#### 2. Scalar arbitrary-auxiliary bound

Put $q=\rho^2$ in (0,1), let X,N be independent standard normals, $Y=\rho$ X+$\sqrt{1-q}$N, and V−X−Y be any standard-Borel auxiliary with finite $r=I$(X;V). Conditional EPI, followed by Jensen for the strictly convex function $s\mapsto \ln(q \exp(2s)+2\pi e(1-q))$, gives

$$
h(Y|V) \ge (1/2)\ln(q \exp(2h(X|V))+2\pi e(1-q)).
$$

Consequently $I(Y;V) \le f_q(r):=-(1/2)\ln(1-q+q \exp(-2r))$. This is an arbitrary-auxiliary inequality, not optimization confined to Gaussian encoders. Conditional densities and entropies are legitimate almost everywhere because finite relative information to a standard normal implies finite conditional KL almost everywhere and finite average conditional entropy; truncation/extended-entropy EPI gives the same limit if needed.

The function $r-\beta f_q(r)$ is strictly convex for $\beta >0$; its derivative is $1-\beta q \exp(-2r)/(1-q+q \exp(-2r))$. Its unique minimizer is $r=0$ if $\beta q\le 1$. Otherwise

$$
d_q=\exp(-2r_q)=(1-q)/[(\beta -1)q],
$$

$$
r_q=(1/2)\ln[(\beta -1)q/(1-q)],
$$

$$
j_q=(1/2)\ln[(\beta -1)/(\beta (1-q))],
$$

$$
b_\beta (q)=r_q-\beta j_q<0.
$$

Set $r_{q}=j_{q}=b_{\beta}(q)=0$ on inactive modes. The normalized encoder $U_q=\sqrt{1-d_q}X+\sqrt{d_q}Z$ with independent standard Gaussian Z attains the active frontier. At critical equality $\beta q=1$, only $r=0$ minimizes.

#### 3. Tensorization and actual infinite-dimensional optimum

Enumerate the independent pairs. For any admissible U put $V_i=(U,Y_1,...,Y_{i-1})$. The scalar Markov relation $V_i-X_i-Y_i$ holds. Independence of pairs and data processing imply

$$
\sum_{i\le n} I(X_i;V_i) \le \sum_{i\le n} I(X_i;U,X_{<i}) = I(X_{\le n};U).
$$

Here $(U,Y_{<i})$ is a randomized postprocessing of $(U,X_{<i})$ by noises independent of the whole X and U. Also

$$
\sum_{i\le n} I(Y_i;V_i)=I(Y_{\le n};U).
$$

Apply the scalar inequality termwise to obtain

$$
I(X_{\le n};U)-\beta I(Y_{\le n};U) \ge \sum_{i\le n}b_\beta (q_i).
$$

Both informations converge monotonically to the full-sequence informations, by continuity of relative entropy on increasing generating $\sigma$-fields. They are finite because $I(Y;U)\le I(X;U)<\infty$. Only finitely many $b$ terms are nonzero since $\rho_{i}\to 0$. Taking $n\to\infty$ proves the global lower bound. Independent active scalar encoders attain it by information additivity; their output is a finite-dimensional Gaussian vector, not a finite alphabet.

The source's $I(X;Y)=-(1/2)\sum_i \ln(1-q_i)$ is finite by summability and strict noise. For this source even auxiliaries with infinite $I(X;U)$ cannot improve the value: their objective is +infinity since $I(Y;U)\le I$(X;Y)<infinity.

Finite output nonattainment: place an active coordinate first in the ordering. Equality in the global bound forces its scalar minimum and scalar EPI/Jensen equality. Thus $X_i|U=u$ must be Gaussian with common variance $d_{i}<1$. If U is finite, the standard Gaussian $X_{i}$ would be a finite mixture of Gaussians of common variance $d_{i}$. Deconvolution of characteristic functions forces the finite-valued mean $E[X_i|U]$ to be a nondegenerate Gaussian of variance 1−$d_{i}$, impossible. Therefore no finite alphabet attains the optimum when an active mode exists. When none is active the constant output does attain zero.

There is also a separate fixed-cardinality gap argument, which must not be inferred from nonattainment alone. For prescribed M, write an encoder as M functions $k_j(X)\in [0,1]$ with sum 1. This closed bounded convex simplex is weakly compact in $L^2(P_X)^M$. Let $Tk=E[k(X)|Y]$. In the product Hermite bases T has singular values $\prod_i \rho _i^{\alpha _i}$ for finite-support multiindices $\alpha$. Its squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm is $\prod_i(1-\rho _i^2)^{-1}<\infty$, using the assumed summability. Thus weakly convergent encoder functions have strongly convergent $Tk_{j}$. Writing mutual information as $\sum_j E[k_j \ln k_j]-\sum_j p_j \ln p_j$, the X-information is weakly lower semicontinuous, whereas the Y-information is continuous by the strong convergence, bounded range and continuity of t $\ln$ t on [0,1]. The objective therefore attains a minimum at each M. If any mode is active, nonattainment of the unrestricted value proves this fixed-M minimum is strictly larger. No quantitative gap or formula for that constrained minimum is asserted. In particular the dimension m of a continuous optimal Gaussian vector is not an m-bit output budget.

#### 4. Cutoff, discrepancy, effective variable, and response dictionary

Let $P_{\mathrm{N}}$ retain $n\le N$. Use the same source and noise coordinates for $(X_N,Y_N)=(P_{NX},P_{NY})$. Their Gaussian IB optimum is $\sum_{n_i\le N}b_\beta (q_i)$, so it equals the continuum value as soon as every active mode is retained. For the explicit source activity is exactly $n^2<(1/2)\ln(\beta /4)$ with the usual strict inequality; none are active at $\beta \le 4$. For $\beta >4$ the exact number of active real coordinates is $m=1+2 \max(0,\lceil \sqrt{(1/2)\ln(\beta /4)}\rceil-1)$: the constant mode counts once and each positive frequency twice. This ceiling convention excludes a frequency at exact threshold. The displayed formula is mathematical, not a uniform comparison algorithm on arbitrary precision-name $\beta$; equality cases require exact data or a comparison promise. In particular the $\beta =8$ witness has an elementary strict threshold margin. A general precision-name spectrum near equality likewise needs its own comparison promises.

For the $L^{2}$ field norm the source cutoff discrepancy obeys

$$
E||X-X_N||^2=E||Y-Y_N||^2=T_N:=2\sum_{n>N}\exp(-2n^2) \le 2\exp(-2(N+1)^2)/(1-\exp(-2(2N+3))).
$$

The same estimate with Sobolev weights provides stronger smooth-test bounds. In particular $W_2(\operatorname{Law}(Y),\operatorname{Law}(Y_N))=\sqrt{T_N}$ in the $L^{2}$ norm: projection coupling attains the bound and every coupling must carry the orthogonal tail. For a joint bounded 1-Lipschitz response on $H\times H$ with its sum norm, expectation discrepancy is at most $2\sqrt{T_N}$ under this coupling. Full-field total variation is instead 1: the truncated law has zero tail and the full law does not. These topologies must not be confused.

With active normalized output u define the finite-rank posterior-mean field

$$
m_\beta (u)=\sum_{i \mathrm{active}} \sqrt{a_i}\rho _i \sqrt{1-d_i}u_i e_i.
$$

The conditional covariance $C_{\beta}$ is diagonal with coefficient $a_i v_i$, where $v_i=1-q_i(1-d_i)$ on active modes and $v_{i}=1$ otherwise. The exact predictive response kernel is

$$
R_\beta (u)=\operatorname{Law}(Y|U=u)=N(m_\beta (u),C_\beta ).
$$

For every $h\in H$ its characteristic response is $\exp(i\langle h,m_\beta (u)\rangle-\langle h,C_\beta h\rangle/2)$. Equivalently all bounded Borel tests $g$ have response $R_\beta g(u)=\int g(y)R_\beta (u,dy)$. The map $u\mapsto m_{\beta}(u)$ is injective on the active finite-dimensional space, so the posterior mean together with the registered fixed covariance is a response-equivalent effective field. This proves preservation of the **chosen bottleneck's** predictive responses. It does not assert that $U$ is sufficient for the entire $X\to Y$ source: finite $\beta$ intentionally loses information.

Once N retains active modes, the finite optimal kernel and mean are identical. Appending the independently specified Gaussian Y-tail gives exactly $R_{\beta}$; zero-tail embedding instead gives a bounded-Lipschitz error ≤$\sqrt{T_N}$, uniformly in u. This is an explicit lifting kernel and limiting response dictionary. Sampling the infinite residual field is an ideal mathematical service, not finite-register machinery.

This provides a free-source spectral coarse-graining/effective-variable map. It does not establish a renormalization flow with spatial rescaling, universality, interacting fixed points, or derivation of the source from PU. Those stronger meanings of RG are not interchangeable with this construction.

#### 5. Output quantization with explicit information and response error

Let $m$ be the number of active real coordinates. Quantize each standard-normal $U_{i}$ by a clipped uniform grid in $[-L,L]$ with spacing at most $\Delta$, including endpoints and saturation cells. There are at most $K=\lceil 2L/\Delta \rceil+2$ labels per coordinate; $Q$ denotes the joint output with $M\le K^m$ labels. Let $\hat{u}_{i}(Q)$ be its reconstruction and $D_i=E(U_i-\hat{u}_i)^2$.

For $L\ge 1$, writing $\phi$ for standard-normal density,

$$
D_i \le \Delta ^2/2 + 8 \phi (L)/L^3.
$$

Indeed $|U-\hat{u}|\le \Delta /2+(|U|-L)_+$; the tail second moment is at most $4\phi (L)/L^3$ by substituting $|U|=L+t$ and using $\exp(-Lt-t^2/2)\le \exp(-Lt)$. The displayed bound follows by $(a+b)^2\le 2a^2+2b^2$.

For a Gaussian regression $Z=\kappa U+\eta$ with $\eta$ independent and variance $v>0$, comparison to $N(\kappa \hat{u}(Q),v)$ proves

$$
I(Z;U|Q) \le \kappa^2 E(U-\mathrm{hat} u(Q))^2/(2v).
$$

The logarithmic improvement $(1/2)\ln(1+\kappa^2 E \operatorname{Var}(U|Q)/v)$ follows from maximum entropy and Jensen, but is not needed for the bounds. The multivariate diagonal version follows by Gaussian KL and gives, with $c_{X,i}=(1-d_i)/d_i$, $c_{Y,i}=q_i(1-d_i)/v_i$,

$$
L_X:=I(X;U)-I(X;Q) \le (1/2)\sum_i c_{X,i} D_i,
$$

$$
L_Y:=I(Y;U)-I(Y;Q) \le (1/2)\sum_i c_{Y,i} D_i.
$$

The source tails are independent of U and do not contribute. Exact chain rules and global optimality yield

$$
0\le B(Q)-B^* = -L_X+\beta L_Y \le (\beta /2)\sum_i c_{Y,i} D_i.
$$

Moreover $E_U \operatorname{TV}(R_\beta (U),\operatorname{Law}(Y|Q)) \le \sqrt{L_Y/2}$ by conditional KL and Pinsker. This controls every bounded predictive decision response on average; it is not a uniform-in-u claim.

For any $\delta\in(0,1]$, choose $\Delta =\sqrt{\delta}$, $L=\sqrt{2\ln(16/\delta)}$; then each $D_{i}\le\delta$. Output memory is at most $\lceil m \log_2 K\rceil$ bits, with $\log K=O(\log(1/\delta)+\log \log(1/\delta))$. These labels approximate ideal continuous $U$; they do not supply its analog acquisition or noise service.

#### 6. Finite input access and finite random bits

The following inequalities are mathematical statements for every fixed finite $\beta$. The effective table-construction claim is restricted to computable supplied parameters and an effectively identified active set, such as the separated $\beta =8$ or $\beta =64$ witnesses above, or to explicitly supplied comparison/oracle data. The exact source specification alone does not make a table computable for an arbitrary noncomputable real $\beta$, nor decide threshold equality from an arbitrary precision name.

Quantize the m active standard input coordinates $\xi_{i}$ to A, with reconstruction mean-square errors $E_{i}$ and a finite input alphabet of cardinality J. Let Q be the ideal output quantizer from part 5. Define the averaged table

$$
T(q|a)=P(Q=q|A=a).
$$

Generate Q' from T using only A, independently of the original source conditional on A. This preserves the joint law of (A,Q), and

$$
D(P_{X,Y,Q} || P_{X,Y,Q'}) = I(X;Q|A) \le I(X;U|A) \le (1/2)\sum_i c_{X,i} E_i.
$$

The first equality follows by cancelling the unchanged source density and recognizing the averaged kernel; Y is conditionally independent of Q given X. The second follows from Q being a function of U. Thus joint $\operatorname{TV}$ is at most $\tau _{\mathrm{in}}=(1/2)\sqrt{\sum_i c_{X,i} E_i}$.

Approximate each row $T$ by dyadic masses of denominator $2^b$: round the first $M-1$ masses down and put the residual in the last entry. Row $\operatorname{TV}$ is at most $(M-1)2^{-b}$. If actual certified numerical table entries have additional row-$\operatorname{TV}$ error $\gamma$, add $\gamma$ separately. Let the final encoder output be $\widetilde Q$ and set

$$
\tau =\tau _{\mathrm{in}}+(M-1)2^{-b}+\gamma \le 1/2.
$$

Its joint source/output law is within $\tau$ of the ideal (X,Y,Q). For any source variable V with unchanged marginal, conditional coupling and the mismatch indicator give $|I(V;Q)-I(V;\widetilde Q)|\le 2g_M(\tau )$, where $g_M(t)=h_2(t)+t \ln M$. This remains valid for continuous V because only the output entropy is finite. Hence

$$
0\le B(\widetilde Q)-B^* \le (\beta /2)\sum_i c_{Y,i} D_i + 2(1+\beta )g_M(\tau ).
$$

The lower bound follows from admissibility $\widetilde Q-X-Y$; the upper bound compares to the ideal $Q$. For any bounded $|f|\le 1$ source/output response, the table approximation changes expectation by at most $2\tau$. Combined with part 5, this gives an explicit average response-error budget. Conditional posteriors of $Q$ versus $\widetilde Q$ need care when their output marginals differ; the unconditional joint-response bound is the stated robust claim. Neither joint $\operatorname{TV}$ nor average posterior $\operatorname{TV}$ nor field-tail Wasserstein/bounded-Lipschitz estimates imply uniform conditional accuracy on arbitrarily rare output labels.

An elementary implementation stores a $J$-by-$M$ table with at most $b+1$ bits per mass numerator (or cumulative entry, including the endpoint $2^b$), at most $O(JM(b+1))$ persistent bits, input/output addresses requiring $\lceil \log_2 J\rceil$ and $\lceil \log_2 M\rceil$ bits, $b$ fresh unbiased random bits per draw, a $b+1$-bit comparison register and finite lookup/comparison circuitry. A sequential scan needs at most $M$ comparisons per sample; tree lookup can reduce comparisons after appropriate table organization. The random word uniformly selects one of $2^b$ intervals, so no ideal continuous random register is required for this finite encoder.

For fixed $\beta$ and fixed m, a conservative accuracy design uses $\delta_{\mathrm{out}}=O(\epsilon)$, $\tau=O(\epsilon/\log(1/\epsilon))$, $\delta_{\mathrm{in}}=O(\tau^2)$, and $b\ge\log_2((M-1)/\tau)$ plus a constant margin. Then output bits are $O(m \log(1/\epsilon ))$, input bits are $O(m \log(1/\epsilon ))$, random bits are $O((m+1)\log(1/\epsilon ))$, and the dense table grows polynomially in $1/\epsilon$ for fixed m, with logarithmic factors. Explicit choices should use the displayed inequalities rather than hide $\beta$-dependent constants or activation-near-boundary effects.

The entries are finite Gaussian rectangle integrals divided by positive Gaussian input-cell probabilities, all computable for the explicit source; certified integration must budget its own $\gamma$ and preprocessing effort. For effective implementation, first compute rational stochastic rows within $\gamma$ and then round those rational rows dyadically. Do not require deciding whether a true computable-real probability equals a dyadic boundary. We assert a finite existence/computability construction and explicit storage/random-bit counts, not a measured execution time or a uniform efficient integration algorithm. Every saturation cell is retained. No discarded-overflow postselection is allowed.

#### 6a. Actual finite X,Y,Z laws converging to the continuum optimum

The preceding construction still had continuous task readout $Y$. Here is the additional finite-readout step needed to connect to Definition M.6.12a itself. Let $A$ be the finite active-input quantizer and $\widetilde Q$ the finite dyadic-table output from part 6. Quantize each active normalized readout $\eta_{i}$ into a finite $B_{i}$, with reconstruction $\hat{\eta}_{i}(B_i)$ and mean-square error $E_{B,i}=E(\eta _i-\hat{\eta} _i)^2$. Put $B=(B_{i})$. The finite source law is the actual law of $(A,B)$, independently obtained by these quantizers from the supplied Gaussian source, not a fitted law chosen to force an optimum.

Because $\widetilde Q$ is generated only from $A$ by a fresh random word, $I(X;\widetilde Q)=I(A;\widetilde Q)$ exactly. Inactive $Y$ coordinates are independent of the entire active source and encoder. Hence conditional data processing gives

$$
I(Y;\widetilde Q)-I(B;\widetilde Q) = I(Y_{\mathrm{active}};\widetilde Q|B) \le I(Y_{\mathrm{active}};X_{\mathrm{active}}|B).
$$

For the reverse Gaussian source regression $\xi _i=\rho _i \eta _i+\sqrt{1-q_i}E_i$, compare conditional distributions with a Gaussian centered at $\rho _i \hat{\eta} _i(B_i)$. The same KL decomposition as before yields

$$
I(Y_{\mathrm{active}};X_{\mathrm{active}}|B) \le (1/2)\sum_{i \mathrm{active}} [q_i/(1-q_i)] E_{B,i}.
$$

Equivalently conditional variances can replace reconstruction errors, but the displayed errors have the explicit clipped-grid bounds of part 5. This estimate does not depend on the output alphabet or on Gaussianity of the finite table encoder.

Let $v_{A,B}$ be the genuine finite-law optimum over all finite stochastic descriptions of $A$ with target $B$, exactly the contract of M.6.12a. Every such kernel lifts to a valid continuum encoder by reading $A(X)$. Its input information is unchanged and its relevance cannot decrease when $B$ is replaced by the full $Y$. Thus its finite-law objective is at least $v_{\mathrm{cont}}$, the continuum minimum. Conversely our table channel is an admissible finite description, so

$$
v_{\mathrm{cont}} \le v_{A,B} \le v_{\mathrm{cont}} + E_{\mathrm{enc}} + (\beta /2)\sum_{i \mathrm{active}}[q_i/(1-q_i)]E_{B,i},
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{enc}}=(\beta /2)\sum_i c_{Y,i} D_i+2(1+\beta )g_M(\tau )$ is the part-6 bound. Sending the input, output and readout errors to zero, with the stated dyadic/probability precision, proves convergence of actual finite-alphabet optima to the continuum value. These finite-law optima themselves are attained by the support bound of Theorem M.6.12h; that does not contradict nonattainment of the limiting continuum optimum by any single finite alphabet. This finite-law optimization admits every finite output alphabet; a separately imposed fixed M may exclude the constructed encoder and retains its separate gap.

For the $\beta =8$ witness all objective constants become elementary: $c_X=4/3$, $c_Y=1/6$, $q/(1-q)=1/3$. Thus

$$
0\le v_{A,B}-v_{\mathrm{cont}} \le (2/3)D_{\mathrm{out}} + 18g_M(\tau ) + (4/3)E_B,
$$

$$
\tau =\sqrt{E_A/3}+(M-1)2^{-b}+\gamma \le 1/2.
$$

The same bound holds for v_($A_{\mathrm{N}}$,$B_{\mathrm{N}}$) once $N\ge 0$, with the separate field-discrepancy budgets below. This is a fully specified nonempty finite-law approximation certificate rather than just convergence notation.

For full-field source discrepancy, fix N containing every active mode and quantize **all** normalized source/readout coordinates with $n\le N$ into $A_{\mathrm{N}}$,$B_{\mathrm{N}}$. Continue to use a channel depending only on the active subvector of $A_{\mathrm{N}}$. Inactive coordinate pairs are independent of the active block, so this channel has the same information values and the same upper bound. Every arbitrary $A_{\mathrm{N}}$ encoder still lifts to the continuum, so the same lower bound holds for the full finite-law optimum v_($A_{\mathrm{N}}$,$B_{\mathrm{N}}$). The quantized joint law is computable for computable grids and the separated witnesses, using finite Gaussian rectangle probabilities; irrational entries are valid precision-name data for M.6.12h, not silently rational inputs to M.6.12e.

Define reconstructed source fields $\widehat X_N=\sum_{n_i\le N}\sqrt{a_i}\hat{\xi} _i(A_N)e_i$ and $\widehat Y_N=\sum_{n_i\le N}\sqrt{a_i}\hat{\eta} _i(B_N)e_i$. Under the original common-source coupling,

$$
E||X-\widehat X_N||^2=T_N+\sum_{n_i\le N}a_i E_{A,i},
$$

$$
E||Y-\widehat Y_N||^2=T_N+\sum_{n_i\le N}a_i E_{B,i}.
$$

These are explicit $W_2$-squared upper bounds; the cutoff tail $T_{\mathrm{N}}$ is the numerical expression from part 4 above. Joint bounded 1-Lipschitz responses in the sum norm differ by at most the sum of the square roots. They can be combined with the table's joint-$\operatorname{TV}$ response error $2\tau$ when comparing the relevant ideal and finite encoder laws. This is convergence of field reconstructions and joint/average responses, not full-field total variation convergence or uniform conditional accuracy at rare labels.

The full-field finite source record needs 2N+1 input-coordinate quantizers and 2N+1 readout-coordinate quantizers. If each uses at most $K_{\mathrm{A}}$ or $K_{\mathrm{B}}$ labels, the source/readout register capacities are at most $\lceil (2N+1)\log_2 K_A\rceil$ and $\lceil (2N+1)\log_2 K_B\rceil$ bits. The compressed encoder table can still ignore inactive indices and retain the active-input storage bound in part 6; preserving the larger source/readout records is a separately counted acquisition/storage task. No sensor count is hidden by the fact that only m effective coordinates matter for the optimum.

For example take $N\to\infty$ and a common reconstruction-error bound $\max_{n_i\le N}\{E_{A,i},E_{B,i}\}\le \delta_N\to 0$, achieved by a common clipped grid, together with dyadic/probability errors tending to zero at the part-6 rate. The source norm convergence follows because the quantization contribution is at most $\delta_N \sum_i a_i$ and $T_{\mathrm{N}}\to 0$, while the objective error uses only finitely many active readout errors. Mere pointwise accuracy on each fixed coordinate is not substituted for this common bound as the cutoff grows. This gives the promised continuum discrepancy and finite-law optimization bridge with independently fixed source and $\beta$; it still supplies no physical calibration or apparatus realization.

#### 7. Full resource and source boundary

The continuum theorem presumes exact access to the field and an exact Gaussian randomization kernel; finite m is not finite precision. The finite-table encoder replaces its output/randomness but still presumes a specified m-channel measurement/ADC interface to the source. Its physical measurement disturbance, sensor response, calibration, sampling/switching time, error correlations, data transport, controller/lookup hardware, preparation, reset, memory retention, noise generation, clock, work and heat have not been supplied by mathematics.

The Gaussian covariance-inverse action $(1/2)\langle F,C^{-1}F\rangle=(1/2)\sum_i \xi _i^2$ is infinite almost surely, as expected from the Cameron–Martin support distinction. This is not automatically a physical Hamiltonian and does not prove infinite physical energy. If a consumer independently nominates that quadratic action as its physical energy, its $N$ cutoff has mean $(2N+1)/2$ in the nominated units and an equipartition divergence follows. By contrast an independently nominated $L^{2}$ or fixed-Sobolev quadratic energy has finite expectation for this smooth source. The source law itself does not choose among those energy assignments. Physical energy, preparation costs and apparatus admission remain unspecified; no physical impossibility or finite total realization follows just from the Gaussian measure.

The OU clock is specified mathematically. Rescaling both drift and noise preserves the equal-time law while changing the lag correlation, hence the optimal active set at a fixed named physical delay; therefore a physical clock calibration is consequential. Likewise $\beta$ is supplied, not selected by PCE. The field source, task readout, normalization and costs do not follow from mutual information.

The continuous Gaussian optimum and finite-alphabet approximation are distinct results. The finite-alphabet problem attains each finite-stage optimum; the stated continuum value is approached through the displayed physical refinements, with their full resource and error bounds.

<a id="theorem-m612l-same-source-finite-controlled-hamiltonian-compiler-and-precision-ledger"></a>**Theorem M.6.12l (Same-Source Finite Controlled-Hamiltonian Compiler and Precision Ledger).**

#### 2. Retained mathematical source and approximation record

Use Theorem M.6.12k’s original circle, normalized Haar measure, real Fourier basis, and independent stationary OU modes:

- $a_{n}=\exp(-2n^2)$, $\lambda_{n}=n^{2}+\ln 2$;
- $\rho_{n}=\exp(-\lambda _n)=\exp(-n^2)/2$;
- $F_{t}=\sum_{i}\sqrt{a_i}\,\xi_{i}(t)\,e_{i}$, with each $\xi$ a stationary variance-one OU process;
- $X=F_{0}$ and $Y=F_{1}$;
- $\beta=8$ for the simplest separated witness, or $\beta=64$ for a nonconstant three-real-mode effective field.

The source is fixed before $\beta$ and before the description kernel. At cutoff N let $A_{\mathrm{N}}$ and $B_{\mathrm{N}}$ be the original clipped finite coordinate quantizers of X and Y. Retain every saturation cell. Let $p_{\mathrm{N}}(a,b)$ be their exact Gaussian rectangle law, and let $T_{\mathrm{N}}(z|a)$ be k's finite dyadic encoder table, generated from independent randomness. All positive-mass input states are retained. Write $p_{a}=\sum_{b}p_{\mathrm{N}}(a,b)$, $W(b|a)=p_{\mathrm{N}}(a,b)/p_{a}$. Then the exact target finite law is

$$
P_N(a,b,z)=p_a W(b|a)T_N(z|a)
\tag{M.6.12l.1}
$$

This is a registered finite joint law; it is not obtained by optimizing or fitting the source to an encoder. In the Gaussian source all nonempty quantizer cells have positive probability. Rectangle probabilities and their ratios are computable reals; exact equality to a dyadic boundary is never needed. The encoder uses rational-row approximation before dyadic rounding, as k requires.

For $\beta =8$, if M is the encoder alphabet size, its objective satisfies the registered bound

$$
0 \le B_N(T_N) - v_{\mathrm{cont}} \le (2/3)D_{\mathrm{out}} + 18 g_M(\tau ) + (4/3)E_B,
$$

$$
\tau = \sqrt{E_A/3} + (M-1)2^{-b} + \gamma \le 1/2,
$$

$$
g_M(t)=h_2(t)+t \ln M
$$

This statement concerns the displayed constructed encoder; the actual finite optimum is between $v_{\mathrm{cont}}$ and that constructed objective. With all modes through N quantized, the field reconstruction errors are

$$
\begin{gathered}
E||X-\widehat X_N||^2 = T_{\mathrm{tail},N} + \sum_{i\le N} a_i E_{A,i},\\E||Y-\widehat Y_N||^2 = T_{\mathrm{tail},N} + \sum_{i\le N} a_i E_{B,i},
\end{gathered}
$$

$$
T_{\mathrm{tail},N} \le 2 \exp(-2(N+1)^2)/(1-\exp(-2(2N+3)))
\tag{M.6.12l.2}
$$

We use these already proved convergence estimates unchanged.

#### 3. Finite physical compilation theorem

*Statement.* For any finite computable law (M.6.12l.1), there is an explicitly described finite-dimensional controlled quantum experiment whose retained classical records have exactly law (M.6.12l.1). It uses three independent initially blank environment registers, three explicitly computable reflection pulses, no erasure, positive specified durations, and a source register unchanged by both readout and encoder operations. Its output has the exact finite-law response kernel, and its mathematical field reconstructions inherit (M.6.12l.2) and k's information bounds. No external analog field sensor, uniform refinement-energy bound, autonomous clock or interacting RG is asserted.

**Physical model.** The permitted finite system has computable-real Hamiltonian matrix entries, ideal finite projective record instruments and an externally specified laboratory pulse schedule. Physical constants $\hbar>0$, time unit $t_0>0$, field unit $f_0>0$ and length unit $\ell_0>0$ are separately supplied calibration data. This is the same kind of formally controlled finite-dimensional model admitted in X04; admitting this model is an explicit premise, not a derived physical law.

Let $J=|A_{\mathrm{N}}|$, $K=|B_{\mathrm{N}}|$, $M=|Z|$. Registers $A,E_{\mathrm{A}}$ have dimension $J$; $B,E_{\mathrm{B}}$ have dimension $K$; $Z,E_{\mathrm{Z}}$ have dimension $M$. Their joint initial state is the named pure product blank. Use an ordinary label, say 0, for each blank; it need not be outside the outcome alphabet. Dimension is

$$
D = J^2 K^2 M^2,
\tag{M.6.12l.3}
$$

before optional copies and an orthogonal classical pulse-stage flag. A four-state stage flag raises this to 4D. We use no unspecified lookup hardware: the finite Hamiltonian matrices below are the compiled apparatus descriptor. Finite coefficient algorithms and the finite matrix indexing grammar are its program. This is not a claim of efficient or local hardware synthesis.

For a real nonnegative unit vector v and basis blank o, define $R_{v}$ as follows. If $v=o$, set $R_{v}=I$. Otherwise let $w=(o-v)/\sqrt{2(1-\langle o,v\rangle)}$ and $R_{v}=I-2|w\rangle\langle w|$. Then $R_{v}$ is Hermitian unitary and $R_{v}o=v$. In the strictly positive Gaussian source/readout cells, $v=o$ cannot occur unless the relevant alphabet is trivial. For the dyadic table it is exactly decidable. Thus no undecidable computable-real equality is introduced.

Preparation pulse on A,$E_{\mathrm{A}}$ uses

$$
v_p = \sum_a \sqrt{p_a}|a,a\rangle,  U_p=R_{v_p}
$$

The source register A is then a classical pointer with reduced law $p_{a}$; its purifying environment $E_{\mathrm{A}}$ is retained, inaccessible to the description or readout controls. The encoder and readout are controlled reflections

$$
\begin{gathered}
U_Z = \sum_a |a\rangle\langle a|_A \otimes R_{v_a^Z},\\v_a^Z = \sum_z \sqrt{T_N(z|a)}|z,z\rangle_{Z,E_Z},
\end{gathered}
$$

$$
\begin{gathered}
U_B = \sum_a |a\rangle\langle a|_A \otimes R_{v_a^B},\\v_a^B = \sum_b \sqrt{W(b|a)}|b,b\rangle_{B,E_B}
\end{gathered}
$$

Each unitary acts identically on unlisted registers. They are block-diagonal Hermitian unitaries. $U_{\mathrm{Z}}$ and $U_{\mathrm{B}}$ commute and leave the A pointer projectors invariant. Consequently after all pulses the state is

$$
\begin{gathered}
\sum_{a,b,z} \sqrt{p_a W(b|a)T_N(z|a)}\\|a,a\rangle_{A,E_A}|b,b\rangle_{B,E_B}|z,z\rangle_{Z,E_Z}
\end{gathered}
\tag{M.6.12l.4}
$$

Tracing the three inaccessible environments gives exactly the diagonal record density operator with law (M.6.12l.1). This proves the Markov cut Z−A−B, including the physical restriction forbidding $E_{\mathrm{A}}$, B or $E_{\mathrm{B}}$ as encoder inputs. It is stronger than merely preparing a joint entangled state and assuming that arbitrary access to its purification respects the intended cut.

Measuring the commuting record projectors is a complete finite instrument. All outcomes are retained, including saturation cells. An optional further permanent record copy uses a controlled modular-addition unitary into another blank register of the same size; this requires additional declared dimension and a pulse, not a free environment. The primary records in (M.6.12l.4) already suffice, so no such copies are needed for (M.6.12l.3).

**Response theorem.** For $P_{\mathrm{N}}(z)>0$ the physical retained readout response is exactly

$$
P_N(b|z)=\sum_a p_a T_N(z|a)W(b|a)/\sum_a p_a T_N(z|a)
\tag{M.6.12l.5}
$$

Any bounded finite-record payoff has its mathematical expected value with no implementation-law error. Reconstructing the fields and comparing with k's Gaussian effective variable therefore gives exactly its joint/average response and Wasserstein/bounded-Lipschitz convergence statements. There is no full-field total-variation convergence: a finite reconstruction remains finitely supported. Nor does (M.6.12l.5) imply uniform conditional convergence at rare labels.

**Effective coefficients.** Square roots of nonnegative computable reals are computable. The strict nontriviality above supplies a positive denominator for each nonidentity reflection and a terminating search for a certified positive lower bound. Finite Gaussian integrals supply p and W. Thus every Hamiltonian entry has a rational-interval algorithm at any requested accuracy. Exact computable coefficients are allowed by the declared formal model. A finite precision laboratory implementation adds an error budget; it is not silently exact.

#### 4. Actual clock, Hamiltonian, work and apparatus ledger

Choose source-preparation duration $\tau_{p}>0$, a named laboratory lag $t_0>0$, encoder pulse duration $t_0/4$, idle duration $t_0/2$, and readout duration $t_0/4$. Source time zero is the END of preparation. $Z$ is available at $t_0/4$, and $B$ is available at the actual elapsed time $t_0$. The preparation prefix is owned and counted: experiment duration is $\tau_{p}+t_0$. Pointer registers are stationary during idle ($H=0$). The Gaussian time lag 1 is represented by the supplied physical interval $t_0$. This is a compiled two-time law, not proof that the apparatus evolves as a continuum OU process between those endpoints.

For a Hermitian unitary U and duration $\tau$ use the actual positive Hamiltonian

$$
H_U = (\pi \hbar/(2\tau ))(I-U)
$$

Since U's eigenvalues are ±1, $\exp(-i H_U \tau /\hbar)$=U exactly and

$$
0 \le H_U \le (\pi \hbar/\tau )I
\tag{M.6.12l.6}
$$

Controlled reflections have the same bound, regardless of the number of controls. The explicit three-pulse ceiling is

$$
E_{\mathrm{peak}} \le \max\{\pi \hbar/\tau _p, 4\pi \hbar/t_0\},
$$

$$
\int ||H(t)|| dt \le 3\pi \hbar
\tag{M.6.12l.7}
$$

These are operator-energy and integrated-norm bounds, not thermodynamic preparation-cost bounds or complexity bounds. Arbitrary nonlocal control is admitted, so the apparent dimension-independent bound does not certify cheap scalable laboratory hardware.

At switch-on/switch-off the external driver supplies work. For a pulse, 0<=$\operatorname{Tr}(\rho H_U)$<=||$H_{\mathrm{U}}$||. Evolution under fixed $H_{\mathrm{U}}$ conserves that expectation. Ideal sudden switching therefore has equal and opposite on/off work and zero net work for this isolated pulse; absolute work throughput is at most 2||$H_{\mathrm{U}}$||. Summing gives the conservative bound

$$
W_{\mathrm{absolute}} \le 2\pi \hbar(1/\tau _p+8/t_0)
\tag{M.6.12l.8}
$$

No extraction of usable work, zero total service cost, or reset cost follows from cancellation. The driver must support the positive energy excursion and recover or dissipate it on the declared schedule. If a driver dissipates instead of recovering energy, its waste store and work supply are additional finite resources selected independently of (M.6.12l.1). Equations (M.6.12l.6)–(M.6.12l.8) cover the registered ideal external drive only.

The complete finite experiment resource record consists of:

1. The six finite registers of (M.6.12l.3), their specified pure blank inventory, and their inaccessible-environment partition.
2. The three finite computable Hamiltonian descriptors, pulse ordering and the externally calibrated clock schedule.
3. The external reversible ideal work supply with peak excursions bounded in (M.6.12l.7) and throughput in (M.6.12l.8).
4. The three pointer records retained to the end, with no reset or erasure. Preparation of the blank inventory is a separately supplied initial resource, not a free thermodynamic operation. A run starts with a new stated inventory.
5. The reconstruction map in physical units $f_0\sum\sqrt{a_i}\,\hat{\xi}_{i}\,e_{i}(x/\ell_0)$, on circumference $2\pi\ell_0$; memory for the finite labels is bounded by $\lceil\log_2 J\rceil+\lceil\log_2 K\rceil+\lceil\log_2 M\rceil$ bits, with equal-capacity retained purifiers separately counted.
6. An ideal complete pointer readout instrument; if an external observer's memory is requested, add its blank register and copy pulse explicitly as above.

The external clock, drive and readout interfaces are declared physical control primitives. Their internal autonomous manufacture, battery Hamiltonian, thermal reset and laboratory accuracy are NOT supplied by this controlled-model theorem. In particular “complete apparatus” is complete only relative to that declared model; it does not discharge a stricter autonomous-apparatus contract. Assigning a finite fee $E_{\mathrm{fee}}$ per service would be an independently supplied accounting convention, not a PCE derivation or an experimentally measured heat budget.

#### 5. Refinement and finite precision

For each $N$ choose k's common coordinate reconstruction-error bound $\delta_{\mathrm{N}}\to 0$, with its output quantization, probability-table and readout errors tending to zero at the stated rates. Compile that exact finite law by sections 3–4. The physical recorded law equals the corresponding mathematical finite law at every $N$, so k's convergence transfers without a new limit interchange. The physical reconstructed field error is $f_0^{2}$ times (M.6.12l.2); test-function bounds scale accordingly. The physical time lag is always $t_0$ and circumference always $2\pi\ell_0$.

If the three pulse unitaries are approximated by $\tilde U_{j}$ with operator errors $\epsilon_{j}$, telescoping gives $\lVert\tilde U_{3}\tilde U_{2}\tilde U_{1}-U_{3}U_{2}U_{1}\rVert\le\sum\epsilon_{j}$. Trace distance of the final states and total variation of all record outcomes are at most that sum (plus any initial-state trace-distance error). For approximate Hamiltonians over equal durations, Duhamel gives $\epsilon_{j}\le\tau_{j}\lVert\tilde H_{j}-H_{j}\rVert/\hbar$. These provide finite accuracy specifications. For growing finite alphabets, choose total law error $\epsilon_{\mathrm{N}}$ so that $\epsilon_{\mathrm{N}}\log(JKM)\to 0$; finite-alphabet entropy continuity then transfers objective convergence as well. Merely $\epsilon_{\mathrm{N}}\to 0$ without alphabet control would not suffice.

This law convergence is same-source in the precise sense that each ($A_{\mathrm{N}}$,$B_{\mathrm{N}}$) is the actual quantized pushforward of the SAME k Gaussian pair law, rather than an encoder-fitted substitute. It is not provenance identity with a preexisting physical OU field, nor a measurement/ADC realization of an externally provided physical field. The apparatus synthesizes the registered law. A sensor-based realization needs its own nondisturbance, calibration and acquisition proof. A multi-time OU process needs jointly consistent multi-time experiments; reproducing one two-time law does not prove the Markov process at intermediate physical times.

#### 6. Exact nonentailment and obstruction results

#### 6.1 Clock nonidentification

For any $c>0$ the rescaled process $d\xi=-c\lambda\xi\,dt+\sqrt{2c \lambda }\,dW$ has the SAME equal-time standard Gaussian law. Its physical-lag-$t_0$ correlations are $\exp(-c \lambda t_0)$. Thus equal-time source covariance, field regularity and entropy alone cannot choose a clock. At $\beta =8$ and $t_0=1$, $c=1$ makes the constant mode active ($8/4>1$), whereas $c=2$ makes every mode inactive ($8/16<1$). Any claim to derive the same effective variable from the equal-time law without an independent clock is therefore false. Section 4 supplies a clock; it does not derive it.

#### 6.2 Energy nonidentification

Under the common source law of Theorem M.6.12k, the nominated cutoff energies $E_{\mathrm{N}}^{CM}=(E_0/2)\sum_{i\le N}\xi_{i}^2$ have mean $E_0(2N+1)/2$, diverging as $N\to\infty$. The independently nominated $L^{2}$ energies $E_{\mathrm{N}}^{L2}=(E_0/2)\sum_{i\le N}a_{i}\xi_{i}^2$ have bounded mean tending to $(E_0/2)\sum_{i}a_{i}$. Both are nonnegative quadratic observables on every finite cutoff, with the same field law. Therefore this law alone entails neither divergent physical energy nor bounded total physical cost. Section 4 chooses an explicit third, pulse-based physical realization; its energy is not inferred from a covariance inverse.

#### 6.3 PCE/source choice nonidentification

Mutual information is invariant under invertible relabelings and contains no energy or time units. Supplying a Gaussian joint law and a mathematical $\beta$ determines a mathematical optimum but supplies no operational PCE valuation that selects that law or $\beta$. For example the very same source has only the constant mode active at $\beta =8$ and additionally both $n=1$ real modes active at $\beta =64$. The corresponding effective fields differ. No claim that PCE uniquely chooses one of them can follow from source covariance plus information theory without an extra valuation premise. This is nonentailment, not a no-go theorem against possible PCE selections.

#### 6.4 Interaction obstruction under the accepted marginalization operations

Every finite-mode marginal of a jointly Gaussian field is Gaussian. Every linear spatial transformation and every independent Gaussian encoder applied to such a field remains jointly Gaussian. Consequently all connected cumulants of order $\ge 3$ vanish for every such retained field. This follows directly from the Gaussian $\log$ characteristic function being quadratic. Whenever the requested interacting effective field has any nonzero connected cumulant of order $\ge 3$, it cannot be produced as that field by only k's cutoff, linear reconstruction, Gaussian bottleneck and independent Gaussian tail lifting. A nonlinear observation can of course be non-Gaussian; no such map, interacting action or response-preserving identification is supplied here. This is an exact obstruction to promoting THESE operations to that interacting-field claim, not a proof that all Gaussian-driven apparatus cannot simulate interactions.

#### 6.5 Rescaled RG underdetermination

The cutoff law of Theorem M.6.12k integrates out independent modes, and its exact effective quadratic action on the retained finite coordinates is simply $(1/2)\sum_{i}x_{i}^2/a_{i}$ plus normalization. This is genuine Gaussian marginalization, with composition $P_LP_N=P_{\min(L,N)}$. It supplies no chosen spatial dilation, field-strength rescaling, running coupling space or fixed-point criterion. Those additional maps are essential inputs to any rescaled-RG assertion.

A concrete warning: the explicitly defined mode-decimation-and-relabeling map $(D_{b}F)_n=cF_{bn}$, $b\ge 2$ integer, would transform variances to $c^{2}\exp(-2b^2n^2)$. Equality with k's original variances at $n=0$ forces $c^{2}=1$; equality at $n=1$ would force $b^{2}=1$, impossible. Thus even this particular clearly specified rescaling-like map does not preserve the registered source under any single field normalization. This map is NOT claimed to be a standard Wilson RG; its role is to falsify the idea that scale invariance follows automatically from the existing Gaussian formula. A nontrivial running-coupling family may accommodate it, but that family and its interpretation would be new premises.

<a id="theorem-m612m-funded-proper-score-pce-selection-with-complete-account-and-common-window"></a>**Theorem M.6.12m (Funded Proper-Score PCE Selection with Complete Account and Common Window).**

#### 9. Constructive extension: registered paid PCE sector, not a uniqueness premise

Theorem M.6.12l supplies the exact compiler and its nonentailment safeguards. The following registered PCE choice and funded costs apply to that same source; Theorem M.6.12n supplies the rescaled free RG.

This use of registration is authorized by Definition 15 in Section 6.1.2: PCE declares an objective on a “specified admissible comparison class,” maximizing registered predictive benefit while charging registered acquisition, representation, processing, update, maintenance and adaptation costs. Definition M.6.12a explicitly chooses $I(A;Z)-\beta I(B;Z)$. Neither definition requires unique derivation of $\beta$ or a universal interacting-field classification.

#### 9.1 Fixed comparison class and physical tariff

At each refinement fix the SAME source law $p_{\mathrm{N}}(a,b)$, the SAME $J,K,M$ registers, and a denominator $2^b$. The admissible comparison class $C_{\mathrm{N}}$ is every $J$-by-$M$ stochastic dyadic table of that denominator, including zero entries, padded to the common dimensions.
