This is a finite, source-independent class. All tables have a fixed-length stored description of $JM(b+1)$ bits. Set $M$ and $b$ large enough for k's constructed table; increase them along refinement as k specifies. The source and readout table are unchanged across $C_{\mathrm{N}}$.

Register a positive physical energy unit e0, $\beta =8$ or 64, and six nonnegative source-service tariffs

$c_{\mathrm{acq}}$,N, $c_{\mathrm{reprbase}}$,N, $c_{\mathrm{process}}$,N, $c_{\mathrm{update}}$,N, $c_{\mathrm{maint}}$,N, $c_{\mathrm{adapt}}$,N.

For definiteness take each equal to e0 times one plus the number of binary storage cells assigned to that service. The finite assignment is part of the apparatus descriptor: acquisition owns A,$E_{\mathrm{A}}$,B,$E_{\mathrm{B}}$; representation owns Z,$E_{\mathrm{Z}}$ and the fixed-length table; processing owns the fixed pulse controller and payment ancillas; update owns its finite stage flag; maintenance owns holding these resources through $\tau_{p}$+t0+$\tau_{\mathrm{pay}}$; adaptation owns offline installation of the selected fixed-length table. Overlap is avoided by assigning each physical register to exactly one category and charging holding/installation as time/service fees rather than counting it twice as acquisition. A simpler admissible uniform tariff is $c_{\mathrm{category}}$,N=e0 for each of six services; we choose this latter exact tariff here. The actual physical registers and time/energy ledger remain separately and completely reported. No claim equates the tariff to irreducible manufacture cost or Landauer heat.

Each of these six service fees is actually transferred, not merely written beside an equation: a funded two-level donor of gap e0 starts excited, its service recipient starts in the ground state, and a resonant swap transfers one quantum e0. All twelve fee-bank qubits and their initial excitation inventory are part of the apparatus. Thus $C_{\mathrm{N}}$=6e0 is the actual fixed registered service debit, independent of T. Refinement requires larger apparatus and new blank inventory even though this chosen service tariff is flat; the resource quantities are not claimed bounded or equated to monetary price.

Register an additional representation charge e0 $I(A;Z)$. Its value is computable from the exact source law and the finite dyadic table. It is between 0 and e0 $\ln$ J. For $J>1$, take a donor/recipient pair of gap $\Delta_{\mathrm{rep}}$=e0 $\ln$ J and a fresh retained coin with probability $r_{\mathrm{rep}}=I$(A;Z)/$\ln$ J. A controlled resonant swap transfers this quantum exactly when the coin is one. Its expected actual debit is precisely e0 $I(A;Z)$. For $J=1$ omit this zero charge. The payment is randomized, but the PCE objective is explicitly expected net energy, and the complete payment distribution is retained.

#### 9.2 Operational predictive benefit and funded proper-score reward

The prediction supplied at record $z$ is the exact table $q_{\mathrm{T}}(b|z)$ in (M.6.12l.5). Because $W(b|a)>0$ for every Gaussian quantizer cell, $q_{\mathrm{T}}(b|z)>0$ whenever $P(z)>0$. Choose a certified rational $w_*>0$ smaller than $\min_{a,b}W(b|a)$, and put $L=-\ln w_*>0$. Then both $q_{\mathrm{T}}(b|z)$ and $p_{\mathrm{B}}(b)$ lie in $[w_*,1]$, uniformly over every $T$ in $C_{\mathrm{N}}$. Therefore the realized logarithmic score improvement

$$
s_T(b,z)=\ln q_T(b|z)-\ln p_B(b)
$$

lies in [−L,L], and its expected value is $I(B;Z)$. Labels z with $P(z)=0$ are impossible and may use any prediction. Whether a label is impossible is decidable because $p_{a}>0$ and T is dyadic: it is exactly an all-zero column.

The reward sponsor funds a pair of gap $\Delta_{\mathrm{rew}}=2\beta e_0L$. After the actual retained (b,z) record, prepare a fresh coin with probability $r_{\mathrm{rew}}(b,z)=(s_{T}(b,z)+L)/(2L)$, retain its purification and result, and transfer the quantum to the recipient exactly when the coin is one. Thus the expected actual reward is $\beta e_0[I(B;Z)+L]$. Charge also an unconditional baseline participation quantum $\beta e_0L$ from the user to the sponsor. This baseline is the same for every T and cancels the added reward offset. Consequently

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text{expected total debit minus reward}\\= 6e_0 + e_0 I(A;Z) - \beta e_0 I(B;Z)
\end{gathered}
\tag{M.6.12m.9}
$$

Every term in (M.6.12m.9) is now an actual registered expected transfer on the same experiment. The predictive component is a proper $\log$-score improvement on its actual task readout; the charge component is a declared finite-service/representation tariff. This constructs a legitimate PCE sector, rather than asserting that information is intrinsically physical energy.

#### 9.3 Payment dynamics and full additional ledger

Each bank pair has bare Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{bank}}=\Delta(n_{\mathrm{donor}}+n_{\mathrm{recipient}})$. A controlled exchange pulse generated by $\hbar\theta/\tau\,(|10\rangle\langle 01|+|01\rangle\langle 10|)$, with $\theta =\pi/2$, maps $|10\rangle$ to $-i|01\rangle$ and commutes with $H_{\mathrm{bank}}$; phase is irrelevant to retained energy records. The drive's interaction energy is bounded by $\pi\hbar/(2\tau)$. Coin preparation uses the nonsingular real rotation

[[$\sqrt{1-r}$,−$\sqrt{r}$],[$\sqrt{r}$,$\sqrt{1-r}$]].

This has computable coefficients even at $r=0$ or 1 and avoids equality-testing or division. Copy the coin to a fresh retained two-level environment before the controlled swap. Controls depend only on table data for the representation fee and on the already recorded (b,z) for the reward; they cannot feed back into source, encoder or readout. The original law (M.6.12l.1) and Markov cut therefore remain exact.

The payment stock consists of six fixed service pairs (12 qubits), one representation pair if $J>1$, one reward pair, one baseline pair, two fresh coins and two coin purifiers. Thus at most 22 additional two-level systems are required. A finite payment-stage flag and the fixed-length dyadic table memory are additionally counted. These registers multiply (M.6.12l.3) by at most $2^{22+JM(b+1)}$ times the finite flag dimension. Reward-control table entries have finite computable-real descriptors and are treated as control coefficients, just like the Gaussian source coefficients; no analog probability oracle is assumed.

The ready-state bank energy is exactly

$$
E_{banks} = 6e_0 + e_0 \ln J + 3 \beta e_0 L
\tag{M.6.12m.10}
$$

for $J>1$, with the representation term omitted for $J=1$. These are explicitly supplied funded initial excitations present at run start, just like the stated pure blank inventory. The A,$E_{\mathrm{A}}$ preparation pulse does not create them. Their energy and possession are an explicit finite initial resource; manufacture of that stock is not silently assigned zero work. Resetting the banks is outside the single-run class and never assumed free. Bare energy is conserved during swaps. Coin preparations and exchange controls have positive allocated durations, included in $\tau_{\mathrm{pay}}>0$ after the readout completes at t0. Their Hamiltonian norms and absolute switched-work throughput are bounded by the sum of the finite per-pulse bounds of section 4, plus the bank-energy bound. Equation (M.6.12m.10) is the exact initial energy and the energy on the invariant one-excitation-per-bank-pair subspace used by every registered operation. On the full bank Hilbert space the bare Hamiltonian operator norm is 2 $E_{\mathrm{banks}}$; this larger bound can always be used. During settlement the B and Z pointer records are held stationary. All preparation and settlement elapsed time is reported; the source's calibrated readout lag remains exactly t0.

This is a full registered controlled-model resource ledger: sources, blank and excitation stocks, parameters/table memory, controls, timing, retained outcome/environment/payment records, and work are supplied. No autonomous-clock or cyclic thermal-reset claim is needed by the original row. Optional manufacture costs could be added as fixed class-wide acquisition tariffs without changing the minimizer; they may not be silently made kernel-dependent while retaining (M.6.12m.9).

At each N the finite class has an attained minimum of (M.6.12m.9). The PCE accounting boundary is the user/source service account. <a id="theorem-m612n-exact-gaussian-shell-space-field-and-time-renormalization"></a>**Theorem M.6.12n (Exact Gaussian Shell, Space, Field and Time Renormalization).**

#### 10. Genuine Gaussian shell elimination and coordinate/field/time rescaling

We now give the missing rescaled RG map, on a declared family containing the exact source of Theorem M.6.12k as a base point. It is a free Gaussian RG; no interacting or universal-fixed-point claim is made.

Let the spatial circle have physical-coordinate length $L_{x}$, normalized Haar measure, frequencies $k_{n}$=2pi n/$L_{x}$, and real orthonormal Fourier modes. At a UV cutoff $\Lambda$ retain |$k_{n}$|<=Lambda. Specify covariance and relaxation parameters

a(k)=A \exp(-2g k^2), \lambda (k)=D k^2+m,
$$

with A,g,D,$m>0$. Let independent mode processes have stationary variance $a(k)$, OU decay $\lambda (k)$, and noise variance rate 2lambda(k)$a(k)$. The k source is exactly the base point

$$
L_x=2\pi , A=1, g=1, D=1, m=\ln 2, lag t=1,
$$

with $\Lambda=N$ and its increasing-cutoff limit. Physical units $\ell_0,f_0,t_0$ insert the calibrations from section 4; no other source is substituted.

For $b>1$, dynamic exponent $z=2$ and any registered real field exponent $\chi$ (choose $\chi =0$ here), the RG transformation consists of three actual mathematical operations:

1. Integrate out shell modes $\Lambda/b<|k|\le\Lambda$. This is ordinary marginalization of the very same Gaussian source, not a newly fitted covariance.
2. Rescale space $x'=x/b$, so $L_{x}'=L_{x}/b$ and retained frequencies become $k'=bk$, with restored cutoff $|k'|\le\Lambda$.
3. Rescale time $t'=t/b^z$ and field $F'(x',t')=b^\chi F_{\mathrm{low}}(bx',b^z t')$.

The resulting field has the EXACT parameter flow

$$
\begin{gathered}
L_x'=L_x/b, A'=b^{2\chi }A, g'=g/b^2,\\D'=b^{z-2}D, m'=b^z m, t_{\mathrm{lag}}'=t_{\mathrm{lag}}/b^z
\end{gathered}
\tag{M.6.12n.11}
$$

Proof: a'(k')=$b^{2\chi }$ A $\exp(-2g(k'/b)^2)$. An OU mode evaluated at $b^z$ t' has decay $b^z[D(k'/b)^2+m]$ and noise variance rate $b^z$ times its old rate, with the additional $b^{2\chi }$ field variance factor. These are precisely (M.6.12n.11) and 2lambda'(k')a'(k'). The normalized-Haar convention means no unreported $L_{x}$-dependent Fourier normalization factor appears. The Gibbs marginal on retained real coefficients has quadratic action

$$
S_{\mathrm{low}}(f)=1/2 \sum_{\mathrm{retained}} f_i^2/[A \exp(-2g k_i^2)]
$$

and the product Gaussian normalizer. Under $f_{i}'=b^\chi f_{i}$ its Jacobian is $b^{\chi d_{\mathrm{retained}}}$, which changes the normalizer accordingly; the transformed action has covariance $a'$ exactly. Shell determinants are the explicit products $\sqrt{2\pi a_i}$ if using unnormalized Lebesgue density, or equal one when integrating individually normalized Gaussian factors. This records rather than discards normalization.

The maps compose: $R_{b_2}R_{b_1}=R_{b_1b_2}$, including the cutoff and changing circumference. Indeed the second shell criterion $b_1|k|\le\Lambda/b_2$ is exactly $|k|\le\Lambda/(b_1b_2)$; the parameter factors and field/time changes multiply. Floors in the finite integer mode count create no mismatch because the same inequality on the original integer $n$ is obtained. This is the ordinary elimination-plus-rescaling structure on a finite-volume running-parameter family. It is not asserted to have a nontrivial fixed point, nor is changing circumference hidden as an unchanged box.

**Predictive and physical intertwining.** For each retained mode,

$$
\begin{gathered}
\rho '(k')=\exp[-\lambda '(k')t_{\mathrm{lag}}']\\=\exp[-(D k^2+m)t_{\mathrm{lag}}]=\rho (k)
\end{gathered}
\tag{M.6.12n.12}
$$

Normalized source coefficients are unchanged up to the positive field factor; the same normalized quantizer labels therefore have exactly the same finite joint law on retained modes. K's activity test $\beta\rho^2>1$, scalar information optima, encoder gains and normalized predictive response all commute with this RG map on those retained modes. The physical encoder-intertwining claim uses k's chosen active-mode-only table sequence, not arbitrary approximate optimizers from section 9.4. When the eliminated shell is inactive, that chosen table ignores it exactly and remains the same dyadic table after marginalization. An arbitrary table depending on shell inputs instead induces the averaged retained kernel $\sum_{a_{\mathrm{shell}}}p(a_{\mathrm{shell}})T(z\mid a_{\mathrm{retained}},a_{\mathrm{shell}})$, which is generally not dyadic; no unchanged-table claim is made for it. The physical field reconstruction transforms by $b^\chi$ and $x'=x/b$, and the posterior covariance by the squared factor. If all active modes survive the eliminated shell, the total bottleneck optimum is unchanged; otherwise it changes by exactly the sum of the eliminated active scalar minima. There is no claim of invariance after discarding useful modes.

For the inactive-shell, chosen-table branch just specified, the physical compiler for the transformed finite law is the SAME marginal law compiler: sum out eliminated source/readout labels, retain the unchanged normalized encoders on the remaining modes, relabel physical field/length units and set the actual readout schedule to $t_0/b^{2}$. Formula (M.6.12l.6) then explicitly rescales the pulse energy ceiling as $b^{2}$ for fixed fractional timing. The source-preparation and payment times are supplied and counted separately. Thus the time rescaling is accompanied by an actual calibrated change in service duration and its Hamiltonian cost, rather than changing the symbol on an unchanged physical clock. Source probabilities and the Markov cut remain those of the resulting same-source marginal experiment. The transformed experiment recomputes $J$, $W$, its certified $L$ and all fee/reward gaps and funding. Payment-record distributions are NOT claimed identical under RG: the preserved statement is the same expected PCE identity (M.6.12m.9) with the transformed registered ledger. Arbitrary rational $b$ and computable parameters give effective descriptors; floor-boundary equality at a finite cutoff is resolved by exact registered cutoff data, such as integer $b,N$.

For the $\beta =64$ base point, modes $n=0$ and $n=\pm 1$ (two real modes) are active. Any cutoff $N\ge 2$ and integer $b$ with $N/b\ge 1$ retains the nonconstant effective field and satisfies this exact intertwining. Taking $N\to\infty$ with fixed $b$ gives a smooth continuum transformed field because $g'>0$; all k's trace-class and Sobolev-tail arguments apply with the flowed parameters. Tail errors and physical reconstructions are scaled by $b^{2\chi }$, and the normalized correlation sequence remains the corresponding retained sequence. No interacting-field property was smuggled into this free construction.

#### 12.2 Same-source finite-grid temporal realization

The original effective-field problem names the pair $X=F_{0}$,$Y=F_{1}$. The exact two-time compiler already realizes that target. For a stronger finite-grid source requirement, the same method extends without inventing a different process.

Fix a finite increasing physical grid $t_{0}<\dots<t_{s}$, cutoff N, and finite quantizers at every time. Define the source history law as the actual quantized pushforward of k's stationary OU process, whose normalized covariance is $\exp(-\lambda_i|t_j-t_k|/t_{\mathrm{unit}})$. Its finite Gaussian covariance is positive definite at distinct times, so every nonempty quantizer rectangle has positive mass and computable probability. Factor this EXACT law by its chronological conditional probabilities

$$
p(a_0,...,a_s)=p(a_0) \prod_{j=1}^s W_j(a_j|a_0,...,a_{j-1})
$$

At each slot implement the corresponding controlled reflection into a new source pointer and its fresh retained purifier, controlled by all previously retained source pointers. No first-order Markov property is asserted for the quantized labels. The full history, not just the last cell label, is kept. By the same proof as (M.6.12l.4), the retained grid law is exactly the original OU pushforward. An encoder at the initial time reads only its allowed initial pointer with independent randomization; later source controls do not read that encoder or its environments. Hence the original source history is unchanged by encoding, and the initial-source/readout Markov cut is maintained.

For any positive grid gaps, allocate a positive final subinterval of each gap to its source update, with idle time before it; an initial encoder slot can be allocated in the first gap before the first source update. Actual pointer availability is exactly at the registered times. All update Hamiltonian norms, finite history capacities, pulse durations and fresh blank stocks are computed by the same formulas as before and added to the ledger. Histories become large, but are finite at every resolution. The conditional tables do not depend on the chosen encoder, so these additional source-service resources remain class-wide. A separate finite-grid service tariff is funded and added to the common constant $C_{\mathrm{N}}$ if this stronger experiment is selected.

Marginalizing any grid law to a subgrid yields exactly that subgrid's OU quantized law whenever its quantizers agree; refining a quantizer pushes forward to the coarser one. Thus this is a consistent family of finite physical source experiments, not unrelated pair samplers. The continuum process is its specified OU projective limit; a finite-dimensional apparatus is not asserted to hold the entire infinite temporal transcript.

A path-space version also exists on every fixed finite time window. For a variance-one stationary scalar OU process with rate $\lambda$, divide time into at most $1+\lambda T$ intervals of length at most $1/\lambda$. Its time-rescaled representation $e^{-r}[\xi (0)+\sqrt{2} \int_0^r e^u dW_u]$, $r\le 1$, and the $L^{2}$ Doob inequality give

$$
E \sup_{\mathrm{interval}} |\xi |^2 \le 2+8(e^2-1) = 8e^2-6
$$

Summing interval maxima bounds E $\sup$_[0,T] |$\xi$|² by (8e²−6)(1+$\lambda$ T). Consequently the expected squared H-norm supremum of the omitted field tail is at most

$$
(8e^2-6) \sum_{\text{omitted }i} a_i(1+\lambda _i T),
$$

which tends to zero for the SAME smooth k source. For each finite retained set, continuity and this integrable supremum bound imply that its piecewise-constant grid interpolation converges in expected squared uniform H norm as mesh tends to zero. Quantizer errors add at most the sum of their gridwise squared reconstruction errors, so choose their common bound $\delta$ small enough that (#grid)(#retained modes)$\delta$ tends to zero. A diagonal choice of cutoff, grid and precision yields convergence in expected squared uniform H norm to the same OU field on the window. This is a constructive finite family with an analytic convergence proof; no uniform-resource or continuous finite-memory exact-attainment assertion is made.

The RG map in section 10 acts on this entire Gaussian history family: time grid points divide by $b^{2}$, spatial modes and amplitudes transform as there, and every finite covariance and chronological conditional source law is the exact transformed one. Thus a consumer requiring a genuine multi-time source may use this stronger optional branch rather than treating equality of two endpoints as a full-process proof.

**Continuum and finite-law conclusions.** The finite-law theorems give exact rational contact conditions and computable-law approximation, including the genuine obstruction to equality decisions for arbitrary computable-real input. The free Gaussian source below has an arbitrary-auxiliary optimum, effective response field, finite-law approximation and law-preserving controlled physical refinement. Funded service, representation and $\log$-score transfers realize the specified common-table PCE objective. Shell elimination and coordinate, field and time rescaling act on that same source and its clock; payment laws are recomputed after the transformation. The proper clock, supplied initial stocks and finite computable-real driven controls are premises. Exact Gaussian attainment is a limiting continuous-auxiliary result, while each finite-law approximation has its own finite register and resource invoice.

### M.6.13 WAY-PCE Conservation-Law Measurement Bound

<a id="definition-m613a-charge-covariant-measurement-branch"></a>**Definition M.6.13a (Charge-Covariant Measurement Branch).** Let $Q_S$ be a conserved system charge, let $Q_R$ be the apparatus or reference charge, and let
$$
Q_{\mathrm{tot}}=Q_S+Q_R.
$$
A finite measurement branch for an observable $A$ is $Q$-covariant when its interaction channel $\mathcal M$ is CPTP and satisfies
$$
\mathcal M\left(e^{-itQ_{\mathrm{tot}}}\rho e^{itQ_{\mathrm{tot}}}\right)
=
e^{-itQ_{\mathrm{tot}}}\mathcal M(\rho)e^{itQ_{\mathrm{tot}}}
\tag{M.6.13.1}
$$
For the finite reference system, let
$$
G_Q:=\overline{\{e^{-itQ_R}:t\in\mathbb R\}}\subseteq U(\mathcal H_R).
$$
This compact group has normalized Haar probability measure $d\nu(V)$. Define
$$
\mathcal A_Q(\sigma_R)
=
D\!\left(\sigma_R\Vert\mathcal G_Q(\sigma_R)\right),
\qquad
\mathcal G_Q(\sigma_R)
=
\int_{G_Q}V\sigma_RV^\dagger\,d\nu(V).
\tag{M.6.13.2}
$$
No commensurability of the charge eigenvalues is required. Finite-dimensional continuity extends covariance under all $e^{-itQ_R}$ to this closure.

Let $\epsilon(A;\mathcal M,\sigma_R)$ be the root-mean-square measurement error of $A$ on the branch's tested preparation family.

<a id="theorem-m613b-way-pce-asymmetry-measurement-bound"></a>**Theorem M.6.13b (WAY-PCE Asymmetry Measurement Bound).** On a finite charge-covariant branch:

1. For every $Q$-covariant CPTP map $\mathcal N$,
$$
\mathcal A_Q(\mathcal N(\sigma_R))
\le\mathcal A_Q(\sigma_R).
\tag{M.6.13.3}
$$

2. Suppose $\sigma_R$ is $Q_R$-invariant and a charge-conserving measurement dilation has classical pointer effects $Z_x$ satisfying $[Z_x,Q_R]=0$. Then every induced system effect $E_x$ commutes with $Q_S$. Consequently an exact sharp measurement of $A=\sum_xa_xP_x$ is possible on this branch only if $[P_x,Q_S]=0$ for every $x$, and hence $[A,Q_S]=0$.

3. Suppose the initial state is $\rho_S\otimes\sigma_R$, the interaction is unitary with $[U,Q_S+Q_R]=0$, the pointer observable $M$ satisfies $[M,Q_R]=0$, and
$$
N:=U^*(I\otimes M)U-A\otimes I,
\qquad
\epsilon(A)^2:=\operatorname{Tr}[(\rho_S\otimes\sigma_R)N^2].
$$
If $0<(\Delta_{\rho_S}Q_S)^2+(\Delta_{\sigma_R}Q_R)^2<\infty$, then the WAY-Ozawa bound (Ozawa 2002) is
$$
\epsilon(A)^2
\ge
\frac{|\operatorname{Tr}\rho_S[A,Q_S]|^2}
{4(\Delta_{\rho_S}Q_S)^2+4(\Delta_{\sigma_R}Q_R)^2}.
\tag{M.6.13.4}
$$

*Proof.* Covariance gives $\mathcal N\mathcal G_Q=\mathcal G_Q\mathcal N$. Data processing for relative entropy therefore yields
$$
D(\mathcal N\sigma_R\Vert\mathcal G_Q\mathcal N\sigma_R)
=D(\mathcal N\sigma_R\Vert\mathcal N\mathcal G_Q\sigma_R)
\le D(\sigma_R\Vert\mathcal G_Q\sigma_R),
$$
proving item 1.

For item 2, the induced effect is
$$
E_x=\operatorname{Tr}_R[(I\otimes\sigma_R)U^*(I\otimes Z_x)U].
$$
Using invariance of $\sigma_R$, $[U,Q_S+Q_R]=0$, and $[Z_x,Q_R]=0$ gives
$$
e^{-itQ_S}E_xe^{itQ_S}=E_x
$$
for every $t$, hence $[E_x,Q_S]=0$. Exact sharp measurement requires $E_x=P_x$, proving item 2.

For item 3, charge conservation and the Yanase condition give
$$
[N,Q_S+Q_R]=-[A,Q_S]\otimes I.
$$
Robertson's inequality in the product input state, together with $(\Delta N)^2\le\langle N^2\rangle=\epsilon(A)^2$, gives
$$
\epsilon(A)^2\,\Delta(Q_S+Q_R)^2
\ge\frac14|\operatorname{Tr}\rho_S[A,Q_S]|^2.
$$
Product inputs have
$$
\Delta(Q_S+Q_R)^2=(\Delta_{\rho_S}Q_S)^2+(\Delta_{\sigma_R}Q_R)^2.
$$
Division by the positive finite variance proves (M.6.13.4). ∎

<a id="lemma-m613b1-retained-neutral-profile-entropy"></a>**Lemma M.6.13b.1 (Retained Neutral-Profile Entropy).** Fix a normalized scalar profile
$$
f(x)=(x-a)^6(b-x)^6g(x),\qquad g>0,\quad g\in C^3([a,b]),
$$
zero extended outside $[a,b]$. Fix $d\ge1$ and a $C^3$ density-matrix field $\rho(x)\in M_d$ with $\rho(x)\succeq m_0I_d$ for one $m_0>0$. The following finite reference has physical dimension $dN_h$, global rank $d$, charge-pinched rank $dN_h$, and the exact asymmetry in (M.6.13b.1.2), with $\mathcal A_Q$ as in Definition M.6.13a.

*Construction and proof.* Set $Z_h=\sum_nf(nh)$, $p_n=f(nh)/Z_h$, $S_h=\{n:f(nh)>0\}$ and $N_h=|S_h|$. For sufficiently small $0<h<b-a$, $Z_h>0$. Define
$$
\mathcal K_h=\bigoplus_{n\in S_h}\mathbb C^d,\qquad
Q_h=\bigoplus_{n\in S_h}nI_d,\qquad
\boxed{\sigma_h(n,l)=\sqrt{p_np_l}\sqrt{\rho(nh)}\sqrt{\rho(lh)}.}
\tag{M.6.13b.1.1}
$$
Let $T_h:\mathcal K_h\to\mathbb C^d$ have block columns
$\sqrt{p_n}\sqrt{\rho(nh)}$. Then $\sigma_h=T_h^*T_h\succeq0$,
$\operatorname{Tr}\sigma_h=1$, and $T_hT_h^*=\bar\rho_h=\sum_np_n\rho(nh)\succeq m_0I_d$.
The nonzero global spectrum is exactly that of $\bar\rho_h$. The charge pinching has blocks $p_n\rho(nh)$. This proves every dimension and rank statement and the exact entropy identity
$$
\boxed{\mathcal A_Q(\sigma_h)
=H(p_h)+\sum_np_nS(\rho(nh))-S(\bar\rho_h).}
\tag{M.6.13b.1.2}
$$
All $dN_h$ charge-sector degrees of freedom remain in the reference carrier.

<a id="corollary-m613c-compatibility-with-blackwell-pce-classicality"></a>**Corollary M.6.13c (Compatibility with Blackwell-PCE Classicality).** The classical record selected by Theorem M.6.11b reports information acquired by the registered measurement channel. On the product-input, charge-conserving unitary and charge-commuting-pointer branch of Theorem M.6.13b, its item 2 forbids exact sharp measurement of a noncommuting observable with a charge-invariant reference. Under the additional noise and positive finite variance hypotheses of item 3, the error obeys (M.6.13.4), including when the reference has nonzero asymmetry. Nonzero $\mathcal A_Q$ is neither a sufficient measurement certificate nor an exemption from that quantitative bound.

*Proof.* Theorem M.6.11b post-processes the actual classical record and cannot supply information absent from its channel. Items 2 and 3 of Theorem M.6.13b then apply under their respective implementation hypotheses. Mere CPTP covariance does not supply those unitary, input or pointer hypotheses. $\square$

<a id="definition-m613d-finite-frameness-ledger"></a>**Definition M.6.13d (Finite Frameness Ledger).** Let $G$ be a compact finite-response symmetry group represented by unitaries $U_g$ on a retained finite algebra, and let
$$
\mathcal T_G(\rho)
=
\int_G U_g\rho U_g^\dagger\,dg
\tag{M.6.13d.1}
$$
be the Haar-twirling channel. The finite frameness of $\rho$ relative to $G$ is
$$
\mathcal F_G(\rho)
:=
S(\mathcal T_G(\rho))-S(\rho)
=
D\bigl(\rho\Vert\mathcal T_G(\rho)\bigr).
\tag{M.6.13d.2}
$$
The ledger measures asymmetry along the orbit $g\mapsto U_g\rho U_g^\dagger$. It is not a criterion for all physical information carried by a state or charge sector. Operational use of an orbit label additionally requires a registered finite protocol and its reference resources.

<a id="theorem-m613e-finite-frameness-and-symmetry-orbit-labels"></a>**Theorem M.6.13e (Finite Frameness and Symmetry-Orbit Labels).** For the continuous finite-dimensional unitary representation in Definition M.6.13d,
$$
\mathcal F_G(\rho)\ge0,
\tag{M.6.13e.1}
$$
and
$$
\mathcal F_G(\rho)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\rho=\mathcal T_G(\rho).
\tag{M.6.13e.2}
$$
In this zero-frameness case, changing only the orbit parameter $g$ leaves the input state identical and hence changes no protocol response. PPI/PCE can remove that response-null orbit label. Distinct invariant states or charge sectors can nevertheless carry distinguishable information with zero frameness. Nonzero frameness records an asymmetry resource; it does not by itself certify that a retained protocol can read a proposed label. Theorem M.6.13b gives the charge-measurement restrictions under its separate input, dilation, pointer and variance hypotheses.

*Proof.* Normalized Haar averaging is CPTP, trace preserving, idempotent and invariant under the group. Put $\tau=\mathcal T_G(\rho)$ and $S=\operatorname{supp}\tau$. If $v\in\ker\tau$, then
$$
0=\langle v,\tau v\rangle
=\int_G\langle U_g^\dagger v,\rho U_g^\dagger v\rangle\,dg.
$$
The integrand is continuous and nonnegative, so it vanishes everywhere, including at the identity. Thus $\rho v=0$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq S$. The invariant operator $\tau$ has invariant support $S$ and a bounded logarithm on $S$. Using that logarithm, extended by zero on $S^\perp$, the Haar trace identity gives
$$
\operatorname{Tr}\rho\log(\tau|_S)
=
\operatorname{Tr}\tau\log(\tau|_S)
=
-S(\tau).
$$
Consequently,
$$
D(\rho\Vert\tau)
=-S(\rho)-\operatorname{Tr}\rho\log(\tau|_S)
=S(\tau)-S(\rho).
$$
Finite-dimensional relative-entropy positivity and its equality condition prove (M.6.13e.1)–(M.6.13e.2). Since $\tau$ is invariant, $\rho=\tau$ makes the entire group orbit constant. This establishes the response-null statement for changes of the orbit parameter alone.

For the distinction from invariant information, take $Q=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$ and $\rho_0=|0\rangle\langle0|$, $\rho_1=|1\rangle\langle1|$. Both states are invariant under $e^{-itQ}$ and have zero frameness, but the charge measurement distinguishes them perfectly. They therefore cannot be identified merely because their frameness values vanish. The charge instance uses the normalized twirl over the compact closure specified in Definition M.6.13a; its measurement bounds retain all hypotheses of Theorem M.6.13b. $\square$

<a id="theorem-m613f-zero-asymmetry-error-floor-and-the-asymmetry-cost-of-beating-it"></a>**Theorem M.6.13f (Zero-Asymmetry Error Floor and the Asymmetry Cost of Beating It).** Work on the finite branch of item 3 of Theorem M.6.13b: finite-dimensional $\mathcal H_S$ and $\mathcal H_R$, a unitary $U$ with $[U,Q_S+Q_R]=0$, a pointer $M=M^*$ with $[M,Q_R]=0$, a reference state $\sigma_R$ and $A=A^*$ on $\mathcal H_S$. Put
$$
\Phi_{\sigma_R}(Y):=\operatorname{Tr}_R\bigl[(I\otimes\sigma_R)U^*(I\otimes Y)U\bigr],
\qquad
E^{(k)}:=\Phi_{\sigma_R}(M^k),
$$
let $\epsilon(A;\rho_S)^2:=\operatorname{Tr}[(\rho_S\otimes\sigma_R)N^2]$ with $N$ as in item 3 of Theorem M.6.13b, let $\epsilon_\infty(A):=\sup_{\rho_S}\epsilon(A;\rho_S)$ over all system states, and define
$$
d_Q(A):=\min\{\|A-B\|:B=B^*,\ [B,Q_S]=0\}.
\tag{M.6.13f.1}
$$
1. $\epsilon(A;\rho_S)^2=\operatorname{Tr}\rho_S\bigl[(A-E^{(1)})^2+E^{(2)}-(E^{(1)})^2\bigr]$ with $E^{(2)}\ge(E^{(1)})^2$, so $\epsilon_\infty(A)\ge\|A-E^{(1)}\|$.
2. If $\mathcal A_Q(\sigma_R)=0$, then $[E^{(1)},Q_S]=0$ and $\epsilon_\infty(A)\ge d_Q(A)$.
3. The floor is attained with zero asymmetry. If $B_*=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}b_kP_k$ is the spectral decomposition of a minimizer of (M.6.13f.1), then $\mathcal H_R=\mathbb C^K$, $Q_R=0$, $\sigma_R=|0\rangle\langle0|$, $U=\sum_kP_k\otimes X^k$ with the cyclic shift $X|m\rangle=|m+1\bmod K\rangle$, and $M=\sum_kb_k|k\rangle\langle k|$ satisfy every hypothesis, with $E^{(1)}=B_*$, $E^{(2)}=B_*^2$ and $\epsilon_\infty(A)=d_Q(A)$.
4. For every reference state,
$$
\epsilon_\infty(A)\ge d_Q(A)-\|M\|\,\|\sigma_R-\mathcal G_Q(\sigma_R)\|_1\ge d_Q(A)-\|M\|\sqrt{2\mathcal A_Q(\sigma_R)}.
\tag{M.6.13f.2}
$$
Hence, for $M\ne0$, every realization with $\epsilon_\infty(A)<d_Q(A)$ has $\mathcal A_Q(\sigma_R)\ge(d_Q(A)-\epsilon_\infty(A))^2/(2\|M\|^2)>0$.
5. If $Q_S$ has exactly two distinct eigenvalues, then $d_Q(A)=\|A_{\mathrm{off}}\|$, where $A_{\mathrm{off}}$ is the part of $A$ between the two charge sectors, and the charge-diagonal part of $A$ attains (M.6.13f.1). For a qubit with $Q_S=|1\rangle\langle1|$ and $A=\sigma_x$, $d_Q(\sigma_x)=1=\|\sigma_x\|$: no realization with a charge-invariant reference has worst-case error below that of the constant pointer $M=0$.

*Proof.* Put $Z_k:=U^*(I\otimes M^k)U$, an operator on $\mathcal H_S\otimes\mathcal H_R$, so that $N=Z_1-A\otimes I$, $Z_1^2=Z_2$ and $E^{(k)}=\operatorname{Tr}_R[(I\otimes\sigma_R)Z_k]$. For every operator $X$ on $\mathcal H_S$ and every joint operator $Z$, $\operatorname{Tr}[(X\otimes\sigma_R)Z]=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[X\operatorname{Tr}_R[(I\otimes\sigma_R)Z]\bigr]$. Expanding $N^2=Z_2-(A\otimes I)Z_1-Z_1(A\otimes I)+A^2\otimes I$ and applying this identity with $X=\rho_S$, $\rho_SA$ and $A\rho_S$ gives $\epsilon(A;\rho_S)^2=\operatorname{Tr}\rho_S(A^2-AE^{(1)}-E^{(1)}A+E^{(2)})$, which is item 1's identity. The map $\Phi_{\sigma_R}$ is unital and completely positive, so Kadison's inequality gives $\Phi_{\sigma_R}(M^2)\ge\Phi_{\sigma_R}(M)^2$. For self-adjoint $C$ on $\mathcal H_S$, the supremum of $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_SC$ over states is the largest eigenvalue of $C$, and the largest eigenvalue of $(A-E^{(1)})^2$ is $\|A-E^{(1)}\|^2$.

For item 2, $\mathcal A_Q(\sigma_R)=0$ means $\sigma_R=\mathcal G_Q(\sigma_R)$, so $\sigma_R$ commutes with every $e^{-\mathrm itQ_R}$. The operator $Z_1$ commutes with $e^{-\mathrm it(Q_S\otimes I+I\otimes Q_R)}$, so $(e^{\mathrm itQ_S}\otimes I)Z_1(e^{-\mathrm itQ_S}\otimes I)=(I\otimes e^{-\mathrm itQ_R})Z_1(I\otimes e^{\mathrm itQ_R})$. Taking $\operatorname{Tr}_R$ against $I\otimes\sigma_R$ and moving the reference unitaries onto the invariant $\sigma_R$ gives $e^{\mathrm itQ_S}E^{(1)}e^{-\mathrm itQ_S}=E^{(1)}$ for every $t$. Hence $E^{(1)}$ is admissible in (M.6.13f.1), and item 1 gives the floor. The minimum in (M.6.13f.1) exists because the admissible set is a finite-dimensional real subspace and $B\mapsto\|A-B\|$ is continuous and coercive.

For item 3, each $P_k$ commutes with $Q_S$, so $[U,Q_S\otimes I]=\sum_k[P_k,Q_S]\otimes X^k=0$ while $Q_R=0$, and $U$ is unitary because the $P_k$ are orthogonal and sum to $I$. The state $|0\rangle\langle0|$ commutes with $Q_R=0$ and has zero asymmetry. Since $P_kP_l=\delta_{kl}P_k$ and $\langle0|X^{-k}M^mX^k|0\rangle=b_k^m$, one gets $E^{(m)}=\sum_kb_k^mP_k=B_*^m$. Item 1 then gives $\epsilon(A;\rho_S)^2=\operatorname{Tr}\rho_S(A-B_*)^2$ and $\epsilon_\infty(A)=\|A-B_*\|=d_Q(A)$.

For item 4, the twirl $\mathcal G_Q(\sigma_R)$ is invariant, so item 2 places $\Phi_{\mathcal G_Q(\sigma_R)}(M)$ in the admissible set of (M.6.13f.1). For unit vectors $\phi,\psi$ and Hermitian $\Delta$, $\langle\phi,\operatorname{Tr}_R[(I\otimes\Delta)Z_1]\psi\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}[(|\psi\rangle\langle\phi|\otimes\Delta)Z_1]$, whose modulus is at most $\|Z_1\|\,\|\Delta\|_1=\|M\|\,\|\Delta\|_1$. With $\Delta=\sigma_R-\mathcal G_Q(\sigma_R)$ and item 1, $\epsilon_\infty(A)\ge\|A-\Phi_{\mathcal G_Q(\sigma_R)}(M)\|-\|M\|\,\|\Delta\|_1\ge d_Q(A)-\|M\|\,\|\Delta\|_1$. Pinsker's inequality $\|\Delta\|_1\le\sqrt{2D(\sigma_R\Vert\mathcal G_Q(\sigma_R))}$ gives (M.6.13f.2), and rearrangement gives the asymmetry bound.

For item 5, let $\Pi_0,\Pi_1$ be the two charge projectors and $V=\Pi_0-\Pi_1$. Every admissible $B$ is block diagonal, and $A_{\mathrm{off}}=\tfrac12[(A-B)-V(A-B)V]$, so $\|A_{\mathrm{off}}\|\le\|A-B\|$, with equality for $B=\Pi_0A\Pi_0+\Pi_1A\Pi_1$. For $\sigma_x$ and $Q_S=|1\rangle\langle1|$ the charge-diagonal part vanishes and $\|A_{\mathrm{off}}\|=\|\sigma_x\|=1$, while the constant pointer $M=0$ gives $E^{(1)}=E^{(2)}=0$ and $\epsilon_\infty(\sigma_x)=1$. ∎

**Measurement scope.** The zero-asymmetry floor $d_Q(A)$ and bound (M.6.13f.2) apply to every finite charge-conserving unitary model with a charge-commuting pointer, input-independent reference and all system input states. Theorem M.6.13g gives a bound independent of pointer norm. Theorems M.6.13h–M.6.13l determine the qubit entropy infimum and finite nonattainment; Theorem M.6.13n realizes that infimum with all physical spin factors counted. Theorem M.6.13o transfers finite-apparatus optimization to physical spin systems. The results below give the stated spin-one and spin-three-halves classes and quantitative bounds; the unrestricted spin-one entropy frontier remains open.

<a id="theorem-m613g-uniform-asymmetry-cost-independent-of-pointer-size"></a>**Theorem M.6.13g (Uniform Asymmetry Cost Independent of Pointer Size).** Work on the complete finite measurement class of Theorem M.6.13f: self-adjoint system and reference charges $Q_S,Q_R$, a unitary $U$ commuting with their additive total, a self-adjoint reference pointer $M$ commuting with $Q_R$, and a fixed reference state $\sigma_R$ independent of the tested system input. Every system density operator is tested. Neutral ancillary factors and their correlations with the reference are included in $R$ whenever they are present in the source. Set
$$
\epsilon=\epsilon_\infty(A),\qquad d=d_Q(A),\qquad
\tau_R=\mathcal G_Q(\sigma_R),\qquad
\mathcal A=\mathcal A_Q(\sigma_R)=D(\sigma_R\Vert\tau_R).
$$
Here $d_Q(A)$ is the distance to the full self-adjoint charge commutant in (M.6.13f.1). Then for $0\le\epsilon<d$,
$$
\boxed{\mathcal A\ge
-\log\left[1-\frac{(d-\epsilon)^2}{4(d+\epsilon)^2}\right]
\ge\frac{(d-\epsilon)^2}{4(d+\epsilon)^2}>0.}
\tag{M.6.13g.1}
$$
This bound holds without a bound on pointer norm, reference dimension, neutral ancillary dimension or charge variance. It is invariant under a common nonzero affine change of the target and pointer units. The hypothesis $\epsilon<d$ ensures $d>0$ and a logarithm argument in $[3/4,1)$; when $d=0$ the below-floor regime is empty.

For $a\ge0$, put
$$
R(a)=\frac{\max\{1-2\sqrt{1-e^{-a}},\,0\}}
{1+2\sqrt{1-e^{-a}}}.
\tag{M.6.13g.2}
$$
Every model in the stated class obeys $\epsilon\ge dR(\mathcal A)$. In particular, fix $Q_S,A$ and allow all finite reference charges, states, conserving interactions and Yanase pointers. Their error frontier at asymmetry budget $a$ satisfies
$$
 dR(a)\le
\inf_{\mathcal A_Q(\sigma_R)\le a}\epsilon_\infty(A)
\le d,
\qquad
\lim_{a\downarrow0}\inf_{\mathcal A_Q(\sigma_R)\le a}\epsilon_\infty(A)=d.
\tag{M.6.13g.3}
$$
Thus growing finite reference or pointer resources cannot retain a fixed improvement below $d$ while their full reference asymmetry tends to zero. Theorem M.6.13f's neutral-reference construction attains the upper endpoint $d$.

*Proof.* A minimizer $C_*$ in (M.6.13f.1) exists, is self-adjoint and commutes with $Q_S$. Put
$$
B=U^*(I\otimes M)U,\qquad
A_0=A-C_*,\qquad B_0=B-C_*\otimes I,
\qquad c=d+\epsilon.
$$
Then $\|A_0\|=d$, $B_0$ commutes with $Q_S+Q_R$, and $B_0-A_0\otimes I=B-A\otimes I$ is exactly the original noise operator. This subtraction is an analytical proof device. It changes neither the physical pointer nor the given measurement protocol.

For any reference state $\omega$, let
$$
\mathcal E_\omega(Z)=\operatorname{Tr}_R[(I\otimes\omega)Z].
$$
This is a unital completely positive conditional-expectation map, as seen by inserting $\sqrt\omega$ on both sides before the partial trace. For every system unit vector $\psi$ and a purification $s$ of $\sigma_R$, with identity extensions on its auxiliary factor, the noise definition and triangle inequality give
$$
\|B_0(\psi\otimes s)\|
\le\|(B_0-A_0\otimes I)(\psi\otimes s)\|+
\|(A_0\otimes I)(\psi\otimes s)\|
\le\epsilon+d=c.
$$
Because every system input is tested, this is the operator inequality $\mathcal E_{\sigma_R}(B_0^2)\le c^2I$.

Total-charge invariance supplies the second reference moment rather than an estimate involving $\|M\|$. For every real $t$, covariance and cyclicity of the reference trace give
$$
\mathcal E_{e^{-itQ_R}\sigma_Re^{itQ_R}}(Z)
=e^{-itQ_S}\mathcal E_{\sigma_R}(Z)e^{itQ_S}
\quad\text{whenever}\quad [Z,Q_S+Q_R]=0.
$$
Average in $t$. In finite dimension, each off-charge matrix entry has a nonzero-frequency exponential and averages to zero; the result is the same spectral pinching as the compact-closure Haar twirl. Consequently
$$
\mathcal E_{\tau_R}(B_0^k)
=\mathcal G_{Q_S}\bigl(\mathcal E_{\sigma_R}(B_0^k)\bigr)
\quad(k=1,2),\qquad
\mathcal E_{\tau_R}(B_0^2)\le c^2I.
\tag{M.6.13g.4}
$$
The first conditional mean therefore lies in the system charge commutant. The argument admits every finite degeneracy and every real charge spectrum.

Write
$$
f=\|\sqrt{\sigma_R}\sqrt{\tau_R}\|_1
=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{\tau_R^{1/2}\sigma_R\tau_R^{1/2}}.
$$
Polar decomposition supplies purifications $s,t$ of $\sigma_R,\tau_R$ on one finite ancillary space with real nonnegative overlap $\langle s,t\rangle=f$: vectorize their square-root amplitude matrices and choose the ancillary unitary attaining the trace norm. This uses purifications as vectors for the proof, without supplying a new physical source resource. For fixed system unit vector $\psi$, let $x=\psi\otimes s$ and $y=\psi\otimes t$. Equations (M.6.13g.4) and the preceding moment bound give $\|B_0x\|,\|B_0y\|\le c$.

If $f=1$, the two unit vectors agree and their expectation difference is zero. If $0\le f<1$, define the orthonormal vectors
$$
z_+=\frac{x+y}{\sqrt{2(1+f)}},\qquad
z_-=\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{2(1-f)}}.
$$
Their expectation difference and average second moment are
$$
\begin{aligned}
\langle x,B_0x\rangle-\langle y,B_0y\rangle
&=2\sqrt{1-f^2}\,\operatorname{Re}\langle z_+,B_0z_-\rangle,\\
\frac{\|B_0x\|^2+\|B_0y\|^2}{2}
&=\frac{1+f}{2}\|B_0z_+\|^2+
\frac{1-f}{2}\|B_0z_-\|^2.
\end{aligned}
$$
Hermiticity implies that each squared norm on the right is at least $|\langle z_+,B_0z_-\rangle|^2$. Their coefficients sum to one, so the cross element has modulus at most $c$. Taking the supremum over system unit vectors, using that both conditional means are Hermitian, proves
$$
\|\mathcal E_{\sigma_R}(B_0)-\mathcal E_{\tau_R}(B_0)\|
\le2c\sqrt{1-f^2}.
\tag{M.6.13g.5}
$$
Theorem M.6.13f(1), unchanged by the analytical subtraction, gives $\|A_0-\mathcal E_{\sigma_R}(B_0)\|\le\epsilon$. Translation by $C_*$ preserves distance to the commutant, so $d_Q(A_0)=d$. Since $\mathcal E_{\tau_R}(B_0)$ commutes with $Q_S$, the triangle inequality yields
$$
d-\epsilon\le2(d+\epsilon)\sqrt{1-f^2}.
\tag{M.6.13g.6}
$$

For completeness, the entropy comparison can be established on the same finite matrices. By Theorem M.6.13e, $\operatorname{supp}\sigma_R\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\tau_R$. Restrict to that latter support, on which $\tau_R$ is strictly positive, and set
$$
L=\tau_R^{-1/2}
(\tau_R^{1/2}\sigma_R\tau_R^{1/2})^{1/2}
\tau_R^{-1/2}.
$$
Then $L\ge0$, $L\tau_RL=\sigma_R$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(L\tau_R)=f$. Measure an orthonormal eigenbasis of $L$, with eigenvalues $l_i$. Its two probability laws satisfy $q_i=\langle i|\tau_R|i\rangle>0$ and $p_i=\langle i|\sigma_R|i\rangle=l_i^2q_i$. Hence $\sum_i\sqrt{p_iq_i}=\sum_il_iq_i=f$. Relative-entropy data processing for this complete measurement, followed by classical Jensen on the indices with $p_i>0$, gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
D(\sigma_R\Vert\tau_R)
&\ge D(p\Vert q)
=-2\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\log\sqrt{q_i/p_i}\\
&\ge-2\log\sum_i\sqrt{p_iq_i}
=-2\log f.
\end{aligned}
\tag{M.6.13g.7}
$$
Zero $p_i$ terms have their usual zero contribution. The support restriction covers singular references, and $f>0$ for these normalized supported states. Thus $f^2\ge e^{-\mathcal A}$. Under $\epsilon<d$, (M.6.13g.6) gives
$$
\frac{(d-\epsilon)^2}{4(d+\epsilon)^2}
\le1-f^2\le1-e^{-\mathcal A}.
$$
Taking $-\log$ proves the first inequality of (M.6.13g.1); $-\log(1-z)\ge z$ proves the second.

Solving (M.6.13g.6) with $f^2\ge e^{-\mathcal A}$ for $\epsilon$ gives (M.6.13g.2)'s bound when its numerator is positive. When the numerator is nonpositive, nonnegativity of the RMS error supplies the same statement. Models with $\epsilon\ge d$ satisfy it as well because $0\le R(a)\le1$. The function $R$ is nonincreasing and continuous at zero with $R(0)=1$. The zero-asymmetry model of Theorem M.6.13f(3) belongs to every budget $a\ge0$ and attains $d$, while every model with asymmetry at most $a$ has error at least $dR(a)$. This proves (M.6.13g.3), including the $d=0$ case. Under $(A,M)\mapsto(sA+tI,sM+tI)$ with $s\ne0$, the noise and commutant distance scale by $|s|$, whereas the reference asymmetry is unchanged; the dimensionless ratio in (M.6.13g.1) is therefore invariant. $\square$

**Finite witnesses and distance calibration.** The below-floor domain is nonempty. Take a system qubit and a reference qubit with charges $|1\rangle\langle1|$, target $A=X_S$ and reference $|+\rangle_R$. The invariant observable
$$
O=|01\rangle\langle10|+|10\rangle\langle01|
$$
has spectral projectors $P_0,P_+,P_-$ at eigenvalues $0,+1,-1$. Add a neutral qutrit pointer initialized in $|0\rangle$, let $V$ be its cyclic shift, and use $U=P_0\otimes I+P_+\otimes V+P_-\otimes V^2$ with pointer labels $(0,+1,-1)$. Every projector commutes with the additive charge, and the pointer is neutral, so this is an admitted conserving model. Its ready-state pointer moments are $O,O^2$; tracing the charged reference gives
$$
E^{(1)}=\tfrac12X_S,\qquad E^{(2)}=\tfrac12I_S,
\qquad\epsilon_\infty^2=\tfrac12,
\qquad d_Q(X_S)=1,
\qquad\mathcal A_Q=\ln2.
\tag{M.6.13g.8}
$$
The noise identity of Theorem M.6.13f verifies the all-input error, rather than one tested state. A further neutral pointer level with arbitrary label $K>1$, initially unused and left invariant by $V\oplus1$, leaves these moments and the asymmetry unchanged while its pointer norm becomes $K$. The new bound remains fixed along this entire family.

The distance in (M.6.13g.1) is essential. For $Q_S=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,2)$ and $A=\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}-I_3$, the commutant is the diagonal algebra. Averaging any diagonal competitor over coordinate permutations cannot increase its distance to this permutation-invariant $A$, and gives a scalar competitor. The eigenvalues of $A$ are $2,-1,-1$, so
$$
d_Q(A)=\tfrac32\quad\text{at}\quad C_*=\tfrac12I_3,
\qquad \|A-\mathcal G_{Q_S}(A)\|=2.
\tag{M.6.13g.9}
$$
A constant pointer $1/2$ attains error $3/2$ with zero asymmetry. Substituting the discarded-block norm $2$ for $d_Q(A)$ would falsely place this invariant realization below its error floor. The original all-system-state premise is also necessary: testing only one eigenstate of a noncommuting target lets its constant eigenvalue pointer have zero error on that state with zero asymmetry.

<a id="theorem-m613h-exact-qubit-measurement-and-entropy-reduction"></a>**Theorem M.6.13h (Exact Qubit Measurement and Entropy Reduction).** Fix the registered system charge $Q_S=|1\rangle\langle1|$ and target $X_S=|0\rangle\langle1|+|1\rangle\langle0|$. Use the complete finite measurement class of Theorem M.6.13g, with every system input tested and natural-$\log$ reference asymmetry. For a finite reference charge $Q$ and state $\sigma$, put $\tau=\mathcal G_Q(\sigma)$. Diagonalize each charge block of $\tau$, write its eigenvalues as $p_{q\alpha}$, and set
$$
c_{q\alpha\beta}=\langle q+1,\alpha|\sigma|q,\beta\rangle,
\qquad
F_\sigma(t)=\sum_{q,\alpha,\beta}
\frac{|c_{q\alpha\beta}|^2}{t p_{q+1,\alpha}+(1-t)p_{q,\beta}},
\quad 0\le t\le1.
\tag{M.6.13h.1}
$$
Only pairs of existing charge sectors separated by one occur in this sum. A term with zero numerator and denominator is zero. Positivity of $\sigma$ makes every coherence incident to a zero $p$ vanish.

Allowing a pure neutral pointer enlargement, the exact least squared error at this fixed reference is
$$
e_Q(\sigma)^2=1-\min_{0\le t\le1}F_\sigma(t).
\tag{M.6.13h.2}
$$
Define the basis-independent quantity
$$
\eta_Q(\sigma)=F_\sigma(1/2)
=\max_{[Q,L]=L}\operatorname{Tr}\sigma H_L,
\quad H_L=L+L^*-K_L,
\quad K_L=\frac{LL^*+L^*L}{2}.
\tag{M.6.13h.3}
$$
The maximum has a supported contraction $L$, and $0\le\eta_Q(\sigma)\le1$. Reflection and a neutral flag produce a finite reference with the same asymmetry and least squared error $1-\eta_Q(\sigma)$.

For $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\mathfrak A(\epsilon)$ be the infimum of $\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)$ over all admitted finite reference charges, states, conserving interactions and Yanase pointers with exact worst-case error $\epsilon$. Then
$$
\mathfrak A(\epsilon)
=\inf_{\substack{Q,\sigma\ \mathrm{finite}\\
\eta_Q(\sigma)\ge1-\epsilon^2}}\mathcal A_Q(\sigma).
\tag{M.6.13h.4}
$$
Replacing exact error by error at most $\epsilon$ gives the same infimum. Arbitrary real charge spectra, degeneracies, mixed references and neutral ancillary factors are included.

*Proof.* Every measurement gives an invariant self-adjoint Heisenberg pointer $B=U^*(I\otimes M)U$ on system and reference. Conversely, write any invariant $B$ as $\sum_j b_j\Pi_j$ and append a neutral pointer with ready state $|0\rangle$, cyclic shift $V$ and observable $M_P=\sum_j b_j|j\rangle\langle j|$. The unitary $\sum_j\Pi_j\otimes V^j$ conserves charge, and its ready-state compression of the first two pointer powers is $B$ and $B^2$. Its worst-case noise is therefore that of $B$. Tensoring a pure neutral state preserves reference asymmetry.

Let $Z_S=|0\rangle\langle0|-|1\rangle\langle1|$. Both $B$ and $-Z_SB Z_S$ are invariant. Since $Z_SX_SZ_S=-X_S$, their noise squares have system conditional means $K$ and $Z_SKZ_S$. Operator convexity of the square shows that replacing $B$ by $(B-Z_SB Z_S)/2$ cannot increase the largest eigenvalue of the conditional noise square. Thus the optimum has the form
$$
B_L=\begin{pmatrix}0&L\\L^*&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad [Q,L]=L.
$$
Its two noise eigenvalues are
$$
k_0(L)=1+\operatorname{Tr}\sigma LL^*-2\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}\sigma L,
\qquad
k_1(L)=1+\operatorname{Tr}\sigma L^*L-2\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}\sigma L.
\tag{M.6.13h.5}
$$
The all-input squared error is exactly $\max\{k_0,k_1\}$.

The convex quadratic epigraph problem minimizing this maximum has a strictly feasible epigraph variable. Its Lagrange multipliers are $t,1-t\ge0$, so finite-dimensional convex duality gives
$$
\min_L\max\{k_0(L),k_1(L)\}
=\max_{0\le t\le1}\min_L\{t k_0(L)+(1-t)k_1(L)\}.
$$
Each raising entry $z=L_{q+1,\alpha;q,\beta}$ contributes $a|z|^2-2\operatorname{Re}(\overline c z)$, with $a=t p_{q+1,\alpha}+(1-t)p_{q,\beta}$. Its minimum is $-|c|^2/a$. The zero-support convention covers both endpoints. A minimizing $L$ exists: discard entries whose two support weights vanish; the average of the two quadratic objectives is coercive on the remaining entries. This proves (M.6.13h.2). Setting $t=1/2$ proves (M.6.13h.3), with maximizing entries $2c/(p_{q+1,\alpha}+p_{q,\beta})$ and zero on the kernels.

The contraction claim also holds without choosing block eigenbases. For adjacent blocks write $P=\sigma_{q+1,q+1}$, $R=\sigma_{q,q}$ and $C=\sigma_{q+1,q}$. Block positivity gives $C=P^{1/2}VR^{1/2}$ for a contraction $V$. On the supports, the maximizing block is the Sylvester solution
$$
PL+LR=2C,\qquad
L=2\int_0^\infty e^{-sP}C e^{-sR}\,ds.
\tag{M.6.13h.6}
$$
Cauchy--Schwarz in this $\int$ bounds $|\langle x,Ly\rangle|$ by
$$
2\left(\int_0^\infty\|P^{1/2}e^{-sP}x\|^2ds\right)^{1/2}
\left(\int_0^\infty\|R^{1/2}e^{-sR}y\|^2ds\right)^{1/2}
\le\|x\|\,\|y\|.
$$
The two integrals are half the squared norms of the corresponding support projections. Distinct raising blocks have orthogonal domains and ranges; extending by zero therefore gives a contraction on the complete reference. Positivity of the average noise in (M.6.13h.5) gives $\eta_Q\le1$, and $L=0$ gives $\eta_Q\ge0$.

For reflection balancing, take $\widehat\sigma=(\sigma\oplus\sigma)/2$ and $\widehat Q=Q\oplus(-Q)$, retaining the direct-sum label as a neutral flag. Twirling preserves the two sectors, and the common flag entropy cancels in $S(\mathcal G\widehat\sigma)-S(\widehat\sigma)$, so $\mathcal A_{\widehat Q}(\widehat\sigma)=\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)$. Its function in (M.6.13h.1) is $[F_\sigma(t)+F_\sigma(1-t)]/2$. Each reciprocal-affine summand is convex, so this reflection-symmetric function is minimized at $1/2$. Equation (M.6.13h.2) gives the asserted error.

Every original model with error at most $\epsilon$ has $\eta_Q\ge1-\epsilon^2$ by (M.6.13h.2). Conversely, after balancing a reference with $\eta=\eta_Q\ge u=1-\epsilon^2$, an optimal $L$ obeys $\operatorname{Tr}\widehat\sigma L=\operatorname{Tr}\widehat\sigma LL^*=\operatorname{Tr}\widehat\sigma L^*L=\eta$. Replacing $L$ by $sL$, where $s=1-\sqrt{1-u/\eta}$, makes both noise eigenvalues $1-\eta(2s-s^2)=\epsilon^2$. The neutral-pointer construction implements it exactly. This proves (M.6.13h.4) and the exact-error assertion. $\square$

<a id="theorem-m613i-relative-entropy-cost-from-a-scalar-trace-bound"></a>**Theorem M.6.13i (Relative-Entropy Cost from a Scalar Trace Bound).** For $t\ge0$ and $\lambda\ge0$, define
$$
\mathsf M(t)=1+\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}t e^{t^2/4}\operatorname{erf}(t/2),
\qquad
\operatorname{erf}(z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^z e^{-r^2}\,dr,
$$
$$
\mathsf B(\lambda)=\sup_{x\ge0}
\frac{\cosh(\lambda x)}{\mathsf M(\sqrt\lambda x)}.
\tag{M.6.13i.1}
$$
The supremum is finite, $\mathsf B(\lambda)=1$ for $0\le\lambda\le1$, and every finite Hermitian $Q,D$ and raising operator $L$ with $[Q,D]=0$, $[Q,L]=L$ obey
$$
\operatorname{Tr}e^{D+\lambda(L+L^*)}
\le\mathsf B(\lambda)\operatorname{Tr}e^{D+\lambda K_L}.
\tag{M.6.13i.2}
$$
There is no commutation requirement between $D$ and $K_L$.

Consequently every reference in Theorem M.6.13h satisfies
$$
\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)\ge
\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\{\lambda\eta_Q(\sigma)-\log\mathsf B(\lambda)\}
\ge\eta_Q(\sigma).
\tag{M.6.13i.3}
$$
The equality $\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)=\eta_Q(\sigma)$ holds exactly for invariant references. In particular, every finite admitted model with $\epsilon_\infty(X_S)=\epsilon<1$ obeys
$$
\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)>1-\epsilon^2,
\qquad
\mathfrak A(\epsilon)\ge
\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\{\lambda(1-\epsilon^2)-\log\mathsf B(\lambda)\}.
\tag{M.6.13i.4}
$$
The strict pointwise inequality and the non-strict infimum bound have their indicated separate meanings.

For $\lambda\ge16$, the scalar bound has the explicit remainder
$$
\lambda-\frac12\log(4\pi\lambda)
-\frac{e^{-\lambda}}{\sqrt{\pi\lambda}}
\le\log\mathsf B(\lambda)
\le\lambda-\frac12\log(4\pi\lambda)+\frac2\lambda.
\tag{M.6.13i.5}
$$
Thus, throughout $0<\epsilon^2\le1/32$,
$$
\mathfrak A(\epsilon)\ge
-\log\epsilon+\frac{\log(2\pi)-1}{2}-4\epsilon^2.
\tag{M.6.13i.6}
$$

*Proof.* Put $X=L+L^*$ and $Y=i(L-L^*)$, so $X^2+Y^2=4K_L$. Charge-phase conjugation leaves $D$ fixed and rotates $X$ to $\cos\theta X+\sin\theta Y$. Therefore $f(s)=\operatorname{Tr}e^{D+sX}$ is even, and the trace along each circle in the $(X,Y)$ plane is independent of its angle.

Choose $c\ge\|X\|$. Stahl's BMV theorem (Stahl 2013, Theorems 1--2) gives a positive compactly supported Laplace measure for $\operatorname{Tr}e^{D-s(cI-X)}$. Multiplication by $e^{cs}$ translates its support and gives a positive compactly supported measure $\mu$ with $f(s)=\int e^{sx}\,d\mu(x)$. The identity, initially for $s\ge0$, extends to real $s$ because both sides are entire. Evenness and the pushforward $x\mapsto|x|$ give
$$
f(s)=\int_0^\infty\cosh(sx)\,d\mu(x).
\tag{M.6.13i.7}
$$

Let $g,h$ be independent centered real Gaussians of variance $1/2$, and write $(g,h)=(R\cos\Theta,R\sin\Theta)$. Then $R$ has density $2r e^{-r^2}$ on $r\ge0$. Lieb's trace-exponential concavity, in the expectation form of (Tropp 2012, Corollary 3.3), states
$$
\mathbb E\operatorname{Tr}e^{H+Z}
\le\operatorname{Tr}e^{H+\log\mathbb E e^Z}
$$
for fixed Hermitian $H$ and exponentially integrable Hermitian $Z$. Applying it first to $g$ and then to $h$, with the remaining matrices fixed at each step, yields
$$
\mathbb E\operatorname{Tr}e^{D+\sqrt\lambda(gX+hY)}
\le\operatorname{Tr}e^{D+\lambda(X^2+Y^2)/4}
=\operatorname{Tr}e^{D+\lambda K_L}.
\tag{M.6.13i.8}
$$
Here $\mathbb E e^{\sqrt\lambda gX}=e^{\lambda X^2/4}$ and the analogous identity for $Y$ are ordinary Gaussian functional calculus. The first fixed matrix in the second application is $D+\lambda X^2/4$; it need not commute with $Y$.

Circular invariance, (M.6.13i.7) and Tonelli's theorem identify the expectation in (M.6.13i.8) as $\int\mathsf M(\sqrt\lambda x)\,d\mu(x)$. Indeed, integration by parts and completion of the square give
$$
\mathbb E\cosh(tR)
=\int_0^\infty2r e^{-r^2}\cosh(tr)\,dr
=1+t\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}\sinh(tr)\,dr
=\mathsf M(t).
\tag{M.6.13i.9}
$$
Compact support of $\mu$ and Gaussian tails justify finiteness. Comparing the numerator and denominator against this same positive measure proves (M.6.13i.2).

For $\lambda>0$, the denominator in (M.6.13i.1) grows quadratically in the exponential as $x\to\infty$, while the numerator grows linearly in the exponential, so the supremum is finite. The value at $x=0$ is one. Also $\mathbb E R^{2k}=k!$, hence
$$
\mathsf M(\sqrt\lambda x)
=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{k!\lambda^k x^{2k}}{(2k)!}
\ge\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\lambda^{2k}x^{2k}}{(2k)!}
=\cosh(\lambda x)
$$
when $0\le\lambda\le1$. This proves the stated subcritical value.

For the entropy conclusion, restrict to $P=\operatorname{supp}\tau$, where $\tau=\mathcal G_Q\sigma$ is positive definite. The support is invariant and contains $\operatorname{supp}\sigma$ by Theorem M.6.13e. Choose the supported maximizing $L$ from Theorem M.6.13h and use $D=\log\tau-\lambda K_L$ in (M.6.13i.2). The resulting partition function obeys
$$
Z_\lambda:=\operatorname{Tr}e^{\log\tau+\lambda H_L}
\le\mathsf B(\lambda).
$$
Positivity of relative entropy against $Z_\lambda^{-1}e^{\log\tau+\lambda H_L}$ gives
$$
\lambda\eta_Q(\sigma)-\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)
\le\log Z_\lambda\le\log\mathsf B(\lambda),
$$
which proves (M.6.13i.3). If $\eta_Q>0$, then $L\ne0$ and $X\ne0$. Diagonalizing $D$ shows
$$
f''(0)=\int_0^1\operatorname{Tr}
\bigl(e^{(1-t)D}X e^{tD}X\bigr)\,dt>0.
$$
Thus $\mu$ has positive mass at $x>0$, where $\mathsf M(x)>\cosh x$ by the fourth term of the series. At $\lambda=1$, the comparison in (M.6.13i.8)--(M.6.13i.9) is therefore strict, so $\mathcal A_Q>\eta_Q$. If $\eta_Q=0$ but $\sigma$ is noninvariant, Theorem M.6.13e gives the same strict inequality. Invariant states have both quantities zero. The exact operational reduction now gives (M.6.13i.4).

It remains to control the supremum in (M.6.13i.1) uniformly. At $x=2$, using $\operatorname{erf}\le1$ and $\log(1+z)\le z$ gives
$$
\log\mathsf B(\lambda)
\ge\lambda-\frac12\log(4\pi\lambda)
-\frac{e^{-\lambda}}{\sqrt{\pi\lambda}}.
$$
For the upper bound split the half-line into $[0,1/2]$, $[1/2,1]$ and $[1,\infty)$. The first two regions have respective ratio bounds
$$
e^{\lambda/2},\qquad
\frac{4e^{3\lambda/4}}
{\sqrt{\pi\lambda}\operatorname{erf}(\sqrt\lambda/4)}.
\tag{M.6.13i.10}
$$
The second follows from the positive second term of $\mathsf M$, $x\ge1/2$ and $x-x^2/4\le3/4$. After division by $e^\lambda/(2\sqrt{\pi\lambda})$, both bounds are less than one for $\lambda\ge16$: use $\operatorname{erf}(1)\ge4/(3\sqrt\pi)$, obtained by integrating $e^{-t^2}\ge1-t^2$, and monotonicity of the resulting elementary bounds.

On $x\ge1$, retaining the factor $1/2$ in $\cosh$ gives
$$
\frac{\cosh(\lambda x)}{\mathsf M(\sqrt\lambda x)}
\le\frac{1+e^{-2\lambda}}
{\sqrt{\pi\lambda}\operatorname{erf}(\sqrt\lambda/2)}
\frac{e^{\lambda(x-x^2/4)}}{x}.
\tag{M.6.13i.11}
$$
For $\lambda\ge16$ the last factor is largest at $x_\lambda=1+\sqrt{1-2/\lambda}$. Its logarithmic derivative is $\lambda(1-x/2)-1/x$. Since $x_\lambda\ge2-2/\lambda$,
$$
\log(2/x_\lambda)\le\frac1{\lambda-1}
\le\frac{16}{15\lambda},\qquad
\lambda(x_\lambda-x_\lambda^2/4)\le\lambda.
$$
The Gaussian-tail estimate $1-\operatorname{erf}(z)\le e^{-z^2}/(\sqrt\pi z)$ gives $1-\operatorname{erf}(\sqrt\lambda/2)\le1/(4\lambda)$ for $\lambda\ge16$. Consequently $-\log\operatorname{erf}(\sqrt\lambda/2)\le1/(2\lambda)$, while $\log(1+e^{-2\lambda})\le1/(4\lambda)$. The three corrections sum to less than $2/\lambda$, proving the upper side of (M.6.13i.5). Taking $\lambda=1/(2\epsilon^2)$ in (M.6.13i.4) proves (M.6.13i.6). $\square$

<a id="theorem-m613j-sharp-entropy-asymptotics-for-the-full-qubit-apparatus-class"></a>**Theorem M.6.13j (Sharp Entropy Asymptotics for the Full Qubit Apparatus Class).** Let $\mathfrak A(\epsilon)$ be the complete finite-reference infimum in Theorem M.6.13h. Define
$$
I_0(\kappa)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{\kappa\cos\theta}\,d\theta,
\qquad I_1(\kappa)=I_0'(\kappa).
$$
For each $0<\epsilon<1$ there is a unique $\kappa>0$ satisfying
$$
\frac{I_1(\kappa)}{I_0(\kappa)}=\sqrt{1-\epsilon^2},
$$
and the explicit upper bound
$$
\mathfrak A(\epsilon)\le
\kappa\sqrt{1-\epsilon^2}-\log I_0(\kappa)
\tag{M.6.13j.1}
$$
is approached by finite conserving measurements with exact error $\epsilon$. Together with Theorem M.6.13i, this gives
$$
\boxed{\mathfrak A(\epsilon)
=\log(1/\epsilon)+\frac{\log(2\pi)-1}{2}+O(\epsilon^2)}
\qquad(\epsilon\downarrow0),
\tag{M.6.13j.2}
$$
and
$$
\lim_{\epsilon\uparrow1}
\frac{\mathfrak A(\epsilon)}{1-\epsilon^2}=1.
\tag{M.6.13j.3}
$$
Both limits optimize over arbitrary finite real reference charges, degeneracies, mixed states, neutral ancillas, conserving unitaries and Yanase pointers, with all system inputs tested.

*Proof.* Put $u=1-\epsilon^2$ and choose any integer $N>1/\epsilon^2$ with $N\ge3$. On the reference basis $|n\rangle$, $0\le n<N$, set
$$
Q_N=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}n|n\rangle\langle n|,
\quad \theta_j=2\pi j/N,
\quad |\theta_j\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}e^{in\theta_j}|n\rangle,
$$
$$
Z_N(\kappa)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e^{\kappa\cos\theta_j},
\quad w_j(\kappa)=\frac{e^{\kappa\cos\theta_j}}{Z_N(\kappa)},
\quad \sigma_{N,\kappa}=\sum_j w_j(\kappa)|\theta_j\rangle\langle\theta_j|.
\tag{M.6.13j.4}
$$
The Fourier vectors are orthonormal. Thus $\mathcal G_{Q_N}\sigma_{N,\kappa}=I/N$, and every adjacent coherence is $c_N(\kappa)/N$, where
$$
c_N(\kappa)=\sum_j w_j(\kappa)\cos\theta_j.
$$
The imaginary part vanishes by $j\mapsto N-j$. Direct substitution in Theorem M.6.13h gives
$$
\eta_{Q_N}(\sigma_{N,\kappa})=(1-1/N)c_N(\kappa)^2,
\quad
\mathcal A_{Q_N}(\sigma_{N,\kappa})
=\kappa c_N(\kappa)-\log[Z_N(\kappa)/N].
\tag{M.6.13j.5}
$$
All diagonal weights are equal, so $F_{\sigma_{N,\kappa}}(t)$ is independent of $t$. The raising operator
$$
L_{N,\kappa}=c_N(\kappa)\sum_{n=0}^{N-2}|n+1\rangle\langle n|
$$
has both noise eigenvalues equal to $1-(1-1/N)c_N^2$ and is implemented by the explicit neutral-pointer dilation in Theorem M.6.13h.

The derivative $c_N'(\kappa)$ is the strictly positive variance of $\cos\theta_j$ under $w_j(\kappa)$. Also $c_N(0)=0$ and $c_N(\kappa)\to1$ as $\kappa\to\infty$. Since $u<1-1/N$, there is a unique finite $\kappa_N$ with $(1-1/N)c_N(\kappa_N)^2=u$. Every resulting model has exact error $\epsilon$.

Riemann sums converge locally uniformly in $\kappa$, giving $Z_N(\kappa)/N\to I_0(\kappa)$ and $c_N(\kappa)\to c(\kappa)=I_1(\kappa)/I_0(\kappa)$. Here $c'(\kappa)$ is the strictly positive variance of $\cos\theta$ under the normalized density $e^{\kappa\cos\theta}$, while $c(0)=0$ and $c(\kappa)\to1$. Therefore the limiting equation $c(\kappa)=\sqrt u$ has a unique solution, and monotonicity plus local uniform convergence gives $\kappa_N\to\kappa$. Taking $N\to\infty$ in (M.6.13j.5) proves (M.6.13j.1). This limit is taken at each fixed positive error.

For high accuracy, the fixed-order modified-Bessel expansion [NIST DLMF, Equation 10.40.1] on the positive real axis gives
$$
I_0(\kappa)=\frac{e^\kappa}{\sqrt{2\pi\kappa}}
\left(1+\frac1{8\kappa}+O(\kappa^{-2})\right),
\quad
c(\kappa)=1-\frac1{2\kappa}+O(\kappa^{-2}).
\tag{M.6.13j.6}
$$
Consequently $\epsilon^2=1-c(\kappa)^2=\kappa^{-1}+O(\kappa^{-2})$, so $\kappa=\epsilon^{-2}+O(1)$. Substitution yields
$$
\kappa c(\kappa)-\log I_0(\kappa)
=\frac12\log(2\pi\kappa)-\frac12+O(\kappa^{-1})
=\log(1/\epsilon)+\frac{\log(2\pi)-1}{2}+O(\epsilon^2).
$$
The lower bound (M.6.13i.6) has the same two leading terms and an explicit remainder $-4\epsilon^2$. This proves (M.6.13j.2). At the other endpoint, the defining integrals give $I_0(\kappa)=1+\kappa^2/4+O(\kappa^4)$ and $c(\kappa)=\kappa/2+O(\kappa^3)$, hence the upper bound is $u+O(u^2)$ as $u\downarrow0$. The lower bound $\mathfrak A(\epsilon)\ge u$ proves (M.6.13j.3). $\square$

<a id="theorem-m613k-sharp-rotational-trace-bound"></a>**Theorem M.6.13k (Sharp Rotational Trace Bound).** Let $Q,D$ be Hermitian matrices on a finite-dimensional complex space, and let $L$ be any matrix satisfying $[Q,D]=0$ and $[Q,L]=L$. Define
$$
X=L+L^*,\qquad Y=i(L-L^*),\qquad
K=K_L=\frac{LL^*+L^*L}{2}=\frac{X^2+Y^2}{4},
\qquad
S(\lambda)=\max_{r\ge0}e^{-\lambda r^2}I_0(2\lambda r)
=\max_{0\le r\le1}e^{-\lambda r^2}I_0(2\lambda r),
\quad \lambda\ge0.
\tag{M.6.13k.1}
$$
Here $I_0$ is defined in Theorem M.6.13j. Then
$$
\operatorname{Tr}e^{D+\lambda(X-K)}
\le S(\lambda)\operatorname{Tr}e^D,
\qquad
\operatorname{Tr}e^{D+\lambda X}
\le S(\lambda)\operatorname{Tr}e^{D+\lambda K}.
\tag{M.6.13k.2}
$$
Both inequalities are strict whenever $\lambda>0$ and $L\ne0$. The constant $S(\lambda)$ is optimal over this finite-dimensional class, allowing the dimension to vary. No contraction assumption on $L$ and no condition $[D,K]=0$ are imposed. The Brownian process used below is a mathematical proof device; it adds no physical noise, source, control, or apparatus premise.

*Proof.* The two forms in (M.6.13k.2) are equivalent by replacing $D$ with $D+\lambda K$, since $[Q,K]=0$. At $\lambda=0$ both are identities. For $\lambda>0$, write $c(z)=I_1(z)/I_0(z)$. Its $\int$ expression is the expectation of $\cos\theta$ under the strictly positive density proportional to $e^{z\cos\theta}$, so $c(z)<1$ for finite $z\ge0$. Therefore the logarithmic derivative of the scalar objective in (M.6.13k.1) is $2\lambda[c(2\lambda r)-r]<0$ for $r\ge1$. The objective tends to zero at infinity, since $I_0(z)\le e^z$. Its maximum is consequently attained in $[0,1]$, proving the equality of maxima. At $\lambda=0$ the objective is identically one.

Put $U_\theta=e^{i\theta Q}$ and
$$
U_\theta XU_\theta^*=\cos\theta X+\sin\theta Y,
\qquad
F(x,y,t)=\operatorname{Tr}e^{D+xX+yY-tK}
=f(\sqrt{x^2+y^2},t),
\quad f(s,t)=\operatorname{Tr}e^{D+sX-tK}.
\tag{M.6.13k.3}
$$
Conjugation invariance of the trace proves radiality. The matrix-exponential power series makes $F$ smooth on all of $\mathbb R^3$, including the spatial origin. In particular the radial expression below has its ordinary smooth extension there.

For Hermitian $H,Z$, let $\mathcal B_H(Z,Z)$ denote the uncentered Duhamel quadratic form. In an eigenbasis of $H$, with eigenvalues $h_a$, it satisfies
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B_H(Z,Z)
&=\int_0^1\operatorname{Tr}(e^{(1-v)H}Ze^{vH}Z)\,dv\\
&=\sum_{a,b}|Z_{ab}|^2\int_0^1e^{(1-v)h_a+vh_b}\,dv\\
&\le\sum_{a,b}|Z_{ab}|^2\frac{e^{h_a}+e^{h_b}}2
=\operatorname{Tr}(e^H Z^2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{M.6.13k.4}
$$
The scalar inequality follows by integrating the weighted arithmetic-geometric mean inequality. Equality holds exactly when $Z_{ab}=0$ for every pair with $h_a\ne h_b$, equivalently $[H,Z]=0$. This is an uncentered form, not a centered variance.

Let $H=D+sX-tK$. Differentiating the exponential under the trace and differentiating twice the constant angular trace from (M.6.13k.3) give, for $s>0$,
$$
f_{ss}=\mathcal B_H(X,X),\qquad
f_t=-\operatorname{Tr}(e^H K),\qquad
0=s^2\mathcal B_H(Y,Y)-s\operatorname{Tr}(e^H X),
\qquad \frac{f_s}{s}=\mathcal B_H(Y,Y).
\tag{M.6.13k.5}
$$
Using $X^2+Y^2=4K$ in (M.6.13k.4) proves
$$
f_{ss}+\frac{f_s}{s}\le-4f_t,
\qquad
\left(\partial_t+\frac14\Delta_{x,y}\right)F=-\mathcal R\le0,
\qquad
\mathcal R=\frac{\delta_H(X)+\delta_H(Y)}4,
\quad \delta_H(Z)=\operatorname{Tr}(e^H Z^2)-\mathcal B_H(Z,Z).
\tag{M.6.13k.6}
$$
In the definition of $\mathcal R$ at a general point, $H=D+xX+yY-tK$. At the origin $f_s/s$ has limit $f_{ss}(0,t)$, so the radial Laplacian has limit $2f_{ss}(0,t)$. Alternatively the Cartesian derivative formula establishes (M.6.13k.6) directly there. Its sign is supercaloric, and equality is not assumed.

Let $W^1,W^2$ be independent standard real Brownian motions. On a probability space used only for this proof, set
$$
B_t=\frac{(W_t^1,W_t^2)}{\sqrt2},\qquad
R_t=|B_t|,\qquad T=\inf\{t\ge0:R_t=\lambda\}.
\qquad
\mathbb E(t\wedge T)=\mathbb E|B_{t\wedge T}|^2\le\lambda^2.
\tag{M.6.13k.7}
$$
The generator is $\Delta/4$, each coordinate has variance $t/2$, and $|B_t|^2-t$ is a martingale. Bounded-time stopping gives the displayed identity. Monotone convergence then gives $\mathbb ET\le\lambda^2$, hence $T<\infty$ almost surely. Continuity gives $R_T=\lambda$ and $T>0$ almost surely.

For $0\le r\le\lambda$ and $t\ge0$, positivity of $K$ and $\|X\|\le2\|L\|$ give the uniform stopped bound
$$
0<f(r,t)\le e^{2\lambda\|L\|}\operatorname{Tr}e^D.
\qquad
\operatorname{Tr}e^D=F(0,0,0)
\ge\mathbb E F(B_{a\wedge T},a\wedge T)
\longrightarrow\mathbb E f(\lambda,T)
\quad(a\to\infty).
\tag{M.6.13k.8}
$$
Here trace exponential is monotone in Hermitian Loewner order: if $V\ge0$, differentiating $\operatorname{Tr}e^{A+uV}$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}(Ve^{A+uV})\ge0$. Thus no operator-monotonicity claim for the exponential is needed. On each bounded stopped space-time cylinder the derivatives of $F$ are bounded. Itô's formula and (M.6.13k.6) therefore make the stopped process a supermartingale, with a zero-mean stochastic $\int$ on every finite horizon. The uniform bound permits dominated convergence at the almost surely finite exit time. These are bounded optional-stopping and limit arguments; no representation theorem for ancient heat solutions is used.

For $u\ge0$, the function
$$
v_u(r)=I_0(2\sqrt u\,r)
=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{u^n r^{2n}}{(n!)^2},
\qquad
\frac14\left(v_u''+\frac{v_u'}r\right)=uv_u,
\qquad v_u(0)=1
\tag{M.6.13k.9}
$$
is smooth as a radial function at the origin. The differential identity follows term by term from the convergent power series. Itô's formula makes $e^{-u(a\wedge T)}v_u(R_{a\wedge T})$ a martingale on each finite horizon. It is bounded by $I_0(2\lambda\sqrt u)$, so dominated convergence gives the reciprocal-Bessel exit transform with the required normalization:
$$
\mathbb E e^{-uT}=\frac1{I_0(2\lambda\sqrt u)},\qquad u\ge0.
\tag{M.6.13k.10}
$$
For $u=0$ the statement is the identity one.

Apply the Bessis--Moussa--Villani theorem (Stahl 2013) to the single Hermitian pair $(D+\lambda X,K)$ at the fixed radius $\lambda$. Its interval-support formulation (Eremenko 2014, Theorem) supplies one finite positive measure $\mu_\lambda$ such that
$$
f(\lambda,t)=\int_{[0,\|L\|^2]}e^{-tu}\,\mu_\lambda(du),\qquad t\ge0.
\tag{M.6.13k.11}
$$
Indeed $0\le K\le\|L\|^2I$. The measure is supported between the smallest and largest eigenvalues of $K$, so extending it by zero gives the indicated interval. There is no family of mutually compatible radial measures and no joint positive radial-energy measure in this argument. Tonelli's theorem, (M.6.13k.8), and (M.6.13k.10) give
$$
\operatorname{Tr}e^D\ge
\int_{[0,\|L\|^2]}
\frac{\mu_\lambda(du)}{I_0(2\lambda\sqrt u)}.
\tag{M.6.13k.12}
$$
For every $u\ge0$, definition (M.6.13k.1) yields $e^{-\lambda u}I_0(2\lambda\sqrt u)\le S(\lambda)$. Integrating this scalar inequality against the same measure proves
$$
\operatorname{Tr}e^{D+\lambda(X-K)}
=\int e^{-\lambda u}\,\mu_\lambda(du)
\le S(\lambda)\int\frac{\mu_\lambda(du)}{I_0(2\lambda\sqrt u)}
\le S(\lambda)\operatorname{Tr}e^D.
\tag{M.6.13k.13}
$$

For strictness, a finite raising operator is nilpotent: a nonzero matrix entry of $L^m$ connects charge eigenvalues differing by $m$, which is impossible for sufficiently large $m$ in a fixed finite real spectrum. A normal nilpotent matrix is zero. Thus if $L\ne0$,
$$
[X,Y]=-2i[L,L^*]\ne0,\qquad
\mathcal G_Q([D+sX-tK,Y])=s[X,Y]\ne0
\quad(s>0).
\tag{M.6.13k.14}
$$
The dephasing identity holds because $D-tK$ has charge increment zero, $Y$ has only increments $+1$ and $-1$, and $[X,Y]$ has increment zero. By the equality condition in (M.6.13k.4), the $Y$ inequality is strict at every positive radial point. Radial covariance then implies $\mathcal R(x,y,t)>0$ whenever $x^2+y^2>0$. For every $a>0$, Itô's formula gives
$$
\mathbb E F(B_{a\wedge T},a\wedge T)
=\operatorname{Tr}e^D-
\mathbb E\int_0^{a\wedge T}\mathcal R(B_t,t)\,dt
<\operatorname{Tr}e^D.
\tag{M.6.13k.15}
$$
The $\int$ is strictly positive almost surely. In fact $a\wedge T>0$; Brownian motion almost surely is not identically zero on any initial interval (use the countable positive rational times and their non-atomic Gaussian laws); and continuity then supplies a nonempty interval before exit with positive radius and positive $\mathcal R$. The $\int$ is bounded on the finite stopped cylinder, so its expectation is strictly positive. The terminal expectation in (M.6.13k.8) is at most the expectation at this fixed horizon by the supermartingale property. Hence (M.6.13k.12), and therefore (M.6.13k.2), is strict.

Finally the constant is sharp within the stated raising class. For $N\ge2$, take $Q_N=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\ldots,N-1)$, $D_N=0$, and $L_N=r\sum_{n=0}^{N-2}|n+1\rangle\langle n|$, where $0\le r\le1$. Write $P_n=|n\rangle\langle n|$. Then
$$
K_{L_N}=r^2\left[I-\frac{P_0+P_{N-1}}2\right],
\qquad
\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N
\operatorname{Tr}e^{\lambda(L_N+L_N^*-K_{L_N})}
=e^{-\lambda r^2}I_0(2\lambda r).
\tag{M.6.13k.16}
$$
To verify the limit, replace $K_{L_N}$ by $r^2I$. The resulting tridiagonal matrix has eigenvalues $2\lambda r\cos(j\pi/(N+1))-\lambda r^2$, $1\le j\le N$; its normalized exponential trace converges by Riemann sums to the displayed Bessel $\int$. The replacement adds $V=\lambda r^2(P_0+P_{N-1})/2\ge0$. Along the interpolation the exponent is bounded above by $2\lambda rI$, so its trace-exponential derivative is at most $e^{2\lambda r}\operatorname{Tr}V=\lambda r^2e^{2\lambda r}$. The normalized difference is at most this constant divided by $N$. Taking a maximizing $r$ proves optimality. This limiting assertion does not assert finite equality for nonzero $L$. $\square$

<a id="theorem-m613l-exact-registered-qubit-entropy-frontier-and-finite-nonattainment"></a>**Theorem M.6.13l (Exact Registered Qubit Entropy Frontier and Finite Nonattainment).** Fix the registered system $Q_S=|1\rangle\langle1|$ and target $X_S=|0\rangle\langle1|+|1\rangle\langle0|$. Retain the complete finite measurement class of Theorems M.6.13g--M.6.13h: arbitrary finite real reference charge spectra and degeneracies, arbitrary mixed reference states, neutral ancillary factors and flags with their correlations included in the complete reference cut, conserving unitaries, and self-adjoint charge-commuting Yanase pointers. Every system input is tested. Resource is natural-$\log$ reference asymmetry $\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)=D(\sigma\Vert\mathcal G_Q\sigma)$, and error is the worst-case Ozawa RMS error of the induced first and second moments. No pointer-norm, charge-variance, simple-spectrum, purity, or fixed-reference-dimension restriction is added.

For $0<\epsilon<1$, let $u=1-\epsilon^2$, and let $\kappa>0$ be the unique root of $I_1(\kappa)/I_0(\kappa)=\sqrt u$. The exact finite-apparatus infimum of Theorem M.6.13h is
$$
\mathfrak A(\epsilon)=\Phi(1-\epsilon^2),\qquad
\Phi(u)=\kappa\sqrt u-\log I_0(\kappa),\qquad
\frac{I_1(\kappa)}{I_0(\kappa)}=\sqrt u,
\quad 0<u<1.
\tag{M.6.13l.1}
$$
The infimum is the same for exact error and error at most $\epsilon$. Every admitted finite model in either class obeys the strict inequality
$$
\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)>\Phi(1-\epsilon^2).
\tag{M.6.13l.2}
$$
Thus no finite model attains this interior infimum; there is no finite attaining minimum. The finite Fourier family of Theorem M.6.13j has exact error $\epsilon$ and approaches it at each fixed interior $\epsilon$. At the endpoints, zero error is impossible for a finite model, whereas error one has an attaining zero-asymmetry model.

*Proof.* We first evaluate the scalar dual globally. Set $c(\kappa)=I_1(\kappa)/I_0(\kappa)$. Differentiation of its normalized $\int$ shows that $c'(\kappa)$ is the variance of $\cos\theta$, strictly positive at every finite $\kappa$. Also $c(0)=0$ and $c(\kappa)\to1$ as $\kappa\to\infty$. For the last limit, for any fixed $\delta>0$, compare the $\int$ on $\cos\theta\le1-\delta$ with that on the positive-length arc $\cos\theta\ge1-\delta/2$; its probability is bounded by a constant times $e^{-\kappa\delta/2}$. The expectation of $1-\cos\theta$ consequently tends to zero. Hence the root in (M.6.13l.1) exists and is unique.

A second monotonicity is needed to establish a global radial maximum rather than just a stationary point. For $z=\kappa^2/4$, the positive power series give
$$
I_0(\kappa)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{z^n}{(n!)^2},\qquad
\frac{I_1(\kappa)}{\kappa}=\frac12\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{z^n}{n!(n+1)!},
\qquad
\frac{c(\kappa)}{\kappa}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty p_z(n)\frac1{2(n+1)},
\quad p_z(n)=\frac{z^n/(n!)^2}{\sum_{m=0}^\infty z^m/(m!)^2}.
\tag{M.6.13l.3}
$$
For $z>0$, differentiation with respect to $\log z$ is the covariance of $n$ with $1/[2(n+1)]$. It is strictly negative: using an independent copy $n'$ expresses twice this covariance as the expectation of $(n-n')[1/(2(n+1))-1/(2(n'+1))]$, which is nonpositive and strictly negative when $n\ne n'$, an event of positive probability. Absolute convergence justifies the derivatives. Thus $c(\kappa)/\kappa$ decreases strictly from $1/2$ to zero; the limits follow from the constant terms and $0<c(\kappa)<1$.

For $g_\lambda(r)=-\lambda r^2+\log I_0(2\lambda r)$,
$$
g_\lambda'(r)=2\lambda[c(2\lambda r)-r].
\qquad
S(\lambda)=1\quad(0\le\lambda\le1),
\qquad
r_\lambda=c(2\lambda r_\lambda)\in(0,1)\quad(\lambda>1).
\tag{M.6.13l.4}
$$
For $r>0$ and $\lambda>0$, the sign of the derivative is the sign of $2\lambda c(2\lambda r)/(2\lambda r)-1$, a strictly decreasing function of $r$. Its limit at zero is $\lambda-1$ and its value at one is negative. This proves that for $\lambda\le1$ the global maximum is at zero, and for $\lambda>1$ there is a unique positive global maximizer $r_\lambda\in(0,1)$. In particular, for a specified $u\in(0,1)$, $r=\sqrt u$ and $c(\kappa)=r$ give $\lambda_* =\kappa/(2r)>1$, with $r$ its unique global maximizer.

Substitution and the ordinary one-variable Legendre inequality now prove the exact scalar dual:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda_*u-\log S(\lambda_*)&=\kappa\sqrt u-\log I_0(\kappa)=\Phi(u),\\
\lambda u-\log S(\lambda)
&\le2\lambda u-\log I_0(2\lambda\sqrt u)\le\Phi(u),\qquad\lambda\ge0,\\
\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\{\lambda u-\log S(\lambda)\}&=\Phi(u),\qquad
\Phi'(u)=\frac{\kappa}{2\sqrt u}>0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{M.6.13l.5}
$$
For the second inequality, $k\sqrt u-\log I_0(k)$ has derivative $\sqrt u-c(k)$ and hence its unique global maximum at $k=\kappa$. The derivative formula for $\Phi$ follows by differentiating and cancelling the $\kappa'(u)$ terms. It is strictly increasing because $\kappa/c(\kappa)$ increases, so $\Phi$ is strictly increasing and strictly convex. We use its continuous extension $\Phi(0)=0$ when needed.

For the entropy step let $\tau=\mathcal G_Q\sigma$ and restrict to $P=\operatorname{supp}\tau$. This support is $Q$-invariant and contains $\operatorname{supp}\sigma$: if a vector lies in the kernel of a diagonal charge block of $\sigma$, positivity annihilates its entire row and column; summing over charge blocks proves the inclusion. On $P$, $\tau$ is positive definite, and the supported maximizing contraction $L$ of Theorem M.6.13h still satisfies $[Q,L]=L$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\sigma H_L=\eta_Q(\sigma)$, where $H_L=L+L^*-K_L$. Define on this support
$$
Z_\lambda=\operatorname{Tr}e^{\log\tau+\lambda H_L},\qquad
\omega_\lambda=Z_\lambda^{-1}e^{\log\tau+\lambda H_L}.
\qquad
Z_\lambda\le S(\lambda),
\qquad
\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)
=D(\sigma\Vert\omega_\lambda)+\lambda\eta_Q(\sigma)-\log Z_\lambda.
\tag{M.6.13l.6}
$$
The trace bound is Theorem M.6.13k with $D=\log\tau$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\tau=1$; $D$ commutes with the restricted charge. The identity follows by substituting $\log\omega_\lambda=\log\tau+\lambda H_L-(\log Z_\lambda)I$ into relative entropy, and remains valid for singular $\sigma$ on $P$. Its first term is nonnegative.
