This gives the strict separation and hence a nonzero lower bound (M.6.13em.4) for each fixed such error and any cost budget strictly between the two frontiers. The commuting coefficient space is unrestricted in dimension in this comparison. \(\square\)

<a id="theorem-m613en"></a>

<a id="theorem-m613en-finite-cyclic-conservation-and-a-uniform-pressure-approximation"></a>**Theorem M.6.13en (Finite Cyclic Conservation and a Uniform Pressure Approximation).** Use the complete spin-one problem of Theorems M.6.13dc and M.6.13el. For each integer \(N\ge3\), let \(F_N^{\mathrm{cyc}}(r)\) and \(b_N^{\mathrm{cyc}}(Z)\) be the same noise and entropy infima with only cyclic conservation. In this class the reference is any finite unitary representation of \(\mathbb Z_N\), with generator \(W\) satisfying \(W^N=I\). The observable commutes with \(U_{2\pi/N}\otimes W\), and reference asymmetry is
\[
\mathcal A_N(\sigma)=S\!\left(N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}W^j\sigma W^{-j}\right)-S(\sigma).
\]
The reference representation allows arbitrary finite multiplicities. Every pointer and auxiliary factor is included as in the original complete measurement class. The neutral spectral-pointer construction remains exact for this conservation law.

For \(Z=x|e\rangle\langle e|+y|m\rangle\langle m|+z|f\rangle\langle f|\), \(x,y>0\), \(z\ge0\), put \(s=x+y\), \(M=s/(2\sqrt{xy})\), \(K=(s+z)(M+1)^2\), and \(\theta_j=2\pi j/N\). Then
\[
\begin{split}
b_N^{\mathrm{cyc}}(Z)
&=-\log\sup_{d,\tau,C}
       \frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}
       \operatorname{Tr}\exp(\log\tau-V_{Z,C}(\theta_j)),\\
0\le b(Z)-b_N^{\mathrm{cyc}}(Z)
&\le e^s\,\inf_{a>0}
   \frac{2\exp(K[1+2\cosh a+2\cosh(2a)])e^{-aN}}{1-e^{-aN}}.
\end{split}
\tag{M.6.13en.1}
\]
The supremum is over all finite coefficient dimensions, all normalized \(\tau\succeq0\), and odd Hermitian \(C\) with \(\|C\|\le M\). The singular-support convention and \(V_{Z,C}\) are those of Theorem M.6.13el. At any fixed such tester the error in (M.6.13en.1) is bounded above by \(\exp[-\tfrac12N\log N+O_Z(N)]\). The same bound holds before taking the supremum, uniformly over all those finite matrix dimensions and eigenvalues of \(\tau\).

For every fixed \(0<r<1\), the cyclic conservation relaxation satisfies
\[
F_N^{\mathrm{cyc}}(r)\le F(r),\qquad
0\le F(r)-F_N^{\mathrm{cyc}}(r)\le \frac{C_r}{N}
\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }N ,
\tag{M.6.13en.2}
\]
where an explicit \(C_r\) can be calculated from any finite strict model at squared error \(r_s<r\) and its entropy. If a maximizing tester for the original problem has \(x,y>0\), the superexponential bound in (M.6.13en.1) applies directly to this frontier difference at that tester. These estimates give a sequence of dimension-uniform lower variational approximations to \(F(r)\).

*Proof.* Replace the circle in (M.6.13el.1) by the \(N\)-point phase measure and denote a normalized positive matrix density on it by \(J_j\), with \(N^{-1}\sum_j\operatorname{Tr}J_j=1\). The two phase conversion maps are exact. Given a finite cyclic apparatus, use system parity oddification, then take \(C\) to be its odd observable and \(J_j=W^{-j}\sigma W^j\). Commutation with the total generator gives
\[
(U_{\theta_j}\otimes I)C(U_{\theta_j}^*\otimes I)
=(I\otimes W^{-j})C(I\otimes W^j).
\]
The phase noise is the entire original odd noise matrix and the phase entropy is exactly \(\mathcal A_N\). Conversely let \(|v_j\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{\ell=0}^{N-1}e^{i\ell\theta_j}|\ell\rangle\) in a cycle register, with \(S|\ell\rangle=|\ell+1\bmod N\rangle\) and \(W_0|\ell\rangle=e^{i\theta_\ell}|\ell\rangle\). For the system charge components \(C_k\), \(k=\pm1\), use the observable
\[
B=C_1\otimes S^*+C_{-1}\otimes S,\qquad
\sigma=N^{-1}\sum_j J_j\otimes |v_j\rangle\langle v_j|.
\]
Since \(W_0SW_0^*=e^{2\pi i/N}S\), the observable conserves the total cyclic charge. The eigenvalues of \(S^*,S\) on \(v_j\) are \(e^{i\theta_j},e^{-i\theta_j}\); all their products in the squared noise agree exactly with the phase coefficients. The twirl of the ready state is \(\tau\otimes I_N/N\), where \(\tau=N^{-1}\sum_j J_j\). Its asymmetry is the discrete entropy
\[
H_N(J)=N^{-1}\sum_j\operatorname{Tr}(J_j\log J_j)-\operatorname{Tr}(\tau\log\tau).
\]
Thus the phase pair gives a complete finite cyclic model with identical noise and entropy. Appending the pure neutral spectral pointer keeps this identity and retains its entire carrier. The support, direct-sum and complete finite carrier conditions are preserved.

The supported Sylvester calculation of Theorem M.6.13el, with sums over the \(N\) angles, gives the same cap \(\|C\|\le M\) in the weighted optimization. Specifically, \(-2M Z\preceq ZX+XZ\preceq2MZ\) gives that order bound after every tensor insertion and summation. The supported solution of \(RC+CR=D\) then lies in \([-MI,MI]\). The Gibbs and entropy splitting identities also apply to the discrete normalized measure. This gives the first identity in (M.6.13en.1).

For the comparison of averages, write \(V(\theta)=V_{Z,C}(\theta)=\sum_{k=-2}^{2}V_ke^{ik\theta}\) on the real circle and continue this polynomial to complex \(\theta\). The positive partial test and \(\|C\|\le M\) imply \(\|V(\theta)\|\le K\) on the real circle, hence \(\|V_k\|\le K\) for every coefficient. For \(|\operatorname{Im}\theta|\le a\) it follows that
\[
\|V(\theta)\|\le K[1+2\cosh a+2\cosh(2a)].
\tag{M.6.13en.3}
\]
On \(\operatorname{supp}\tau\), let \(g(\theta)=\operatorname{Tr}\exp(\log\tau-V(\theta))\), with \(V\) compressed to this support. For any complex matrix \(T\) the ordered Duhamel series about \(\log\tau\) gives the dimension-independent bound
\[
|\operatorname{Tr}\exp(\log\tau+T)|\le e^{\|T\|}.
\]
In detail, the term with \(k\) insertions integrates over the ordered simplex of volume \(1/k!\). Its integrand is a trace of a product of \(k\) copies of \(T\) and \(\tau^{u_0},\ldots,\tau^{u_k}\), with \(u_j\ge0\), \(\sum_ju_j=1\). Schatten Hölder bounds it by \(\|T\|^k\prod_j\|\tau^{u_j}\|_{1/u_j}=\|T\|^k\), using the support identity norm at \(u_j=0\). Summing proves the claim. In particular the bound for \(g\) on the strip does not involve the smallest positive eigenvalue of \(\tau\).

Cauchy's contour shift by \(ia\) or \(-ia\) bounds each Fourier coefficient of \(g\) by \(\exp(K[1+2\cosh a+2\cosh(2a)])e^{-a|k|}\). Absolute convergence gives that the \(N\)-point mean and the integral differ only by the sum of Fourier coefficients at nonzero multiples of \(N\), whose total absolute bound is the right side of (M.6.13en.1) before multiplication by \(e^s\). The bound is uniform, so it also controls the difference of the two suprema. Both are at least \(e^{-s}\) using \(C=0\), and the logarithm on \([e^{-s},\infty)\) is \(e^s\)-Lipschitz. For a simple explicit choice, \(1+2\cosh a+2\cosh(2a)\le5e^{2a}\) for \(a\ge0\). If \(N>10K\), take \(a=\tfrac12\log(N/(10K))\) to get a bound
\[
\frac{2 e^{s+N/2}(10K/N)^{N/2}}{1-(10K/N)^{N/2}}.
\]
This proves the fixed-tester rate.

For the one-sided comparison, oddify any original apparatus and pinch its reference into fractional charge classes as in Theorem M.6.13el. Translate to integer charges within each retained class, then take those charges modulo \(N\). This leaves the chosen invariant observable admitted. The cyclic twirl has coarser projections than the integer twirl, so its entropy is at most that of the integer twirl: applying the latter pinching to the cyclic twirl produces the integer twirl, and pinching cannot decrease entropy. The ready-state entropy is unchanged in the reduction modulo \(N\). Consequently \(F_N^{\rm cyc}(r)\le F(r)\) and \(b_N^{\rm cyc}(Z)\le b(Z)\). No larger charge group is required in the cyclic comparison. For every cyclic apparatus and tester, weak duality gives \(F_N^{\rm cyc}(r)\ge b_N^{\rm cyc}(Z)-r\operatorname{Tr}Z\).

Finally, let \(T=a_s/(r-r_s)\) be the trace cap for one optimal original tester \(Z_*\) of Theorem M.6.13dc, using a fixed strict model with entropy \(a_s\). Choose this tester symmetric as in that theorem. If it has \(x,y>0\), the fixed-tester bound follows by the preceding weak duality. In general take \(Z_\epsilon=Z_*+\epsilon(|e\rangle\langle e|+|m\rangle\langle m|)\), \(0<\epsilon\le1\). Monotonicity of \(b\) in the tester gives \(b(Z_\epsilon)-r\operatorname{Tr}Z_\epsilon\ge F(r)-2r\epsilon\). Put \(T_0=T+2\). Its \(s\le T_0\), and \(x,y\ge\epsilon\) imply
\[
M^2=\frac{s^2}{4xy}\le\frac{s^2}{4\epsilon(s-\epsilon)}
\le\frac{T_0}{2\epsilon},\qquad K\le\frac{T_0(T_0+2)}{\epsilon}.
\]
The last inequality uses \((M+1)^2\le 2M^2+2\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}Z_\epsilon\le T_0\). Set \(G_1=1+2\cosh1+2\cosh2\) and \(L=2G_1T_0(T_0+2)\). For \(N\ge L\) choose \(\epsilon=L/N\) and \(a=1\). The pressure difference is then at most \(2e^{T_0}e^{-N/2}/(1-e^{-N})\). Thus
\[
0\le F(r)-F_N^{\rm cyc}(r)
\le\frac{2rL}{N}+\frac{2e^{T_0}e^{-N/2}}{1-e^{-N}} .
\]
This gives (M.6.13en.2) with explicit finite constants. The construction gives finite cyclic variational problems with unrestricted multiplicities. It requires neither an entropy-attaining original apparatus nor a bound on its dimension. \(\square\)

<a id="corollary-m613eo"></a>

<a id="corollary-m613eo-quadratic-frontier-comparison-by-phase-interpolation"></a>**Corollary M.6.13eo (Quadratic Frontier Comparison by Phase Interpolation).** Use the complete spin-one class and cyclic relaxation of Theorem M.6.13en, with arbitrary finite neutral multiplicities. Let \(a=\pi/N\), \(c=\sin(a)/a\), and let
\[
\Delta_N=(c^{-2}-1)(1+\sqrt r)^2.
\]
For any complete finite strict additive apparatus with error \(r_s<r\) and entropy \(a_s\), the cyclic and additive frontiers satisfy the sharper bound
\[
0\le F(r)-F_N^{\mathrm{cyc}}(r)
\le \frac{a_s\Delta_N}{r-r_s+\Delta_N}=O_r(N^{-2}).
\tag{M.6.13eo.1}
\]
*Proof.* Start with any cyclic phase pair \(J_j,C\) with its complete noise at most \(rI\). Extend \(J\) to the full circle by setting \(J_{\theta_j+t}=J_j\) for \(-a\le t<a\). Its mean and entropy are exactly those of the discrete pair. Put \(A_\theta=(U_\theta\otimes I)C(U_\theta^*\otimes I)\), and denote conditional expectation against \(J_j\) on the coefficient factor by \(\mathbb E_j\). Because \(C\) has only the two unit system harmonics,
\[
A_{\theta_j+t}=\cos t\,A_{\theta_j}+\sin t\,A'_{\theta_j},
\qquad A'_{\theta_j}=(U_{\pi/2}\otimes I)A_{\theta_j}(U_{\pi/2}^*\otimes I).
\]
Use \(C/c\) with the extended phase density. The average of the first moment over each symmetric arc is restored to the original one because \(\langle\cos t\rangle=c\) and \(\langle\sin t\rangle=0\), where \(\langle\cdot\rangle\) is the normalized arc average. The mixed terms in the square vanish because \(\langle\cos t\sin t\rangle=0\). Set \(D=N^{-1}\sum_j\mathbb E_j(A_{\theta_j}^2)\). The continuous phase noise is therefore the discrete phase noise plus
\[
\left(\frac{\langle\cos^2t\rangle}{c^2}-1\right)D
+\frac{\langle\sin^2t\rangle}{c^2}\,U_{\pi/2}DU_{\pi/2}^*.
\]
Both coefficients are nonnegative and their sum is \(c^{-2}-1\). For any system vector \(u\), apply the triangle inequality in the direct sum of Hilbert–Schmidt spaces to the components \(N^{-1/2}A_{\theta_j}(u\otimes J_j^{1/2})\), by writing \(A_{\theta_j}=(A_{\theta_j}-X\otimes I)+X\otimes I\). The first term has norm at most \(\sqrt r\|u\|\) by the given cyclic noise bound and the second at most \(\|u\|\) by the normalization of the discrete density and \(\|X\|=1\). Thus \(D\preceq(1+\sqrt r)^2 I\), and the extended phase noise is at most \((r+\Delta_N)I\). Mix this phase model with the phase image of the strict original apparatus at weight \(\Delta_N/(r-r_s+\Delta_N)\) on the strict branch, using the retained direct-sum flag. Its noise is at most \(rI\), while the entropy is at most the cyclic pair's entropy plus that weight times \(a_s\). Theorem M.6.13el applies to the repaired pair. For each positive tolerance choose a cyclic phase pair within that tolerance of its infimum; the correction bound is independent of the pair and its dimension. Letting the tolerance tend to zero proves (M.6.13eo.1). Finally \(c^{-2}-1=a^2/3+O(a^4)\). The sine interpolation is a phase-model proof. Its final additive implementation comes from the conserving finite approximation of Theorem M.6.13el. \(\square\)

<a id="theorem-m613ep"></a>

<a id="theorem-m613ep-finite-word-criterion-for-additive-attainment"></a>**Theorem M.6.13ep (Finite-Word Criterion for Additive Attainment).** Use the spin-one charge basis \(0,1,2\), the complete measurement class of Theorem M.6.13dc, and the phase representation of Theorem M.6.13el. Fix \(0<r<1\), and choose a parity- and reflection-symmetric maximizing tester \(Z\succeq0\) in (M.6.13dc.2). For a finite coefficient dimension \(d\), let \(\tau>0\) be a normalized matrix density, and let \(C=C^*\) on system and coefficients be odd under system parity. Define
\[
P_{\tau,C}=\int_{\mathbb T}\operatorname{Tr}\exp(\log\tau-V_{Z,C}(\theta)),\qquad
J_\theta=P_{\tau,C}^{-1}\exp(\log\tau-V_{Z,C}(\theta)).
\tag{M.6.13ep.1}
\]
Here \(V_{Z,C}\) is the positive weighted error of Theorem M.6.13el, and the circle measure is normalized. Consider these tests:
\[
\begin{gathered}
\int_{\mathbb T}J_\theta=\tau,\qquad P_{\tau,C}=e^{-b(Z)},\\
K_{\rm ph}(J,C)\preceq rI,\qquad
\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[Z(rI-K_{\rm ph}(J,C))\right]=0.
\tag{M.6.13ep.2}
\end{gathered}
\]
In addition use the alphabet consisting of \(\tau\) and the nonzero system blocks \(C_{ij}\), where the degree of \(\tau\) is zero and the degree of \(C_{ij}\) is \(i-j\). It is closed under adjoints, with opposite degree for adjoints. The degree of a word is the sum of the degrees of its letters. Require the finite trace conditions
\[
\operatorname{Tr}w=0\quad\text{for every word of nonzero degree and length at most }2d^2+1.
\tag{M.6.13ep.3}
\]
Then \(F(r)\) has a complete finite additive-charge attainer if and only if there exist \(d,\tau,C\) satisfying (M.6.13ep.2)–(M.6.13ep.3). If there is an attainer, this witness exists for every symmetric maximizing tester. For any particular finite \((\tau,C)\), (M.6.13ep.3) is equivalent to the finite real linear system in a Hermitian unknown \(Q\),
\[
[Q,\tau]=0,\qquad [Q,C_{ij}]=-(i-j)C_{ij}.
\tag{M.6.13ep.4}
\]
A solution can be chosen with integer charge values after charge translations on its reducing blocks. For \(x,y>0\) in the notation of Theorem M.6.13el, a globally saturated phase witness can equivalently be sought with its weighted observable norm cap \(M(x,y)\). The scalar equality \(P_{\tau,C}=e^{-b(Z)}\) compares to the pressure over every finite coefficient dimension. Saturation only within a fixed coefficient dimension does not give that equality.

*Proof.* First prove the trace criterion. If (M.6.13ep.4) holds, conjugating any word by \(e^{-itQ}\) multiplies it by \(e^{it\deg w}\). Trace invariance for every \(t\) forces (M.6.13ep.3), in fact at all word lengths.

Conversely let \(\mathcal A\) be the unital matrix \(*\)-algebra generated by the displayed alphabet. Let \(\mathcal A_\ell\) denote the linear span of words of length at most \(\ell\), with the empty word equal to \(I\). If \(\mathcal A_\ell=\mathcal A_{\ell+1}\), multiplication on the left by each generator preserves \(\mathcal A_\ell\), so all words already belong to it. Until this stabilization, dimensions increase strictly, and \(\dim\mathcal A\le d^2\). Hence words of length at most \(d^2-1\) span \(\mathcal A\). For \(\deg u\ne\deg v\), (M.6.13ep.3) implies that \(\operatorname{Tr}(u^*v)=0\) whenever \(|u|\le d^2-1\), \(|v|\le d^2\), since the product has length at most \(2d^2-1\) and nonzero degree. In particular the spans of short words of different degrees are pairwise orthogonal in the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product. For each \(t\), define the linear map \(\alpha_t\) on those spanning words by \(\alpha_t(w)=e^{it\deg w}w\). Orthogonality makes it well defined, unitary for the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product, and continuous in \(t\). Every word of length at most \(d^2\) belongs to its degree subspace: the same trace test makes its components in every different-degree short span zero. It follows for a generator \(g\) and a short word \(w\) that \(\alpha_t(gw)=\alpha_t(g)\alpha_t(w)\). By linearity this holds for every second argument in \(\mathcal A\), and by induction it holds for every word in the first argument. Thus \(\alpha_t\) is a unital \(*\)-automorphism. It preserves adjoints by the degree sign rule and \(\alpha_{-t}\) is its inverse.

The continuous automorphism group fixes each minimal central projection because their set is finite. Write the finite represented algebra as a direct sum of \(M_n(\mathbb C)\otimes I_m\). The derivative at zero of \(\alpha_t\) is a \(*\)-derivation on each matrix factor and has form \(-i[Q,\cdot]\) for some Hermitian \(Q\) in that factor. For a direct verification of the inner form, if \(\delta\) is a derivation on \(M_n\) with matrix units \(E_{ij}\), set \(T=\sum_i\delta(E_{i1})E_{1i}\). The product rule on \(E_{ab}E_{i1}=\delta_{bi}E_{a1}\) gives \([T,E_{ab}]=\delta(E_{ab})\). The \(*\)-rule implies that \(T+T^*\) is central, so its scalar self-adjoint part can be subtracted and the remainder is \(-iQ\). Extend by identity on the represented multiplicity factor. Since \(\alpha_{2\pi}\) is the identity, \(e^{-2\pi iQ}\) is scalar on each simple matrix block. Its eigenvalues therefore differ by integers. Subtract one eigenvalue on each block to make that block's charges integers, without changing its commutators. On the generators the derivative is \(i\deg(g)g\), giving (M.6.13ep.4). The displayed cutoff is therefore sufficient even when the matrix algebra acts reducibly.

Suppose now that there is a complete finite additive attainer. Use oddification by system parity, which keeps \(K\preceq rI\) and does not increase its cost. Use the complete twirl support and the compression of Theorem M.6.13dc. The state is faithful on that support by its finite-attainment theorem. The compressed observable still conserves additive charge, and its noise does not increase. For any symmetric maximizing tester, the new finite model gives equality in weak duality because its asymmetry is still \(F(r)\). If necessary pinch fractional charge classes as in Theorem M.6.13el. This preserves the odd noise and does not increase the asymmetry. Since the original optimum is a lower bound for the new feasible apparatus, the asymmetry remains \(F(r)\). Translate the fractional charge origins separately on the retained reducing classes. The twirl support, ready-state entropy, and all difference equations are preserved by this operation.

Let \(Q\) be the resulting reference charge, \(\sigma\) its ready state, and \(\tau=\mathcal G_Q\sigma\) on the chosen support. With \(C\) the compressed odd observable, conservation gives (M.6.13ep.4), so the trace test holds. The finite Gibbs equality (M.6.13dc.8) gives
\[
\sigma=e^{\log\tau-V_{Z,C}(0)}/e^{-b(Z)}.
\]
Conjugating by \(e^{-itQ}\) gives precisely the phase density (M.6.13ep.1), since \(V_{Z,C}(t)=e^{-itQ}V_{Z,C}(0)e^{\mathrm{itQ}}\). This covariance follows by rotating the entire system error square before its weighted partial trace and using conservation of \(C\). Hence the phase mean is \(\tau\), its whole noise is the finite apparatus's noise, and complementary slackness supplies all of (M.6.13ep.2). If \(x,y>0\), replace the weighted observable by the supported Sylvester minimizer in Theorem M.6.13dc if needed. On the faithful twirl support its odd quadratic form in each total-charge block is strictly positive, because its middle coefficient is \(y\sigma_{q,q}>0\) whenever a middle coordinate exists. There is consequently a unique odd minimizer on the supported blocks, already realized by the attainer, and it obeys \(M(x,y)\).

Conversely assume the tests. Use (M.6.13ep.3) to construct an integer charge \(Q\) as above. Then \(C\) conserves \(Q_S+Q\). Equation (M.6.13ep.4) makes \(\tau\) invariant and implies the same covariance of \(V_{Z,C}\). Thus \(J_\theta=e^{-iQ\theta}J_0e^{iQ\theta}\). Put \(\sigma=J_0\); its trace is one because the orbit has constant trace and the density in (M.6.13ep.1) is normalized. Its twirl is the mean \(\tau\). The phase and finite additive noise matrices coincide by covariance, and \(H(J)=\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)\). The Gibbs identity and the mean test give
\[
\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)+\operatorname{Tr}(ZK_\sigma(C))
=H(J)+\int\operatorname{Tr}(J_\theta V_{Z,C}(\theta))
=-\log P_{\tau,C}=b(Z).
\]
The scalar budget and the slackness condition therefore give \(\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)=b(Z)-r\operatorname{Tr}Z=F(r)\). The complete neutral spectral pointer and physical energy-host realization in Theorems M.6.13dc and M.6.13df implement this finite additive apparatus. Shifting charge origins on the reducing matrix blocks changes no charge differences or tested observable and can place all reference energies above a finite lower bound. The endpoint conditions are those of the additive apparatus, so the test introduces no wrap transitions or cyclic substitute. \(\square\)

*Finite pass and fail examples.* On \(d=2\), take \(\tau=\operatorname{diag}(p,1-p)\) with \(0<p<1\), and \(C_{01}=a|1\rangle\langle0|\), \(C_{12}=a|1\rangle\langle0|\) for real \(a\ne0\), with their adjoints. The charge \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\) solves (M.6.13ep.4), so this is an additive model with two nonzero adjacent couplings. For a failing candidate let \(C_{01}=aS\), \(C_{12}=aS\), where \(S\) is the two-dimensional cyclic shift, and take \(\tau=I/2\). Each displayed off-diagonal generator has trace zero, but \(C_{01}^2=a^2I\) has degree \(-2\) and nonzero trace. It violates the mixed-word test even though the couplings can be used as phase coefficients or in a cyclic construction. These examples test additive realizability of the coefficient matrices. Global saturation at a specified \(r\) is the separate requirement (M.6.13ep.2).

<a id="theorem-m613eq"></a>

<a id="theorem-m613eq-sharp-unrestricted-high-accuracy-spin-one-entropy"></a>**Theorem M.6.13eq (Sharp Unrestricted High-Accuracy Spin-One Entropy).** For the complete finite spin-one measurement class of Theorem M.6.13dc, let \(F(r)\) be the entropy infimum at squared all-input error at most \(r\). Then
\[
\lim_{r\downarrow0}\left[F(r)-\frac12\log\frac1r\right]
=\frac{\log(2\pi)-1}{2}.
\tag{M.6.13eq.1}
\]
The lower estimate is uniform in every finite reference dimension, real charge spectrum, multiplicity, and complete mixed ready state. Together with Theorem M.6.13cb it shows \(F(r)=\Phi(1-r)+o(1)\) at this endpoint.

*Proof.* Use the full matrix phase representation of Theorem M.6.13el, with a positive coefficient density \(J_\theta\), and a constant odd Hermitian observable
\[
C=\begin{pmatrix}0&A&0\\ A^*&0&B\\0&B^*&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
All angle integrals use \(d\mu=d\theta/(2\pi)\). Suppose the full noise is at most \(rI\). Write \(L=(A+B)/\sqrt2\), \(T=(A-B)/\sqrt2\), and define Hermitian coefficient operators
\[
R_\theta=\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta}L)-I,\quad
I_\theta=\operatorname{Im}(e^{-i\theta}L),\quad
D_\theta=\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta}T),\quad
E_\theta=\operatorname{Im}(e^{-i\theta}T),
\]
where \(\operatorname{Re}V=(V+V^*)/2\), \(\operatorname{Im}V=(V-V^*)/(2i)\). In the system basis \((e,m,f)\) of Theorem M.6.13dc, the rotated error \(U_\theta C U_\theta^*-X\otimes I\) has the exact block matrix
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
0&R_\theta+iE_\theta&0\\
R_\theta-iE_\theta&0&D_\theta-iI_\theta\\
0&D_\theta+iI_\theta&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{M.6.13eq.2}
\]
For example, its \(e,m\) entry is \((e^{-i\theta}A+e^{i\theta}B^*)/\sqrt2-I\), and its \(f,m\) entry is \((e^{-i\theta}A-e^{i\theta}B^*)/\sqrt2\). This fixes the signs without any commutativity assumption.

Put \(S_\theta=R_\theta+iE_\theta\) and \(T'_\theta=D_\theta+iI_\theta\). The three input noise diagonals are the integrated expectations of \(S_\theta S_\theta^*\), \(S_\theta^*S_\theta+{T'_\theta}^*T'_\theta\), and \(T'_\theta {T'_\theta}^*\). Each diagonal is at most \(r\). Since both middle terms are positive, each of the four ordered products separately has integrated expectation at most \(r\). Their pairwise sums satisfy \(S_\theta S_\theta^*+S_\theta^*S_\theta=2(R_\theta^2+E_\theta^2)\) and \(T'_\theta {T'_\theta}^*+{T'_\theta}^*T'_\theta=2(D_\theta^2+I_\theta^2)\). In particular,
\[
\int\operatorname{Tr}J_\theta R_\theta^2\,d\mu\le r,\qquad
\int\operatorname{Tr}J_\theta I_\theta^2\,d\mu\le r.
\tag{M.6.13eq.3}
\]

The classical-quantum law with angle \(\Theta\) and coefficient register \(R\) has angle density \(p(\theta)=\operatorname{Tr}J_\theta\) relative to \(\mu\), and normalized conditional state \(J_\theta/p(\theta)\) when \(p(\theta)>0\). Write \(h(\Theta)\) for differential entropy relative to unnormalized angle measure \(d\theta\), and \(I(\Theta:R)\) for the information of this classical-quantum law. The entropy decomposition gives
\[
H(J)=\log(2\pi)-h(\Theta)+I(\Theta:R).
\tag{M.6.13eq.4}
\]
This identity follows by inserting \(J_\theta=p(\theta)\rho_\theta\) into (M.6.13el.1). It suffices to consider \(H(J)<\infty\), so the differential entropy and all finite-register entropy terms here are finite. For a deterministic finite bin \(G\) of \(\Theta\), the ordinary and classical-quantum chain rules give
\[
H(J)=\log(2\pi)-H(G|R)-h(\Theta|G)+I(\Theta:R|G).
\tag{M.6.13eq.5}
\]
For example, the classical-quantum chain rule follows by grouping the angle integral by the bins and inserting their mean density matrices into the entropy difference. All conditional quantities are averaged over the occupied bins.

Fix a small Cartesian mesh \(\delta>0\). Quantize \(\cos\Theta\) and \(\sin\Theta\) with intervals of length \(\delta\), using shifts of their grids, and let \(G=(G_1,G_2)\) be their joint label. Measuring the Hermitian coefficient observable \(\operatorname{Re}L\) estimates \(\cos\Theta\). Its error operator at angle \(\theta\) is
\[
\operatorname{Re}L-\cos\theta\,I=\cos\theta\,R_\theta-\sin\theta\,I_\theta,
\]
and similarly \(\operatorname{Im}L-\sin\theta\,I=\sin\theta\,R_\theta+\cos\theta\,I_\theta\). The integrated squared errors of these separate projective measurements are at most \(4r\) by (M.6.13eq.3) and the triangle inequality in the integrated Hilbert–Schmidt norm. The outcomes may be clipped to \([-1,1]\) before quantizing, without increasing either error.

For a fixed coordinate, choose its grid shift uniformly over one grid period. For each true coordinate value the probability that it lies within distance \(b\) of a grid boundary is at most \(2b/\delta\), for \(0<b<\delta/2\). Fubini therefore gives a deterministic shift with true-coordinate collar probability at most \(2b/\delta\), for any angle law \(p\). The separate measurement disagrees with that coordinate's bin only on this collar or on an estimation error of magnitude at least \(b\). Its bin error probability is at most \(2b/\delta+4r/b^2\). Choose \(b=r^{1/3}\) for all sufficiently small \(r\). Each bin alphabet has size at most \(2+\lceil2/\delta\rceil\), independently of the shifts, angle law, and coefficient dimension. Data processing and the finite Fano inequality bound \(H(G_i|R)\) by the binary entropy of an error probability tending uniformly to zero, plus that probability times the logarithm of the alphabet size. Quantum conditional entropy subadditivity gives \(H(G_1,G_2|R)\le H(G_1|R)+H(G_2|R)\), by strong subadditivity. Thus \(H(G|R)\le o_\delta(1)\) as \(r\downarrow0\), uniformly over the whole phase class. The two coordinate measurements need not be jointly implemented.

Any nonempty Cartesian bin on the unit circle has pairwise chord distances at most \(\sqrt2\,\delta\). Pick a point of the bin as its angle center \(\varphi_g\). Every angle in that bin lies on the arc \(\theta=\varphi_g+t\), \(|t|\le w_\delta:=2\arcsin(\delta/\sqrt2)\), with an unambiguous representative when \(w_\delta<\pi/2\). Conditional on the bin, measure \(\operatorname{Im}(e^{-i\varphi_g}L)\) on the coefficient register. If the true angle is \(\theta=\varphi_g+t\), its error as an estimate of \(\sin t\) is the Hermitian operator
\[
\operatorname{Im}(e^{-i\varphi_g}L)-\sin t\,I
=\cos t\,I_\theta+\sin t\,R_\theta.
\]
Clip the real outcome to \([-\sin w_\delta,\sin w_\delta]\) and apply \(\arcsin\) on this interval to obtain a real angle estimate \(\widehat t\). By (M.6.13eq.3), the triangle inequality and the Lipschitz constant \(1/\cos w_\delta\) for this inverse, its total mean squared error averaged over bins is at most
\[
D_r=\frac{r(1+\sin w_\delta)^2}{\cos^2 w_\delta}.
\tag{M.6.13eq.6}
\]
The use of the bin here is conditioning in an information inequality. It requires neither a joint measurement of the two coarse coordinates nor a source intervention on the original measurement apparatus.

Let \(Y\) be the outcome of the bin-dependent measurement, with each outcome labeled together with its given bin. Data processing inside each bin gives \(I(\Theta:R|G)\ge I(\Theta:Y|G)\). Entropy of the translated real angle \(t\) in a bin is its arc differential entropy, with Jacobian one. For each conditional outcome law of \(t\), relative entropy against the Gaussian of variance \(D_r>0\) and mean \(\widehat t\) gives a differential entropy upper bound \(\frac12\log(2\pi D_r)+\mathbb E[(t-\widehat t)^2|G,Y]/(2D_r)\). The conditional laws are absolutely continuous on their arcs for occupied outcomes, since the original angle law has a density. The bound also holds if a conditional differential entropy is \(-\infty\). Averaging and (M.6.13eq.6) give \(h(\Theta|G,Y)\le\tfrac12\log(2\pi e D_r)\). Therefore (M.6.13eq.5) implies
\[
H(J)\ \ge\
\frac12\log\frac1r+\frac{\log(2\pi)-1}{2}
-\log\!\frac{1+\sin w_\delta}{\cos w_\delta}-o_\delta(1).
\tag{M.6.13eq.7}
\]
Every constant in the error term comes from the fixed finite bin alphabets and their uniform error estimate. Thus this lower bound applies to the infimum over all finite coefficient dimensions, without interchanging that infimum with an uncontrolled limit. Take \(r\downarrow0\) at each fixed mesh, and then \(\delta\downarrow0\). The resulting lower limit matches the upper limit from Theorem M.6.13cb and the expansion of \(\Phi(1-r)\) in Theorem M.6.13q. This proves (M.6.13eq.1). \(\square\)

<a id="corollary-m613er"></a>

<a id="corollary-m613er-explicit-uniform-high-accuracy-lower-curve"></a>**Corollary M.6.13er (Explicit Uniform High-Accuracy Lower Curve).** For the complete finite spin-one frontier \(F(r)\) of Theorem M.6.13dc and \(0<r<1\), put \(m_\delta=\sqrt{3r/4}/\delta\) and
\[
g(m)=\log(1+2m)+m\log(1+1/m),\qquad g(0)=0.
\]
For every \(0<\delta<1\),
\[
F(r)\ \ge\
\frac12\log\frac1r+\frac{\log(2\pi)-1}{2}
+\frac12\log(1-\delta^2/2)-2g(m_\delta).
\tag{M.6.13er.1}
\]
In particular,
\[
F(r)\ \ge\ \frac12\log\frac1r+\frac{\log(2\pi)-1}{2}
-O\!\left(r^{1/3}\log(1/r)\right).
\tag{M.6.13er.2}
\]
The bound (M.6.13er.1) improves the lower curve in (M.6.13eg.2) for every sufficiently small positive \(r\). It applies uniformly over all finite coefficient dimensions and ready-state multiplicities.

*Proof.* Use \(J_\theta,L,R_\theta,I_\theta\) from the complete phase problem in Theorem M.6.13eq. Define \(v_R=\int\operatorname{Tr}J_\theta R_\theta^2\,d\mu\) and \(v_I=\int\operatorname{Tr}J_\theta I_\theta^2\,d\mu\). In the notation of that theorem the three noise diagonals sum to the integrated expectation of \(2(R_\theta^2+E_\theta^2+D_\theta^2+I_\theta^2)\). Each diagonal is at most \(r\). Together with (M.6.13eq.3), this gives \(v_R,v_I\le r\) and \(v_R+v_I\le3r/2\).

Choose an independent uniform angle \(\alpha\), rotate Cartesian coordinates by \(-\alpha\), and choose each of the two grid offsets independently and uniformly in \([0,\delta)\). Denote these independent public variables by \(S\). At fixed \(S\), let \(G=(G_1,G_2)\) be the integer cell of \((\cos(\Theta-\alpha),\sin(\Theta-\alpha))\) in the shifted square grid of side \(\delta\). The two labels can be estimated separately by measuring the Hermitian operators \(\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\alpha}L)\), \(\operatorname{Im}(e^{-i\alpha}L)\) and applying the corresponding coordinate grids to their real outcomes. Let \(\widehat G_i\) be the result of the respective measurement. The angle-averaged squared coordinate errors, averaged also over \(\alpha\), are each \((v_R+v_I)/2\le3r/4\): for the first coordinate the error operator is \(\cos(\theta-\alpha)R_\theta-\sin(\theta-\alpha)I_\theta\), and for the second it is \(\sin(\theta-\alpha)R_\theta+\cos(\theta-\alpha)I_\theta\). Orthogonality of sine and cosine removes both ordered cross terms on integrating over \(\alpha\).

For fixed true and estimated real coordinates \(x,y\), the expected absolute difference between their integer bins under a uniform shift is \(|x-y|/\delta\). Indeed the difference counts the number of grid boundaries between the two real values, and the expected count for an interval of length \(t\) is \(t/\delta\) by integrating its indicator over a single grid period. The measurements do not depend on the grid offsets. By Cauchy–Schwarz this gives \(\mathbb E|G_i-\widehat G_i|\le m_\delta\). If an integer variable \(D\) has \(\mathbb E|D|\le m\), comparison by relative entropy with the probability law \((1-q)q^{|k|}/(1+q)\), \(q=m/(1+m)\), gives \(H(D)\le g(m)\), with the zero case obtained directly. The comparison applies to arbitrary integer laws, for example first to finite truncations and then by the entropy upper bound and monotone convergence on the nonnegative entropy terms. By data processing for each of the two measurements,
\[
H(G_i|R,S)\le H(G_i|\widehat G_i,S)
=H(G_i-\widehat G_i|\widehat G_i,S)
\le H(G_i-\widehat G_i)\le g(m_\delta).
\]
Strong subadditivity therefore gives \(H(G|R,S)\le2g(m_\delta)\). No joint measurement of the two quadratures is required.

For a realized \(S\) and \(G\), take \(\varphi\) to be the angle of the Euclidean cell center, expressed in the original coordinates. At each true point the displacement from it to the cell center has norm at most \(\delta/\sqrt2\), so that center is nonzero. With \(t=\Theta-\varphi\) chosen in \((-\pi,\pi]\), tangent geometry gives \(|t|\le w_\delta:=\arcsin(\delta/\sqrt2)<\pi/2\). To see this, for a fixed unit point and any center within distance \(\delta/\sqrt2<1\), its angle has positive cosine and its perpendicular distance to the line through the origin and the center is \(|\sin t|\), which is at most the distance to the center itself.

For a fixed true angle \(\theta\), uniform grid offsets make the cell-center displacement in the rotated frame uniform in the centered square of side \(\delta\), independent of \(\alpha\). Uniform \(\alpha\) makes its displacement in the original frame rotationally and reflection invariant. Consequently the conditional distribution of \(t\) is symmetric about zero and independent of \(\theta\). Given \(S,G\), measure \(\operatorname{Im}(e^{-i\varphi}L)\). Its error as an estimate of \(\sin t\) is \(\cos t\,I_\theta+\sin t\,R_\theta\). Since the distribution just proved has \(\mathbb E_S(\sin t\cos t\mid\Theta=\theta)=0\) and constant \(\mathbb E_S(\sin^2t\mid\Theta=\theta)\), the total quadratic loss after averaging \(S,\Theta\) is a convex combination of \(v_I,v_R\), hence at most \(r\). Clip the outcome to \([-\sin w_\delta,\sin w_\delta]\) and apply \(\arcsin\). The resulting angle estimate has mean squared error at most
\[
D_r=\frac{r}{\cos^2w_\delta}=\frac{r}{1-\delta^2/2}.
\]
These measurements are used conditionally in the entropy bound and introduce no additional source operation.

Apply (M.6.13eq.5) at every fixed \(S\) and then average it. Its left side is unchanged because \(S\) was independent of the phase law and its coefficient register. The entropy of the real coordinate \(t\) in each occupied cell is the angle entropy on that arc. Data processing for the cell-dependent measurement and the Gaussian relative entropy bound used in Theorem M.6.13eq, with the same comparison variance \(D_r>0\) in every cell and outcome, give
\[
H(J)\ge\log(2\pi)-H(G|R,S)-\frac12\log(2\pi e D_r).
\]
The estimate holds for all phase laws with finite \(H(J)\), and is automatic at infinite cost. Inserting the uniform bin bound proves (M.6.13er.1). Take \(\delta=r^{1/6}\) for sufficiently small \(r\) to obtain (M.6.13er.2). Finally the lower curve \(\Phi(v_*(r))\) of Theorem M.6.13eg has additive constant \([\log(8\pi/(3+2\sqrt2))-1]/2\) by its expansion there and Theorem M.6.13q. This is smaller than the constant in (M.6.13er.2) by \(\frac12\log[(3+2\sqrt2)/4]>0\). The difference remains positive for all sufficiently small \(r\). \(\square\)

<a id="theorem-m613es"></a>

<a id="theorem-m613es-strict-noncommuting-advantage-at-every-interior-spin-one-error"></a>**Theorem M.6.13es (Strict Noncommuting Advantage at Every Interior Spin-One Error).** For the complete finite spin-one problem of Theorem M.6.13dc and every \(0<r<1\), the exact commuting phase frontier of Theorem M.6.13em is strictly above the unrestricted frontier:
\[
F(r)<F_{\rm com}(r)=\Phi(1-r).
\tag{M.6.13es.1}
\]
At each such error the strict upper improvement is obtained in coefficient dimension two in Theorem M.6.13el. In particular it gives finite additive-charge apparatuses below \(\Phi(1-r)\) at the prescribed error, with their complete physical reference and pointer. Neither the two-dimensional phase optimum nor the unrestricted value is identified.

*Proof.* Fix \(0<r<1\) and let \(t_*=\sqrt{1-r}\). For \(\kappa>0\), write
\[
j_\kappa(\theta)=\frac{e^{\kappa\cos\theta}}{I_0(\kappa)},\qquad
t(\kappa)=\int j_\kappa\cos\theta\,d\mu,\qquad
v(\kappa)=\int j_\kappa\sin^2\theta\,d\mu=\frac{t(\kappa)}{\kappa},
\]
with \(d\mu=d\theta/(2\pi)\). The last identity follows by integrating the derivative of \(\sin\theta\,e^{\kappa\cos\theta}\) over the circle. There is a unique \(\kappa_*>0\) with \(t(\kappa_*)=t_*\) by Theorem M.6.13l, and \(t'(\kappa_*)>0\) because it is the variance of \(\cos\theta\) under the strictly positive density \(j_{\kappa_*}\).

Choose any \(p,q>0\) with \(p+q=1\) and \(p\ne q\), set \(\tau=\operatorname{diag}(p,q)\), and put \(Y=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). For \(|\epsilon|<\sqrt{pq}\) use
\[
J_{\kappa,\epsilon}(\theta)=j_\kappa(\theta)(\tau+\epsilon\sin\theta\,Y).
\tag{M.6.13es.2}
\]
These densities are positive definite, have total mass one and have mean \(\tau\). Their first Fourier moment is
\[
T=\int e^{i\theta}J_{\kappa,\epsilon}(\theta)\,d\mu
=t(\kappa)\tau+i\epsilon v(\kappa)Y.
\tag{M.6.13es.3}
\]

Use an odd constant observable with upper adjacent blocks \(A=C_{01}\), \(B=C_{12}\), and put \(a=1/\sqrt2\). The error for middle input is the integrated sum of the two squared output components \(e^{-i\theta}A-aI\) and \(e^{i\theta}B^*-aI\). The first quadratic has constant \(a^2\), quadratic term \(\operatorname{Tr}(\tau A^*A)\), and linear term \(-2a\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(T^*A)\). It is minimized at \(A=aT\tau^{-1}\). The second, in variable \(B^*\), is minimized at \(B^*=aT^*\tau^{-1}\). Both formulas follow by completing the corresponding matrix squares in the Hilbert–Schmidt norm. Hence the exact middle-input improvement relative to the zero observable is
\[
\frac12\operatorname{Tr}(T\tau^{-1}T^*+T^*\tau^{-1}T)
=t(\kappa)^2+\epsilon^2v(\kappa)^2\left(\frac1p+\frac1q\right).
\tag{M.6.13es.4}
\]
In (M.6.13es.3) the two off-diagonal cross terms in these products cancel, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(Y\tau^{-1}Y)=1/p+1/q\). All remaining noise directions are still tested.

Write \(d_0=1/p+1/q\). The derivative of \(t(\kappa)^2\) at \(\kappa_*\) is strictly positive. The implicit function theorem applied to (M.6.13es.4) therefore gives, for sufficiently small \(\epsilon\), a positive \(\kappa=\kappa(\epsilon)\) near \(\kappa_*\) for which the improvement is \(t_*^2=1-r\). Its squared first scalar moment obeys
\[
t(\kappa(\epsilon))^2=t_*^2-\epsilon^2v(\kappa_*)^2d_0+o(\epsilon^2).
\tag{M.6.13es.5}
\]
At \(\epsilon=0\) the chosen blocks give \(C=t_*X\otimes I\). As in Theorem M.6.13em, its full matrix noise is diagonal in \((e,m,f)\) with middle entry \(r\) and endpoint entries
\[
k_e=\int j_{\kappa_*}(t_*\cos\theta-1)^2\,d\mu,\qquad
k_f=\int j_{\kappa_*}t_*^2\sin^2\theta\,d\mu.
\]
Both are positive and their sum is \(r\). The two endpoint eigenvalues are consequently strictly less than \(r\). Their block is continuous under this perturbation, because \(\tau\) is fixed and faithful, the blocks \(A,B\) are given by (M.6.13es.3), and the density is smooth in the parameters. System parity separates the middle coordinate from the endpoint block for every odd \(C\) and for every \(\theta\): the square of the odd error is even. Thus the middle value stays exactly \(r\) and the endpoint block remains strictly below \(rI\) for sufficiently small \(|\epsilon|\). The full worst-case squared error of the perturbed phase pair is exactly \(r\).

For the entropy, set \(\ell=(\log p-\log q)/(p-q)\). For a real scalar \(u\) near zero the eigenvalues of \(\tau+uY\) near \(p\) and \(q\) respectively are \(p+u^2/(p-q)+O(u^4)\) and \(q-u^2/(p-q)+O(u^4)\). This follows from its quadratic characteristic polynomial. Hence
\[
\operatorname{Tr}[(\tau+uY)\log(\tau+uY)]-\operatorname{Tr}(\tau\log\tau)
=\ell u^2+O(u^4).
\]
The trace of \(\tau+uY\) is one. Factoring out \(j_\kappa\) in (M.6.13es.2) and integrating gives
\[
H(J_{\kappa,\epsilon})=\Phi(t(\kappa)^2)+\epsilon^2 v(\kappa)\ell+O(\epsilon^4),
\]
with bounded remainder for \(\kappa\) near \(\kappa_*\). The derivative of the scalar frontier is \(\Phi'(t_*^2)=\kappa_*/(2t_*)=1/(2v(\kappa_*))\), either by the scalar formula in Theorem M.6.13l or by differentiating its Legendre relation. Substituting (M.6.13es.5) therefore gives
\[
H(J_{\kappa(\epsilon),\epsilon})=
\Phi(1-r)+\epsilon^2 v(\kappa_*)\left(\ell-\frac{d_0}{2}\right)+o(\epsilon^2).
\tag{M.6.13es.6}
\]
Here \(\ell=\int_0^1[(1-u)p+uq]^{-1}\,du\) is strictly less than \((1/p+1/q)/2\), by strict convexity of \(x\mapsto1/x\) between the distinct positive endpoints. The quadratic coefficient in (M.6.13es.6) is strictly negative. Taking sufficiently small nonzero \(\epsilon\) yields a feasible phase pair below the commuting frontier. For such \(\epsilon\) its density matrices at opposite nonzero sine values do not commute, since \([\tau,Y]\ne0\).

Theorem M.6.13el converts this finite-dimensional phase pair to complete finite additive-charge apparatuses with the original error bound and costs converging to its strict entropy improvement. If exact equality in the largest error eigenvalue is required, the continuous rescaling of Theorem M.6.13de preserves asymmetry and the charge constraints. At sufficiently fine finite grades the strict gap survives the approximation. This proves (M.6.13es.1). \(\square\)

<a id="corollary-m613et"></a>

<a id="corollary-m613et-order-r-noncommuting-improvement-and-twirl-conditioning"></a>**Corollary M.6.13et (Order-\(r\) Noncommuting Improvement and Twirl Conditioning).** In the complete finite spin-one class of Theorem M.6.13dc, the unrestricted high-accuracy frontier satisfies
\[
F(r)\le \Phi(1-r)-\frac{\,8/3-2\log 3\,}{100}\,r+O(r^2)
\quad (r\downarrow0).
\tag{M.6.13et.1}
\]
At every \(0<r<1\), consider a complete finite apparatus with \(K\preceq rI\) and \(\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)\le h<\Phi(1-r)\). Let \(k\) be the condition number of its ready-state charge twirl \(\tau=\mathcal G_Q\sigma\) on its support. Then
\[
k>
\frac{1+\sqrt{1-\Phi^{-1}(h)/(1-r)}}
     {1-\sqrt{1-\Phi^{-1}(h)/(1-r)}}.
\tag{M.6.13et.2}
\]
A zero entropy budget at \(r<1\) is infeasible. For each fixed \(r\), Theorem M.6.13es supplies a feasible cost below \(\Phi(1-r)\), so (M.6.13et.2) excludes a nonempty interval of twirl condition numbers from any finite frontier attainer at that error.

*Proof of (M.6.13et.1).* Use the phase family (M.6.13es.2) with \(p=3/4\), \(q=1/4\), and fixed \(\epsilon=1/10\). Write \(t=I_1(\kappa)/I_0(\kappa)\), \(v=t/\kappa\), \(T_0=Y\tau^{-1}\), and \(d_0=1/p+1/q=16/3\). The complete middle-input noise of its minimizing adjacent blocks is
\[
r(\kappa)=1-t^2-\epsilon^2 v^2d_0
=\kappa^{-1}+O(\kappa^{-2}).
\]
The Bessel expansions of Theorem M.6.13q give \(t=1-\frac1{2\kappa}+O(\kappa^{-2})\). The continuous positive function \(r(\kappa)\) tends to zero, so every sufficiently small prescribed \(r>0\) has a solution on its large-\(\kappa\) branch by the intermediate value theorem. Every such solution sufficiently far along satisfies \(\kappa^{-1}=r+O(r^2)\).

It remains to keep both other input errors below \(r(\kappa)\) with \(\epsilon\) fixed. In the basis \((e,m,f)\) the two endpoint-to-middle error blocks, in row \(e\) and row \(f\) respectively, are
\[
S_\theta=(t\cos\theta-1)I+\epsilon v\sin\theta\,T_0,\qquad
D_\theta=i(-t\sin\theta\,I+\epsilon v\cos\theta\,T_0).
\]
They follow directly from (M.6.13es.3) and the two middle-input least-squares coefficients there. The other nonzero error blocks are their adjoints. Conjugating the neutral factor by \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) under \(\theta\mapsto-\theta\) preserves \(J_\theta\) in the reflected comparison, takes \(S_\theta\) to its even transform and \(D_\theta\) to its odd transform. Thus the integrated endpoint off-diagonal of the noise is zero. Its endpoint diagonals \(k_e,k_f\) are the expectations of \(S_\theta S_\theta^*\) and \(D_\theta D_\theta^*\), and the middle diagonal is the expectation of \(S_\theta^*S_\theta+D_\theta^*D_\theta\). Subtracting gives the exact identity
\[
k_e+k_f-r(\kappa)=\epsilon^2v^2\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\tau[T_0,T_0^*]\right)
=\frac{64}{9}\epsilon^2v^2.
\tag{M.6.13et.3}
\]
Indeed the two scalar-plus-operator blocks have commutators \(\epsilon^2v^2\sin^2\theta[T_0,T_0^*]\) and \(\epsilon^2v^2\cos^2\theta[T_0,T_0^*]\), and the neutral mean of \(J_\theta\) is \(\tau\).

For the bright error, under \(j_\kappa\) one has \(\mathbb E(1-\cos\theta)=1-t\) and \(\mathbb E(1-\cos\theta)^2=2-2t-v\). The next term of the fixed-order Bessel expansion used in (M.6.13j.6) gives \(t=1-1/(2\kappa)-1/(8\kappa^2)+O(\kappa^{-3})\): the two bracket series, for \(I_0\) and \(I_1\) after removing their common leading factor, are \(1+1/(8\kappa)+9/(128\kappa^2)+O(\kappa^{-3})\) and \(1-3/(8\kappa)-15/(128\kappa^2)+O(\kappa^{-3})\). Thus the latter moment is \(3/(4\kappa^2)+O(\kappa^{-3})\). Consequently
\[
k_e=\mathbb E_{j_\kappa}(t\cos\theta-1)^2+O(\kappa^{-3})
=\frac{3}{2\kappa^2}+O(\kappa^{-3}).
\]
For the first equality, the neutral trace of the scalar–\(T_0\) cross term is zero against \(\tau\), and its remaining contribution against \(\epsilon\sin\theta\,Y\) is \(O(v\,\mathbb E[\sin^2\theta\,|1-t\cos\theta|])=O(\kappa^{-3})\). This uses \(\sin^2\theta\le2(1-\cos\theta)\), the preceding two moments, and \(1-t\cos\theta=(1-t)+t(1-\cos\theta)\). The quadratic \(T_0\) term is \(O(v^2\mathbb E\sin^2\theta)=O(\kappa^{-3})\). For the second equality, expand \((1-t\cos\theta)^2=[(1-t)+t(1-\cos\theta)]^2\), whose three leading coefficients in units of \(\kappa^{-2}\) are \(1/4,1/2,3/4\). Now (M.6.13et.3) gives
\[
k_f-r(\kappa)=\left(\frac{64}{900}-\frac32\right)\kappa^{-2}+O(\kappa^{-3})<0
\]
for sufficiently large \(\kappa\). Also \(k_e=O(\kappa^{-2})<r(\kappa)\). The full phase model therefore has largest noise eigenvalue exactly \(r(\kappa)\).

The entropy expansion used in Theorem M.6.13es has an error bounded by a constant times \(\epsilon^4\mathbb E_{j_\kappa}\sin^4\theta=O(\kappa^{-2})\) in the present fixed-\(\epsilon\) regime. The bound follows from the fourth-order remainder of the finite \(2\times2\) trace formula on the compact interval \(|u|\le\epsilon<\sqrt{pq}\), and from the above second moment of \(1-\cos\theta\). With \(\ell=(\log p-\log q)/(p-q)=2\log3\), it follows that
\[
H(J_{\kappa,\epsilon})=\Phi(t^2)+\epsilon^2 v\ell+O(\kappa^{-2}).
\]
Since \(1-r=t^2+\epsilon^2v^2d_0\), integration of the scalar derivative \(\Phi'(u)=\kappa(u)/(2\sqrt u)\), where \(I_1(\kappa(u))/I_0(\kappa(u))=\sqrt u\), gives
\[
\Phi(1-r)-\Phi(t^2)=\frac{\epsilon^2d_0}{2}\,\kappa^{-1}+O(\kappa^{-2}).
\]
Indeed \(1-u=\kappa^{-1}+O(\kappa^{-2})\) throughout that interval, so \(\Phi'(u)=\kappa/2+O(1)\) uniformly there. Use \(v=\kappa^{-1}+O(\kappa^{-2})\) and \(\kappa^{-1}=r+O(r^2)\). The phase conversion of Theorem M.6.13el, with its counted finite conserving apparatuses, proves (M.6.13et.1).

*Proof of (M.6.13et.2).* Diagonalize each block of \(\tau\), with its strictly positive occupied eigenvalues \(p_i\). Positivity forces matrix entries of \(\sigma\) touching its zero-population directions to vanish. For each adjacent-charge pair of occupied eigenvectors set
\[
z_{ij}=\frac{p_i-p_j}{p_i+p_j},\qquad
\eta_{ij}=\frac{2|\sigma_{ij}|^2}{p_i+p_j}.
\]
Taking the pure middle-input tester in the two separate square completions of (M.6.13eg.5) gives its exact gain
\[
g_m=\sum_{\rm edges}\frac{\eta_{ij}}{1-z_{ij}^2}.
\]
All sums here are finite, with positive denominators on occupied directions. Equivalently this is the limit \(d\uparrow1\) of (M.6.13eg.5), term by term, with the zero directions deleted, and the same square completion realizes the middle-only infimum. The given all-input budget entails \(g_m\ge1-r\). If \(k\) is the ratio of the greatest to least occupied eigenvalue then
\[
|z_{ij}|\le\frac{k-1}{k+1},\qquad
\eta:=\sum_{\rm edges}\eta_{ij}\ge\frac{4k}{(1+k)^2}(1-r).
\]
The strict one-gap entropy theorem of Theorem M.6.13l gives \(\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)>\Phi(\eta)\) since \(\eta>0\). Thus \(4k/(1+k)^2<\Phi^{-1}(h)/(1-r)\). Solving this inequality for \(k\ge1\) yields (M.6.13et.2). No charge degeneracy, spectral shape, mixed-state or neutral-dimension restriction was added. \(\square\)

<a id="corollary-m613eu"></a>

<a id="corollary-m613eu-uniform-distance-from-commuting-readout-coefficients"></a>**Corollary M.6.13eu (Uniform Distance from Commuting Readout Coefficients).** Use the complete spin-one matrix phase problem of Theorem M.6.13el at \(0<r<1\). For a normalized matrix phase density \(J_\theta\) and two constant odd Hermitian observables \(C,C_0\) on the same system and coefficient space, set
\[
d_J(C,C_0)=\sup_{\|u\|=1}
\left[\int_{\mathbb T}
 \left\|(U_\theta\otimes I)(C-C_0)(U_\theta^*\otimes I)
      (u\otimes J_\theta^{1/2})\right\|_2^2\,d\mu(\theta)\right]^{1/2}.
\tag{M.6.13eu.1}
\]
Here \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is the Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the operator from the coefficient space, \(u\) is a system vector, and \(\mu\) is the normalized circle measure. If \(K_{\rm ph}(J,C)\preceq rI\) and \(H(J)\le h<\Phi(1-r)\), then every \(C_0\) whose neutral coefficient blocks and their adjoints are simultaneously diagonal in one orthonormal basis satisfies
\[
\|C-C_0\|\ \ge\ d_J(C,C_0)\
\ge \sqrt{1-\Phi^{-1}(h)}-\sqrt r>0 .
\tag{M.6.13eu.2}
\]
The bound holds in every finite coefficient dimension. It applies to the phase image of any complete finite additive apparatus. By Theorem M.6.13es, at each interior error there is an entropy budget \(h<\Phi(1-r)\) for which actual finite additive apparatuses satisfy this hypothesis.

*Proof.* For a unit system vector \(u\), the quadratic form of \(K_{\rm ph}(J,C)\) at \(u\) is the integrated squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the error operator applied to \(u\otimes J_\theta^{1/2}\). The triangle inequality in the integrated Hilbert–Schmidt space gives
\[
K_{\rm ph}(J,C_0)\preceq(\sqrt r+d_J(C,C_0))^2 I.
\]
The normalization \(\int\operatorname{Tr}J_\theta\,d\mu=1\) and unitary conjugation also give \(d_J(C,C_0)\le\|C-C_0\|\). Pinch \(J_\theta\) in the common coefficient basis of \(C_0\), writing \(\mathcal E\) for this pinching. Every coefficient of the full rotated square for \(C_0\) is diagonal in that basis, so \(K_{\rm ph}(\mathcal EJ,C_0)=K_{\rm ph}(J,C_0)\) exactly. Relative-entropy data processing gives \(H(\mathcal EJ)\le H(J)\). The commuting frontier of Theorem M.6.13em thus implies
\[
H(J)\ge\Phi\!\left([1-(\sqrt r+d_J(C,C_0))^2]_+\right).
\]
For an error budget at least one this inequality reduces to nonnegativity of \(H\). In the other case it is (M.6.13em.1), with the limiting interpretation at error zero. Inverting the strictly increasing \(\Phi\) proves (M.6.13eu.2). The last strict positivity follows from the hypothesis on \(h\). The comparison uses the candidate's own matrix phase density and the whole error square, including its dark input. It imposes no bound on dimension or on the reference charge spectrum. \(\square\)

<a id="theorem-m613ev"></a>

<a id="theorem-m613ev-exact-degenerate-spin-one-tester-pressures"></a>**Theorem M.6.13ev (Exact Degenerate Spin-One Tester Pressures).** Use the complete finite spin-one reference class of Theorem M.6.13dc, with $Q_S=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,2)$, $X=J_x$ and its symmetric tester basis $e,m,f$. Then
\[
b(x|e\rangle\langle e|+z|f\rangle\langle f|)=0
\quad(x,z\ge0),\qquad
b(y|m\rangle\langle m|)=0\quad(y\ge0).
\tag{M.6.13ev.1}
\]
If $x>0$ on the first face, or $y>0$ on the second ray, no finite model attains the corresponding weighted infimum. The dark-only face $x=y=0$ attains value zero with an invariant ready state and zero observable. Every symmetric maximizing tester of (M.6.13dc.2) at $0<r<1$ therefore has $y>0$, and if $x=0$ it must have $z>0$.

*Proof.* Write an invariant odd observable as
\[
B_{\rm obs}=
\begin{pmatrix}0&A&0\\ A^*&0&B\\0&B^*&0\end{pmatrix}
\]
in the system charge basis. Both reference operators $A,B$ raise charge by one. For a pure ready vector $\psi$, the diagonal noise tested on a unit system vector $v$ is $\|(B_{\rm obs}-X\otimes I)(v\otimes\psi)\|^2$. Use the three reference charges $0,1,2$ and
\[
\psi_\epsilon=\sqrt\epsilon\,|0\rangle+
 \sqrt{1-2\epsilon}\,|1\rangle+\sqrt\epsilon\,|2\rangle,
 \qquad 0<\epsilon<1/2 .
\]
Its asymmetry is the Shannon entropy of $(\epsilon,1-2\epsilon,\epsilon)$, which tends to zero as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

For $y=0$, put $c=\sqrt{1-2\epsilon}/\sqrt{2\epsilon}$, $A=c|2\rangle\langle1|$, and $B=c|1\rangle\langle0|$. Then
\[
A^*\psi_\epsilon=B\psi_\epsilon
=\frac{\sqrt{1-2\epsilon}}{\sqrt2}|1\rangle .
\]
In the system middle component the errors on $e,f$ are respectively $(A^*+B)\psi_\epsilon/\sqrt2-\psi_\epsilon$ and $(A^*-B)\psi_\epsilon/\sqrt2$; the other components are zero. Thus the bright error is $2\epsilon$ and the dark error is zero. For the second ray, write $\psi_n=\langle n|\psi_\epsilon\rangle$. Choose
\[
A=\sum_{n=0}^{1}\frac{\psi_{n+1}}{\sqrt2\,\psi_n}|n+1\rangle\langle n|,
\qquad
B=\sum_{n=0}^{1}\frac{\psi_n}{\sqrt2\,\psi_{n+1}}|n+1\rangle\langle n|.
\]
On $m=|1\rangle$ the error has reference components $(A-I/\sqrt2)\psi_\epsilon$ in system charge zero and $(B^*-I/\sqrt2)\psi_\epsilon$ in system charge two. Their squared norms sum to $(|\psi_0|^2+|\psi_2|^2)/2=\epsilon$. Both constructions conserve additive charge, and their bounded finite observables at each fixed $\epsilon$ admit the complete neutral spectral pointer of Theorem M.6.13dc. The error estimates and the vanishing ready entropy prove (M.6.13ev.1), since both terms in the weighted objective are nonnegative. No bound uniform in $\epsilon$ on the observable norms is needed.

If a finite model attained value zero for a bright weight, its asymmetry would be zero, so its ready state would commute with the reference charge. It suffices to consider odd invariant observables by the parity argument in Theorem M.6.13el, which cannot increase the weighted objective for these testers. In the odd class the expectation of either nonzero reference charge shift in an invariant ready state vanishes. For $m$ the error is a sum of squared distances from the two shifted amplitudes to the unshifted amplitudes of $X$; the cross terms against $X$ vanish, leaving error at least $\|Xm\|^2=1$. For $e$ the same argument in the middle output component leaves error at least $\|Xe\|^2=1$, since $A^*+B$ is a sum of two nonzero reference charge shifts. The argument applies to mixed ready states by linearity in the density matrix. Thus no bright-weighted case can attain zero. In the dark-only case $Xf=0$, so the zero observable with an invariant ready state attains zero.

Finally a tester on either zero-pressure face has dual value $-r\operatorname{Tr}Z\le0$. The complete spin-one frontier has $F(r)>0$ at $0<r<1$ by Theorem M.6.13dc, so neither face can contain a maximizing tester there. $\square$

<a id="theorem-m613ew"></a>

<a id="theorem-m613ew-positive-pressure-on-the-middle-dark-tester-face"></a>**Theorem M.6.13ew (Positive Pressure on the Middle–Dark Tester Face).** Use the complete finite spin-one class of Theorem M.6.13dc. Let $k_m=\langle m,K_\sigma(B)m\rangle$, $k_f=\langle f,K_\sigma(B)f\rangle$ and $a=\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)$. Every admitted model satisfies
\[
\sqrt{k_m}+\sqrt{k_f}\ge [2e^{-a}-1]_+ .
\tag{M.6.13ew.1}
\]
Consequently, for $y,z>0$ and $c=yz/(y+z)$, the middle–dark weighted pressure satisfies
\[
b(y|m\rangle\langle m|+z|f\rangle\langle f|)
\ \ge\ \min_{a\ge0}\{a+c[2e^{-a}-1]_+^2\}>0.
\tag{M.6.13ew.2}
\]
When $c\le1/4$, the minimum on the right equals $c$. This evaluates the displayed lower bound.

*Proof.* Use the Hilbert–Schmidt space of reference matrices as a reference and conjugate spectator, with $B$ acting on the system and the left reference factor. Write $\psi=\sqrt\sigma$, a unit Hilbert–Schmidt vector, and $U_\theta=e^{i\theta Q}$. The action on this space is $L_\theta(\xi)=U_\theta\xi U_\theta^*$, which is the reference rotation together with its conjugate action on the spectator. The operator $B$ commutes with $e^{i\theta Q_S}\otimes L_\theta$: it commutes with the system and left reference rotation by additive conservation, and acts trivially on the spectator. For a system vector $v$, the noise $\langle v,K_\sigma(B)v\rangle$ is $\|(B-X\otimes I)(v\otimes\psi)\|^2$, by the Hilbert–Schmidt trace identity for left multiplication.

Take $\theta=\pi/2$. Then $e^{i\theta Q_S}f=e$ in the spin-one charge basis, and $Xf=0,\ Xm=e$. Covariance of $B$ gives $\|B(e\otimes L_\theta\psi)\|=\|B(f\otimes\psi)\|=\sqrt{k_f}$. By self-adjointness,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle L_\theta\psi,\psi\rangle
&=\langle e\otimes L_\theta\psi,X(m\otimes\psi)\rangle\\
&=\langle e\otimes L_\theta\psi,(X-B)(m\otimes\psi)\rangle
 +\langle B(e\otimes L_\theta\psi),m\otimes\psi\rangle .
\end{aligned}
\]
Both system-reference vectors tested here have norm one. Thus $\sqrt{k_m}+\sqrt{k_f}$ bounds the absolute overlap, which is nonnegative as the trace of the product of two positive matrices.

Let $\tau=\mathcal G_Q\sigma$ and write $\psi=\psi_0+\psi_\perp$, where $\psi_0=\mathcal G_Q(\sqrt\sigma)$ is its Hilbert–Schmidt projection onto the charge-block-diagonal subspace. This subspace is fixed by $L_\theta$, and its orthogonal complement is invariant. Hence
\[
\langle L_\theta\psi,\psi\rangle
=\|\psi_0\|_2^2+\langle L_\theta\psi_\perp,\psi_\perp\rangle
\ge2\|\psi_0\|_2^2-1
\ge2(\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt\sigma\sqrt\tau)^2-1 .
\]
For the last step use $\sqrt\tau$ in the diagonal subspace, with Hilbert–Schmidt norm one. To bound its overlap, write positive eigenvalues of $\sigma$ as $p_i$ with eigenvectors $|i\rangle$, and those of $\tau$ on its support as $q_j$ with eigenvectors $|j\rangle$. The support of $\sigma$ lies in that of $\tau$, so $w_{ij}=p_i|\langle i|j\rangle|^2$ is a probability table on the positive eigenvalues of $\sigma$ and $\tau$. The overlap is $\sum_{ij}w_{ij}\exp[-(\log p_i-\log q_j)/2]$, and $D(\sigma\Vert\tau)=\sum_{ij}w_{ij}(\log p_i-\log q_j)$. Jensen's inequality gives $\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt\sigma\sqrt\tau\ge e^{-a/2}$. This proves (M.6.13ew.1).

Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives $(\sqrt{k_m}+\sqrt{k_f})^2\le (1/y+1/z)(yk_m+zk_f)$. Adding $a$ proves the lower bound in (M.6.13ew.2). Its right side is continuous in $a$, tends to infinity with $a$, and can vanish neither at zero nor at positive $a$. For $0\le a\le\log2$ its derivative is $1-4ce^{-a}(2e^{-a}-1)\ge1-4c$. For $a\ge\log2$ the expression is $a$, proving the asserted weak-weight evaluation of this lower bound. $\square$

<a id="theorem-m613ex"></a>

<a id="theorem-m613ex-high-weight-middle-dark-pressure"></a>**Theorem M.6.13ex (High-Weight Middle–Dark Pressure).** Use the complete finite spin-one class of Theorem M.6.13dc. For a model put $a=\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)$ and $k=\sqrt{k_m}+\sqrt{k_f}$, with $k_m,k_f$ as in Theorem M.6.13ew. Define
\[
I(k)=
\begin{cases}
0,&k=0,\\[1mm]
\dfrac2\pi\left[\arcsin k+k\log\cot\!\left(\dfrac{\arcsin k}{2}\right)\right],&0<k<1,\\[2mm]
1,&k\ge1.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $e^{-a}\le I(k)$ on the complete finite class. For fixed $y,z>0$, put $Z=y|m\rangle\langle m|+z|f\rangle\langle f|$, $c=yz/(y+z)$ and $\gamma_c=\min\{0,(1+\log(2c))/2\}$. For every $t\ge1$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
b(tZ)&\ge\min\left\{tc,\ 
\frac12\log t-\log 2-\log\!\left(1+\frac12\log t\right)+\gamma_c\right\},\\
b(tZ)&\le\frac12\log t+\log\pi+\frac{y+z}{3}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{M.6.13ex.1}
\]
In particular $\lim_{t\to\infty}b(tZ)/\log t=1/2$. The lower bound holds for arbitrary finite real charge spectra, multiplicities and mixed ready states.

*Proof.* Use the Hilbert–Schmidt purification $\psi=\sqrt\sigma$ and its rotated vector $L_\theta\psi=U_\theta\sqrt\sigma U_\theta^*$ as in Theorem M.6.13ew. For the system vector $f_\theta=e^{iQ_S\theta}f$, one has $|\langle f_\theta,e\rangle|=|\sin\theta|$. Covariance and $Xf=0$ give $\|B(f_\theta\otimes L_\theta\psi)\|=\sqrt{k_f}$. Also $Xm=e$ and $\|(X-B)(m\otimes\psi)\|=\sqrt{k_m}$. Self-adjointness and the triangle inequality therefore give
\[
|\sin\theta|\,A(\theta)\le k,\qquad
A(\theta)=\operatorname{Tr}(U_\theta\sqrt\sigma U_\theta^*\sqrt\sigma).
\tag{M.6.13ex.2}
\]
Here $0\le A(\theta)\le1$ by positivity and Hilbert–Schmidt Cauchy–Schwarz. This applies to every real $\theta$.

Let $P_q$ be the projection onto reference charge $q$. The expansion
\[
A(\theta)=\sum_{q,q'} e^{i(q-q')\theta}
                    \|P_q\sqrt\sigma P_{q'}\|_{\rm HS}^{\,2}
\]
is finite. For any nonzero real gap the exponential has vanishing average over $[0,T]$ as $T\to\infty$. Thus the long-time mean of $A$ is $\|\mathcal G_Q(\sqrt\sigma)\|_{\rm HS}^2$, which is at least $e^{-a}$ by the projection and Jensen estimates in Theorem M.6.13ew. In (M.6.13ex.2), bound $A$ above by $\min(1,k/|\sin\theta|)$ away from the sine zeros. This upper bound is periodic, so its long-time mean is its mean over a period. For $0<k<1$ that mean is
\[
\frac2\pi\left[\int_0^{\arcsin k}1\,d\theta+
\int_{\arcsin k}^{\pi/2}\frac{k}{\sin\theta}\,d\theta\right]=I(k).
\]
For $k=0$ the upper bound is zero almost everywhere, and for $k\ge1$ it is one. This proves the claim.

Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives $yk_m+zk_f\ge ck^2$. For $0<k<1$, use $\arcsin k\le\pi k/2$ and $\cot(\arcsin(k)/2)=(1+\sqrt{1-k^2})/k\le2/k$ to obtain $I(k)\le2k(1+\log(1/k))$. The tested objective is then bounded below by
\[
a+t(yk_m+zk_f)\ge
\log(1/k)-\log 2-\log(1+\log(1/k))+tc k^2 .
\]
Write $s=\sqrt t\,k$ and $L=\frac12\log t$. Since
\[
1+\log(1/k)=1+L-\log s
 \le (1+L)(1+[\log(1/s)]_+),
\]
the right side is at least $L-\log2-\log(1+L)$ plus
$cs^2-\log s-\log(1+[\log(1/s)]_+)$. For $0<s\le1$, this last expression is nonnegative because $v-\log(1+v)\ge0$ for $v=-\log s\ge0$. For $s\ge1$, it is $cs^2-\log s$, whose unrestricted minimum over $s>0$ is $(1+\log(2c))/2$ by differentiation. Thus the claimed lower branch holds for $0<k<1$. At $k\ge1$, the objective is at least $tc$; $k=0$ is impossible at finite $a$ by the mean bound. This proves the first inequality of (M.6.13ex.1).

For the upper bound in the scalar phase class of Theorem M.6.13el take $C=X$ and use the constant density $\pi\sqrt t$ on the interval $|\theta|\le t^{-1/2}$, zero elsewhere, with respect to normalized circle measure. Its entropy is $\frac12\log t+\log\pi$. At angle $\theta$, the squared error on $m$ is $2(1-\cos\theta)$, and the squared error on $f$ is $\sin^2\theta$, by the two adjacent entries of $X$. Each is bounded by $\theta^2$, whose mean on the interval is $1/(3t)$. The phase-to-additive approximation of Theorem M.6.13el gives finite apparatuses whose entropies and full noise converge to these quantities, so this bounds the infimum $b(tZ)$ from above. The two bounds give the stated leading coefficient. $\square$

<a id="theorem-m613ey"></a>

<a id="theorem-m613ey-charge-block-lower-bound-for-middle-dark-pressure"></a>**Theorem M.6.13ey (Charge-Block Lower Bound for Middle–Dark Pressure).** Use the complete finite spin-one class of Theorem M.6.13dc. For a ready state $\sigma$ let $a=\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)$, and put $k_m=\langle m,K_\sigma(B)m\rangle$ and $k_f=\langle f,K_\sigma(B)f\rangle$. Then
\[
\sqrt{k_m}+\sqrt{k_f}\ge e^{-a}.
\tag{M.6.13ey.1}
\]
For every $y,z>0$, put $c=yz/(y+z)$ and $Z=y|m\rangle\langle m|+z|f\rangle\langle f|$. For $t>0$ the pressure obeys
\[
b(tZ)\ge
\begin{cases}
tc,&tc\le\tfrac12,\\[1mm]
\tfrac12[1+\log(2tc)],&tc\ge\tfrac12.
\end{cases}
\tag{M.6.13ey.2}
\]
In particular, for fixed $y,z>0$,
\[
\tfrac12\log(2ec)
\ \le\ \liminf_{t\to\infty}\left(b(tZ)-\tfrac12\log t\right)
\ \le\ \limsup_{t\to\infty}\left(b(tZ)-\tfrac12\log t\right)
\ \le\ \tfrac12\log(4\pi(y+z)).
\tag{M.6.13ey.3}
\]
These lower bounds retain every finite real reference charge, mixed ready state and charge multiplicity.

*Proof.* Use the Hilbert–Schmidt purification $\psi=\sqrt\sigma$ of Theorem M.6.13ew. The generator on the reference matrix space acts by $\xi\mapsto Q\xi-\xi Q$, with the right factor acting as a conjugate spectator. The observable acts by left multiplication and commutes with the system charge plus this generator. The purification is used only for the norm calculation on the original reference and introduces no physical spectator or additional charge cost.

Write $\psi=\sum_g\psi_g$ for the orthogonal decomposition by the real gap $g$ of the reference matrix generator, and put $p_g=\|\psi_g\|_{\rm HS}^2$, taking $p_g=0$ for every absent gap. This is a finitely supported probability distribution on the real line. In the total charge $h$ sector define
\[
M_h=|1\rangle\otimes\psi_{h-1},\qquad
E_h=\frac{|0\rangle\otimes\psi_h+|2\rangle\otimes\psi_{h-2}}{\sqrt2},
\qquad
F_h=\frac{|0\rangle\otimes\psi_h-|2\rangle\otimes\psi_{h-2}}{\sqrt2}.
\]
Thus $M_h,E_h,F_h$ are the components of $m\otimes\psi,e\otimes\psi,f\otimes\psi$, respectively. Since $Xm=e$ and $Xf=0$, the components of the two error vectors are
$D_{m,h}=BM_h-E_h$ and $D_{f,h}=BF_h$. Orthogonality of total charge sectors gives $\sum_h\|D_{m,h}\|^2=k_m$ and $\sum_h\|D_{f,h}\|^2=k_f$.

Self-adjointness gives
\[
\frac{|p_h-p_{h-2}|}{2}
=|\langle F_h,E_h\rangle|
\le \|F_h\|\,\|D_{m,h}\|+\|M_h\|\,\|D_{f,h}\| .
\]
Indeed, use $E_h=BM_h-D_{m,h}$ and move $B$ to $F_h$ in the first pairing. Sum over the finite set of nonzero terms. Because $\sum_h\|F_h\|^2=\sum_h\|M_h\|^2=1$, Cauchy–Schwarz yields
\[
\sqrt{k_m}+\sqrt{k_f}\ \ge\ \frac12\sum_h|p_h-p_{h-2}|.
\tag{M.6.13ey.4}
\]
Partition the support and its translate by two into the cosets of $2\mathbb Z$ in $\mathbb R$. On each coset write $p_{g+2n}$ as a finite nonnegative sequence extended by zeros at both ends. Its total absolute variation is at least twice its maximum, by telescoping from each end to an index of maximum. In particular the coset containing zero contributes at least $2p_0$, so the right side of (M.6.13ey.4) is at least $p_0$. The zero-gap block is $\mathcal G_Q(\sqrt\sigma)$. The Hilbert–Schmidt projection and spectral Jensen estimate in Theorem M.6.13ew give $p_0\ge(\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt\sigma\sqrt{\mathcal G_Q\sigma})^2\ge e^{-a}$. This proves (M.6.13ey.1). Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz now gives $yk_m+zk_f\ge c e^{-2a}$. Minimizing $a+tc e^{-2a}$ over $a\ge0$ gives (M.6.13ey.2) by differentiation.

For the upper constant in (M.6.13ey.3), let $s=y+z$ and use $C=X$ in the scalar phase representation of Theorem M.6.13el. Take a scalar angle density proportional to $e^{-ts\theta^2}$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$ relative to normalized circle measure. If $Z_t=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{-ts\theta^2}\,d\theta$, then $Z_t=\sqrt{\pi/(ts)}(1+o(1))$, by rescaling and integrating the real Gaussian. The density relative to circle measure is $2\pi e^{-ts\theta^2}/Z_t$, so its entropy is $\log(2\pi/Z_t)-ts\,\mathbb E\theta^2$. The middle and dark errors are $2(1-\cos\theta)$ and $\sin^2\theta$, respectively. Each is $\theta^2+O(\theta^4)$ on the stated interval. The fourth moment is $O((ts)^{-2})$ by the same Gaussian rescaling. Adding $t$ times the weighted error to the entropy therefore gives $\log(2\pi/Z_t)+O_{y,z}(1/t)$, which has the asserted upper limit. The phase-to-finite approximation in Theorem M.6.13el transfers this upper bound to the original finite infimum, without assuming a finite apparatus attains it. Equation (M.6.13ey.2) supplies the lower limit. $\square$

<a id="theorem-m613ez"></a>

<a id="theorem-m613ez-an-exact-attained-weak-weight-branch-on-the-middle-dark-face"></a>**Theorem M.6.13ez (An Exact Attained Weak-Weight Branch on the Middle–Dark Face).** Use the complete finite spin-one class of Theorem M.6.13dc. Fix $y,z>0$, put $Z=y|m\rangle\langle m|+z|f\rangle\langle f|$, and define
\[
L=y\bigl(1+\max\{3/2,y/z\}\bigr),\qquad
T=\frac{y+z/2}{y^2}.
\]
Then
\[
b(tZ)=ty\quad(0\le t\le 1/L),\qquad
b(tZ)<ty\quad(t>T).
\tag{M.6.13ez.1}
\]
The exact branch is attained by an invariant ready state with zero observable. For $0<t\le 1/L$, every finite attaining ready state is invariant. Moreover, there is an onset $t_0\in[1/L,T]$ such that the equality set in (M.6.13ez.1) is exactly $[0,t_0]$. This bounds $t_0$ without asserting its value.

*Proof.* Use the mathematical Hilbert–Schmidt purification and total-charge decomposition of Theorem M.6.13ey, with gap populations $p_g=\|\psi_g\|_{\rm HS}^2$. Since $\sqrt\sigma$ is Hermitian, $\psi_{-g}=\psi_g^*$ and $p_{-g}=p_g$, also for arbitrary real reference spectra. For each total-charge sector $h$, the self-adjointness identity in that theorem and weighted Cauchy–Schwarz give
\[
y\|D_{m,h}\|^2+z\|D_{f,h}\|^2
\ \ge\
\frac{(p_h-p_{h-2})^2}
 {4\bigl((p_h+p_{h-2})/(2y)+p_{h-1}/z\bigr)} .
\tag{M.6.13ez.2}
\]
A term with zero denominator is assigned zero, because then the numerator also vanishes. In detail, the bound on $|\langle F_h,E_h\rangle|$ is the scalar product of the two nonnegative vectors
$(\|F_h\|/\sqrt y,\|M_h\|/\sqrt z)$ and $(\sqrt y\|D_{m,h}\|,\sqrt z\|D_{f,h}\|)$, while $\|F_h\|^2=(p_h+p_{h-2})/2$ and $\|M_h\|^2=p_{h-1}$.

Set $a_0=p_0$, $b_2=p_2$, $b_1=p_1$ and $\delta=1-p_0$. Retaining just $h=0,2$ and using symmetry of $p_g$ gives
\[
yk_m+zk_f\ge
y\,\frac{(a_0-b_2)^2}{a_0+b_2+(2y/z)b_1}.
\]
For nonnegative $a,b,c$ with $a+b+c>0$,
\[
\frac{(a-b)^2}{a+b+c}-(a-3b-c)=\frac{(2b+c)^2}{a+b+c}\ge0.
\]
The analogous bound holds with a zero denominator under the stated convention. Since $2(b_1+b_2)\le\delta$, one obtains
\[
yk_m+zk_f\ge y\bigl[1-\delta-3b_2-(2y/z)b_1\bigr]\ge y-L\delta .
\tag{M.6.13ez.3}
\]
Let $A=\mathcal A_Q(\sigma)$. The proof of Theorem M.6.13ey gives $p_0\ge e^{-A}$, so $\delta\le1-e^{-A}\le A$, with strict inequality $\delta<A$ when $A>0$. Therefore
\[
A+t(yk_m+zk_f)\ge ty+A-tL\delta\ge ty
\quad(0\le t\le 1/L).
\]
For $t>0$ in that range the bound is strict when $A>0$. An invariant ready state and zero observable give $A=0$, $k_m=1$ and $k_f=0$, so attain $ty$. This proves the exact branch and the necessity of invariance for a finite minimizing state there.

For the upper bound on the onset, use the scalar phase class of Theorem M.6.13el, with $j_u(\theta)=1+2u\cos\theta$ relative to normalized circle measure, $|u|<1/2$, and $C=vX$ for real $v$. Its entropy is $u^2+O(u^4)$, by Taylor expansion and the vanishing odd cosine moments. Direct evaluation of the middle and dark input squares gives
\[
k_m=1+v^2-2uv,\qquad k_f=v^2/2.
\]
Indeed the middle square before integration is $1+v^2-2v\cos\theta$, and the dark square is $v^2\sin^2\theta$. Choosing $v=yu/(y+z/2)$ gives
\[
H(j_u)+t(yk_m+zk_f)
=ty+\left(1-\frac{t y^2}{y+z/2}\right)u^2+O(u^4).
\]
For each $t>T$, a sufficiently small nonzero $u$ makes this strictly less than $ty$. The phase-to-additive approximation of Theorem M.6.13el preserves the strict inequality for a sufficiently accurate complete finite apparatus. Finally, $t\mapsto b(tZ)-ty$ is concave as an infimum of affine functions, finite, and nonpositive by the invariant construction. Its zero set is an interval containing $[0,1/L]$, is bounded above by $T$, and is closed at its positive upper endpoint by continuity of a finite concave function on $(0,\infty)$. This proves the onset claim. $\square$

<a id="theorem-m613fa"></a>

<a id="theorem-m613fa-exact-quadratic-susceptibility-of-the-spin-one-tester-pressure"></a>**Theorem M.6.13fa (Exact Quadratic Susceptibility of the Spin-One Tester Pressure).** Use the complete finite spin-one class of Theorem M.6.13dc. Fix a symmetric tester $Z=x|e\rangle\langle e|+y|m\rangle\langle m|+z|f\rangle\langle f|$, with $x,z\ge0$, $y>0$, and $h=(x+z)/2>0$. Set $s=x+y$ and $k=((y-h)/(y+h))^2$. For a ready state $\sigma$ let
\[
g_Z(\sigma)=s-\inf_{B}\operatorname{Tr}(ZK_\sigma(B)),
\]
where the infimum uses the complete finite conserving observable class on the reference of $\sigma$. For a charge-invariant ready density $\tau$, consider any nonzero Hermitian direction $D$ with $\mathcal G_QD=0$ and $\tau+\varepsilon D\ge0$ for all sufficiently small real $\varepsilon$. The exact supremum of the quadratic gain-to-asymmetry ratio over all finite references and such directions is
\[
\sup_{\tau,Q,D}\ \lim_{\varepsilon\to0}
\frac{g_Z(\tau+\varepsilon D)}{\mathcal A_Q(\tau+\varepsilon D)}
=\Gamma(Z)
:=\frac{s^2}{y+h}\max_{0\le u<1}
   \frac{u}{(1-ku^2)\operatorname{artanh}u}.
\tag{M.6.13fa.1}
\]
The ratio in $u$ is continuously extended at zero with value one. If $k\le1/3$, its unique maximizer is $u=0$. If $k>1/3$, the unique maximizer is the positive $u<1$ determined by the equation
\[
\frac{(1-ku^2)u}{1-u^2}
=(1+ku^2)\operatorname{artanh}u .
\tag{M.6.13fa.2}
\]
In either case the ratio is realized by a quadratic perturbation of a two-charge scalar ready state. For every $t>1/\Gamma(Z)$ one has $b(tZ)<ts$. For every $0<t<1/\Gamma(Z)$ the second variation of the tested objective $A+t\operatorname{Tr}(ZK)$, after optimizing its observable, is strictly positive along every nonzero direction in (M.6.13fa.1). These are statements about the local susceptibility and a strict global upper bound on the end of any linear pressure interval.

*Proof.* Let $E=\operatorname{supp}\tau$. If $\sigma_\varepsilon=\tau+\varepsilon D$ is positive, its twirl is $\tau$ and its support lies in $E$, since a vector in the kernel of a diagonal charge block of a positive matrix has zero row and column. Thus $D$ is supported on $E$. Compressing any candidate observable to the system tensored with $E$ cannot increase its noise: the discarded excursion contributes the expectation of a positive square and the target acts identically on the reference. Conversely extend an observable on $E$ by zero. The reduction is exact, conserves charge, and allows $\tau>0$ on the retained space. This handles arbitrary multiplicities, missing charge gaps, and any retained neutral or classical flags within the original reference.

By parity oddification, the weighted infimum can be taken over
$B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&A&0\\ A^*&0&B_1\\0&B_1^*&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$,
with $[Q,A]=A$, $[Q,B_1]=B_1$. The gain maximized over these two raising operators has the linear term $s\operatorname{Tr}\sigma_\varepsilon(A+A^*+B_1+B_1^*)/\sqrt2$. Its quadratic penalty is the weighted square in (M.6.13ca.3) with weights $x,y,z$ on the corresponding inputs. At $\varepsilon=0$, terms with charge gap two have zero trace. The penalty is exactly
\[
y\operatorname{Tr}\tau(A^*A+B_1B_1^*)
+h\operatorname{Tr}\tau(AA^*+B_1^*B_1).
\]
It is strictly positive definite on the finite real space of allowed raising coefficients whenever that space is nonzero. Its coefficients at $\varepsilon\ne0$ depend affinely on $\varepsilon$, so it remains positive definite for all sufficiently small $|\varepsilon|$ on this fixed support. The linear term vanishes at $\varepsilon=0$. Solving the positive quadratic optimization thus gives $A,B_1=O(\varepsilon)$ and an exact quadratic gain coefficient determined by the displayed unperturbed penalty. If no raising edge is available the gain is identically zero, with the same conclusion below. In particular the proof does not discard the gap-two terms at finite $\varepsilon$.

Diagonalize $\tau$ within its charge blocks and write $p_i>0$ for its eigenvalues and $q_i$ for their charges. With $i,j$ counted once when $q_i=q_j+1$, completing the two independent squares yields
\[
g_Z(\sigma_\varepsilon)=
\varepsilon^2\frac{s^2}{2}
\sum_{q_i=q_j+1}|D_{ij}|^2
\left(\frac1{y p_j+h p_i}+\frac1{y p_i+h p_j}\right)
+O(\varepsilon^3).
\tag{M.6.13fa.3}
\]
For example, the $A_{ij}$ linear coefficient is $\sqrt2\,\varepsilon s\,\operatorname{Re}(\overline{D_{ij}}A_{ij})$ and its penalty coefficient is $y p_j+h p_i$. The other coefficient exchanges the two populations. The error term here is for each fixed finite reference and perturbation.

The entropy derivative of $\operatorname{Tr}\sigma_\varepsilon\log\sigma_\varepsilon$ at zero is zero because $D$ has no charge-diagonal entries, and the twirl is fixed. Its second derivative is the trace pairing of $D$ with the Fréchet derivative of $\log$ at $\tau$ applied to $D$. For the $i,j$ entry the derivative multiplier is $\int_0^\infty (p_i+v)^{-1}(p_j+v)^{-1}dv=(\log p_i-\log p_j)/(p_i-p_j)$, with value $1/p_i$ on equality. Pairing and dividing by two to obtain the quadratic coefficient gives
\[
\mathcal A_Q(\sigma_\varepsilon)=
\varepsilon^2\sum_{i<j,\ q_i\ne q_j}|D_{ij}|^2
\,\frac{\log p_i-\log p_j}{p_i-p_j}
+O(\varepsilon^3).
\tag{M.6.13fa.4}
\]
The sum counts each unordered eigenvector pair once. This identity follows from the resolvent integral for the logarithm on the fixed positive support. Its quadratic coefficient is positive when $D\ne0$.

The ratio of the two coefficients is a weighted mean of adjacent-pair ratios and zero for other gaps. With $u=|p_i-p_j|/(p_i+p_j)$, a single adjacent-pair ratio reduces to
\[
\frac{s^2}{y+h}\frac{u}{(1-ku^2)\operatorname{artanh}u}.
\]
Every $u\in[0,1)$ is realized by the two charge populations $(1+u)/2,(1-u)/2$ and a nonzero off-diagonal perturbation. This proves the supremum formula, including arbitrary finite flags and neutral multiplicities.

To compute its maximizer, minimize $f(v)=(1-kv)\operatorname{artanh}\sqrt v/\sqrt v$ on $0\le v<1$. Its power series is
\[
f(v)=1+\sum_{n\ge1}\left(\frac1{2n+1}-\frac{k}{2n-1}\right)v^n.
\]
For $k\le1/3$ the coefficients are nonnegative and some are positive, so its minimum occurs only at zero. For $1/3<k<1$ the coefficients have a nonempty initial negative segment and an eventual positive segment, with at most one intervening zero. Divide $f'(v)$ by $v^{N-1}$, where $N$ is the last index with a negative coefficient. Every term of the resulting series is nondecreasing on $0<v<1$, and the eventual positive terms make it strictly increasing. Since $f'(0)<0$ and $f(v)\to+\infty$ as $v\uparrow1$, there is exactly one derivative zero. Differentiating in $u=\sqrt v$ gives (M.6.13fa.2). This identifies the maximizer and shows it lies strictly inside the range. The assumption $y,h>0$ ensures $k<1$; the faces $y=0$ and $h=0$ have the separate exact pressures in Theorem M.6.13ev. The formula includes $x=0$ when $z>0$ and $z=0$ when $x>0$.

Finally the optimized cost for $\sigma_\varepsilon$ is $ts+\mathcal A_Q(\sigma_\varepsilon)-t g_Z(\sigma_\varepsilon)$. Equations (M.6.13fa.3)–(M.6.13fa.4) prove strict local positivity when $t<1/\Gamma(Z)$. At $t>1/\Gamma(Z)$, the two-charge maximizing direction gives a negative quadratic coefficient and thus an actual finite strict improvement for sufficiently small nonzero $\varepsilon$.
